messages.subject_clean: QR Reparameterization with Random Slopes?
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, November 1, 2016 at 1:55:52 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> How does the QR reparameterization work when there are random slopes involved?
> Does rstanarm just use the reparameterization for the fixed baseline slopes and then
> add individual corrections for each random slope using the rows of the nominal design
> matrix?

Yes. In the lme4 way of looking at things you have

y = X * beta + Z * b + e = Q * R * beta + Z * b + e = Q * theta + Z * b + e

with Z being a sparse design matrix that is structured in such a way that b represents group-wise deviations from the common beta.

Ben

> Hi Sean,
>
> You're missing a key conceptual bit of the Stan language. In the Stan language, your goal is to define a log joint probability distribution function (up to a additive constant) over the data and the parameters.
>
> What the Stan language does not do is specify some sort of rejection sampler. That is very inefficient. This line:
>   V ~ pareto_type_2(0, 3, 3);
> does not mean, "please draw V from a pareto_type_2 random number generator with arguments (0, 3, 3)." It means this:
>   target += pareto_type_2_lpdf(V | 0, 3, 3);
> The value of target at the end of the model block is the value of the log joint probability distribution function.
>
> If you notice in the first program, you've correctly specified data, which is nothing, parameters, V, and the log joint probability distribution function: V ~ pareto_type_2(0, 3, 3). Also notice that you haven't actually specified how to do inference. That's outside of the language. It's the job of the inference algorithm to fill in the values of each of the parameters at each iteration. To be concrete, at each iteration (and each evaluation of the log probability), the data is known, the parameters are actual values (like 0.1, 1.2, etc.), and the model block evaluates to a number.
>

So this line:  V ~ pareto_type_2(0, 3, 3) or equivalent to target += pareto_type_2_lpdf(V | 0, 3, 3) evaluates to nonsense. Why? Maybe a simpler example from R is: rnorm(NA). messages.body_plain:
> On Nov 1, 2016, at 2:22 PM, Mikey T <tab...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all,
> I'm trying to properly code a marginalized latent discrete parameter and I'm having trouble. I know that I am writing the code improperly, but I'm not sure what is wrong and wondering if someone can please help. The model is as follows:
> Process model:
>
> logit(psi[i]) = mu + X*Beta
>
>
>
> Observation model:
>
> z[i] ~ Bernoulli(psi[i]*rho + (1-psi[i])*(1-phi))
>
>
>
> Data model:
>
> y[i] ~ Bernoulli(z[i]*pi)

The trick is to write the joint density out then just turn the
crank to marginalize, then just code it up directly in Stan.  First,
you have the joint distribution of the latent z and observed y based
on parameters

  p(z, y | mu, X, beta, rho, psi, phi)

  = PRODUCT_i p(z[i], y[i] | ...)

and then you can work on the inner term:

  p(z[i], y[i] | ...)

    = Bernoulli(z[i] | psi[i]*rho + (1-psi[i])*(1-phi))
      * Bernoulli(y[i] | z[i] * pi)

where

  psi[i] = inv_logit(mu + X * Beta);  // sure that's not X[i] * Beta?

and then marginalize out the z[i]:

   = SUM_{k in 0:1}
     Bernoulli(k | psi[i]*rho + (1-psi[i])*(1-phi))
     * Bernoulli(y[i] | k * pi)

Then put it on the log scale:

  log(p(z[i], y[i] | ...)

  = log(SUM_{k in 0:1}
     Bernoulli(k | psi[i]*rho + (1-psi[i])*(1-phi))
     * Bernoulli(y[i] | k * pi)

  = log_sum_exp_{k in 0:1}
    log  Bernoulli(k | psi[i]*rho + (1-psi[i])*(1-phi))
    + log Bernoulli(y[i] | k * pi)

and you can just code that up directly using log_sum_exp
in Stan:

  psi = inv_logit
  log_sum_exp(bernoulli_lpmf(0 | psi[i] * rho + (1-psi[i]) * (1-phi))
              + bernoulli_lpmf(y[i] | 0),
              bernoulli_lpmf(1 | psi[i] * rho + (1-psi[i]) * (1-phi))
              + bernoulli_lpmf(y[i] | pi));

You can also look at the zero-inflation and hurdle models
in the manual, which are similar.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There is no way to stop this if the model allows mixing between
the modes/labels.  What you need to do is define inferences that
aren't sensitive to the labels.  These will go through.

We still worry about convergence running a single model, but we
really don't have great advice (nor does anyone else) about this
label switching issue.  It gets in the way of our trying to evaluate
converegence more than anything else.

- Bob

> On Oct 31, 2016, at 6:04 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Just to add to this: Yes, it's probably due to label switching. You're marginalizing over multiple modes that are equivalent in inference, but labels are switched, so everything winds up being the same when averaged.
> This is *not* an issue if you have between-chain label switching, meaning that chain 1 found and explored 1 mode, and chain 2 found and explored another mode, but neither chain found the other modes.
> If this is the case, your trace plots will tell you pretty quickly --- The traces of the individual chains will just be flipped from one another. In this case, just extract out individual chains or chains that converged to similar modes and look at the posterior summaries.
>
> However, if your chains are switching modes during simulation (chain 1 explores modes 1, 2, 3, ...), you have an issue that I have no idea how to solve from MCMC output itself. I've only stopped this by applying some identifiability constraints that either creates one mode, or pushes the modes further apart so any one given chain is unlikely to 'find' the other one throughout its simulation. It's not ideal, but it works well enough.

> There's a problem with mixture models in general that they don't have
> maximum likelihoods.  If you put one mixture component be responsible
> for one data item, as the scale (std dev param) goes to zero and the location
> (mean param) goes to the data item's value, the likelihood grows.
>
> One way to avoid this is to force the components to have more responsibility.
> You can do this with a prior on the simplex.  Something like Dirichlet(alpha)
> where alpha is a vector values >> 1 can help.  Also putting a prior on the
> scales that explicitly avoids zero (like a lognormal) can help.
>
> - Bob

> > Hi Sean,
> >
> > You're missing a key conceptual bit of the Stan language. In the Stan language, your goal is to define a log joint probability distribution function (up to a additive constant) over the data and the parameters.
> >
> > What the Stan language does not do is specify some sort of rejection sampler. That is very inefficient. This line:
> >   V ~ pareto_type_2(0, 3, 3);
> > does not mean, "please draw V from a pareto_type_2 random number generator with arguments (0, 3, 3)." It means this:
> >   target += pareto_type_2_lpdf(V | 0, 3, 3);
> > The value of target at the end of the model block is the value of the log joint probability distribution function.
> >
> > If you notice in the first program, you've correctly specified data, which is nothing, parameters, V, and the log joint probability distribution function: V ~ pareto_type_2(0, 3, 3). Also notice that you haven't actually specified how to do inference. That's outside of the language. It's the job of the inference algorithm to fill in the values of each of the parameters at each iteration. To be concrete, at each iteration (and each evaluation of the log probability), the data is known, the parameters are actual values (like 0.1, 1.2, etc.), and the model block evaluates to a number.
> >
> > In your second program, V is a local variable. It takes on the value of NaN without defining it. So this line:  V ~ pareto_type_2(0, 3, 3) or equivalent to target += pareto_type_2_lpdf(V | 0, 3, 3) evaluates to nonsense. Why? Maybe a simpler example from R is: rnorm(NA). Just curious, what sort of inferences aren't sensitive to the labels?
Say you're wanting to fit a latent group model from data. You want to
know what probability each person has of belonging to each of K groups,
then the parameters of said K groups. Is there a way of obtaining such
parameters in a way that doesn't have a label switching problem?

On 11/01/2016 05:32 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> There is no way to stop this if the model allows mixing between
> the modes/labels.  What you need to do is define inferences that
> aren't sensitive to the labels.  These will go through.
>
> We still worry about convergence running a single model, but we
> really don't have great advice (nor does anyone else) about this
> label switching issue.  It gets in the way of our trying to evaluate
> converegence more than anything else.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>> On Oct 31, 2016, at 6:04 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Just to add to this: Yes, it's probably due to label switching. You're marginalizing over multiple modes that are equivalent in inference, but labels are switched, so everything winds up being the same when averaged.
>> This is *not* an issue if you have between-chain label switching, meaning that chain 1 found and explored 1 mode, and chain 2 found and explored another mode, but neither chain found the other modes.
>> If this is the case, your trace plots will tell you pretty quickly --- The traces of the individual chains will just be flipped from one another. In this case, just extract out individual chains or chains that converged to similar modes and look at the posterior summaries.
>>
>> However, if your chains are switching modes during simulation (chain 1 explores modes 1, 2, 3, ...), you have an issue that I have no idea how to solve from MCMC output itself. I've only stopped this by applying some identifiability constraints that either creates one mode, or pushes the modes further apart so any one given chain is unlikely to 'find' the other one throughout its simulation. It's not ideal, but it works well enough.
>>
>> On Friday, October 21, 2016 at 11:19:00 PM UTC-5, Shawn Lee wrote:
>> Thank you for your response, I have solved the 0 problem.
>> After sampling, I find all the elements of theta equals to 0.1(I defined there are 10 components).
>> Is it because the label switching problem?
>>
>> 在 2016年10月22日星期六 UTC+8上午2:47:31，Bob Carpenter写道：
>> sigma is occassionally hitting 0 due to underflow in the transforms.
>>
>> There's a problem with mixture models in general that they don't have
>> maximum likelihoods.  If you put one mixture component be responsible
>> for one data item, as the scale (std dev param) goes to zero and the location
>> (mean param) goes to the data item's value, the likelihood grows.
>>
>> One way to avoid this is to force the components to have more responsibility.
>> You can do this with a prior on the simplex.  Something like Dirichlet(alpha)
>> where alpha is a vector values >> 1 can help.  Also putting a prior on the
>> scales that explicitly avoids zero (like a lognormal) can help.
>>
>> - Bob

On Wednesday, November 2, 2016, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I wonder whether there is a standard (or at least recommended) way to plot PPC for discrete outputs. For instance, the target output (1, 2, or 3) follows a categorical distribution. How to visualize the PPC properly after the Stan draws?

For binomial and poison models a lot of the existing plots should be useful. For categorical/multinomial I think it's a bit trickier but going forward we should add some plots specifically for that. One thing you can already do for those models is look at the proportion in a category or set of categories, comparing observed to replicated, e.g. using the functions prefixed with ppc_stat. Jonah

> you have the joint distribution of the latent z and observed y based
> on parameters
>
>   p(z, y | mu, X, beta, rho, psi, phi)

>      * Bernoulli(y[i] | k * pi)

messages.subject: Re: multiple random effect blocks and the decov prior?
messages.subject_clean: multiple random effect blocks and the decov prior?
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, November 2, 2016 at 4:56:13 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>
> Suppose I have a model with two blocks of random effects:
>
> y ~ 1 + cov1 + cov2 + cov3 + (cov1 + cov2 | grouping1 ) + ( cov3 | grouping2 )
>
> So I intend to fit 3 random effects out of which the first two are modeled as correlated while the third is independent of the others.
>
> How do I set the prior_covariance then? Can I give it a list of length of decov priors?

You can't supply a list of decov priors but you can specify a decov prior with vectors as its arguments. For (cov1 + cov2 | grouping), there will be 1 scale parameter, 1 concentration parameter, and 1 regularization (LKJ) parameter. For (cov3 | grouping), there will be 1 scale parameter only. Thus, I think you can pass to decov a vector of length two for its shape and / or scale arguments for the gamma priors on the scale parameters. Then, you would need a scalar for each of the regularization and concentration arguments.

Ben

predictors and y is observed data.  It's the same likelihood calculation
as in the model.

You can do similarity, i.e., Pr[items n and n' belong to same group | x, y].

> Say you're wanting to fit a latent group model from data. You want to
> know what probability each person has of belonging to each of K groups,
> then the parameters of said K groups.

Exactly because of label switching this isn't a valid inference.

> Is there a way of obtaining such
> parameters in a way that doesn't have a label switching problem?

No.  You can't evaluate what the probability is that item n
belongs to mixture component k.  You can get the marginal for a parameter,
such as mu, given item i.  It'll be multimodal.

Another thing I should put in the manual!

In my experience, you *can* do this so long as you specify enough constraints to avoid within-chain label switching.
If each chain settles on one mode without swapping modes, extracting similar chains or unimodal chains seems to work just fine.
I am working on a publication that uses mixtures extensively, using stan, and it appears to work fine on simulated data. A few constraints (valid constraints) keeps it either unimodal or the modes far enough apart that the chains never swap modes during simulation. Some parameters are invariant to label switching, but the latent group membership component of the model, of course, is not invariant and requires the constraint.

If you're going to update the manual, I'd at least be fair to the issue.
The full marginal posterior may not be interpretable if labels switch, but the type of label switching makes a big difference.
If each chain explores separate modes but never switch during simulation, this is ok for inference on EACH of the chains. You can examine the convergence of similar chains, or manually compute Rhat on the MCMC output using the correct columns --- If chain 1 and chain 2 label-switched, you can compute Rhat on, e.g., theta[1] for chain 1 and theta[2] for chain 2; if those converged, you're golden, just make sure you do your posterior inference on either one of the chains or adjust the MCMC output manually and assess convergence across both.

As a followup, I thought I'd mention the constraints that helped me. One is not preferred, but more generally applicable; the other is preferred, but only applicable if you're adding a certain prediction to the model.

1) Ordering constraints; this has been mentioned extensively. Place an ordering constraint on, e.g., gaussian means if that's the more important aspect of the different gaussian distributions to you. Yes, this can lead to bias in some cases, and can create a 'trough' between modes that a chain can get stuck in. If a chain gets stuck in the trough, you can usually tell it in the trace plots (chains 1 and 2 are label-swapped, but chain 3 is exactly between them bouncing endlessly between them). In this case, I've found that discarding chain 3 is 'fine', as it has nothing to do with my inference, per se, and more to do with a sampling problem --- The expectactions indicated by chain 3 are only applicable if I think label switching occurs in the population, which makes no intuitive sense to me, so it's out.

2) If you're predicting latent group membership via, e.g., logistic or softmax regression, impose a positivity constraint on one of the predictors for one of the groups. In the case of softmax, I recommend keeping group 1's log-odds at 0, to set the scale, then group 2's first predictor to be positive. That also seems to work; it works better if the first predictor is actually useful though, of course (otherwise it'll bunch up around 0); if need be, you could run it without the constraint, see which predictors appear to be multimodal (+2, or -2), then set the constraint so that it will find the mode with the beta = +2.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simple "within-subjects" design
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Simple "within-subjects" design
messages.body_plain:
Several months later, and I seem to have solved this finally! At least, for the scenario where you have data in wide format. I'll post the long-data compatible version in a bit, but in the meantime, here is the wide version that also permits missing data:

data {
  # N: number of cases
  int<lower=1> N ;
  # Y: matrix of outcomes for each case & variable
  matrix[N,2] Y ;
  # n_missing: number of instances of missing data
  int n_missing ;
  # indices_of_missing: matrix of the row and column indices of missing data
  int indices_of_missing[n_missing,2] ;
}
parameters {
  # means: vector of population-level means for intercept & slope
  vector[2] means ;
  # sds: vector of population-level sds for intercept & slope
  vector<lower=0>[2] sds ;
  # cor: population-level correlation between intercept & slope
  corr_matrix[2] cor ;
  # imputed: vector of imputed values for missing observations
  vector[n_missing] imputed ;
}
transformed parameters{
  # cov: covariance matrix (derived from cor & sds)
  matrix[2,2] cov ; #used in getting correlation to work
  # Y_with_imputed: matrix of observations including imputed values
  matrix[N,2] Y_with_imputed ;
  # Z: matrix of latent subject-by-subject intercepts & effects
  matrix[N,2] Z ;
  #replace any missing values in Y
  Y_with_imputed = Y ;
  for(i in 1:n_missing){
    Y_with_imputed[indices_of_missing[i][1],indices_of_missing[i][2]] = imputed[i] ;
  }
  #express Z as intercept/slope representation of Y_with_imputed
  for(i in 1:N){
    Z[i,1] = (Y_with_imputed[i,1]+Y_with_imputed[i,2])/2 ;
    Z[i,2] = Y_with_imputed[i,1]-Y_with_imputed[i,2] ;
  }
  #compute covariance matrix from cor & sds
  cov = quad_form_diag(cor,sds) ;
}
model {
  #priors on population parameters; presumes data has been scale()ed
  means ~ normal(0,1) ;
  sds ~ lognormal(0,1) ;
  cor ~ lkj_corr(1) ;
  #assert sampling of case-level outcomes on each variable given
  #  multivariate normal population
  for(s in 1:N){
    Z[s,] ~ multi_normal(means,cov) ;
  }
}

The problem is in this statement,

  if (X[i] >= cpX) {X_bin[i] = 1;} else {X_bin[i] = 0;}

that could've been written more simply as:

differentiability of the log density through X_bin and
down to cpX.

What you want to do is marginalize out the value of X_bin[i]

messages.body_plain:
The argument for stan() in RStan is "thin", not "thinSteps".

Also, after the fact, you can pull out the draws and thin
there.

For (2), your description is not what happens.  We don't
take the posterior mean and plug in, but rather do a full
Bayes computation.

So if you have

generated quantities {
  real ealpha;
  ealpha = exp(alpha);
}

alpha is some parameter, then for each draw for alpha, we compute
exp(alpha) and return the set of draws.  Because exp isn't linear,
the answer won't be the same, because in general, if u is a vector,

  exp(mean(u)) != mean(exp(u))

Jensen's inequality tells you which way it goes.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
messages.subject_clean: Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, October 31, 2016 at 4:23:57 PM UTC-4, jun...@gmail.com wrote:
> Dear RStanians,

>
>
> 1) How I can access only those saved steps? It looks like the extract() extracts all iterations, not those after thinning. So when I was trying to compare the descriptive statistics produced by summarizing across all iterations with those using pring(stan_fit), it's not surprising that they are different.

If you use the "thin" argument when calling the stan() function then afterwards extract should returned the thinned draws. For example

library(rstan)
fit <- stan_demo(
  "eight_schools",
  chains = 4,
  iter = 200,
  warmup = 100,
  thin = 5
)
posterior <- extract(fit)
length(posterior$mu)

For this example length(posterior$mu) should be 4*(200-100)/5 = 80 post-warmup draws. Is that what you get if you run the code?

On another note, thinning is almost never a good idea. Running each chain for 100,000 iterations is very extreme (for Stan) and I would bet that there's a reparameterization of your model that would lead to much more efficient sampling. For some models that already use the most efficient parameterization you may still need a lot of iterations per chain but probably still an order of magnitude smaller than 100K. Regardless, thinning is just throwing away information. So unless you can't fit all the draws in memory or something like that I would avoid thinning.

>
> 2) We can use the "generated quantities { }" block in stan to produce some post-estimation statistics using those means of estimated parameters and their credible intervals. I would assume we should be able to get the same results using the simulated posterior distributions. In this case, it should be the posterior after thinning, right?

Maybe I'm misunderstanding what you mean, but you don't have access to posterior means and credible intervals inside the generated quantities block. The generated quantities block is run once per iteration, but posterior means and credible intervals require the full set of posterior draws and so can't be computed at each iteration. What you can do in generated quantities is compute functions of parameters using the value of the parameters at each iteration. Then after the fact you can get means and intervals for whatever you've defined in generated quantities.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

out.  In each case of the marginalization, you'll know X_bin.  And

you really want a sample as opposed to directly calculating most
expectations of interest.

On Thu, Nov 3, 2016 at 1:26 AM, Bill Harris <bill_...@facilitatedsystems.com> wrote:
> Is it generally true that the mean and sd fall outside the yrep typical set when there's a link function between the linear predictor and y?

Good question, but no I don't think that should necessarily be true in general. For instance, the classic R glm example with log link is a counterexample:

library("rstanarm")
library("bayesplot")

counts <- c(18,17,15,20,10,20,25,13,12)
outcome <- gl(3,1,9)
treatment <- gl(3,3)
fit <- stan_glm(counts ~ outcome + treatment, family = poisson(link="log"))

yrep <- posterior_predict(fit)
ppc_stat_2d(counts, yrep, stat = c("mean", sd"))

messages.subject: Adaptive quadrature (or similar) numerical integration within Stan
messages.subject_clean: Adaptive quadrature (or similar) numerical integration within Stan
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am using a model with a likelihood that involves transformed parameters that are obtained via an integral, for which I do not have an analytic expression (the integral is of the form integral from 0 to t of exp(-(ax)^b-(cx)^d) * x^(b-1) dx, where a, b, c and d are all >0). I can e.g. numerically integrate this using a composite Simpson’s rule with a fixed number of terms and for my one particular integral it is pretty easy to remove any singularities and to turn this into a very nice straightforward problem. However, I cannot easily get any certainty about the quality of the numerical integral, because it is one of those cases where I have trouble to find the maximum of the fourth derivative over the plausible parameter values. Thus, even if I pick some large number of terms (e.g. 50), I am not entirely sure whether the integral approximation is all that good. Normally, one might just use an adaptive Simpson’s rule, but if I understand correctly how Stan works, a choice of the number of integral terms that is conditional on the values in successive iterations would lead to a problem with the automatic differentiation (which some suitably chosen fixed number of terms would not).

Is there some standard trick to deal with this (or a totally different approach that should work)?

Many thanks,
Björn

messages.subject: Re: stopping rule for sampling
messages.subject_clean: stopping rule for sampling
messages.body_plain:
You could examine the posterior distribution of the effect directly without need for model comparison. For example, you could compute the probability that you can infer the sign of the effect (making type-S error small).

WAIC and LOO are asymptotically equal (if n->infty while p_eff->finite). In finite case they mostly differ in the computational approximation PSIS-LOO being more reliable than WAIC (See Vehtari, Gelman and Gabry (2016). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. In Statistics and Computing, doi:10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4. Preprint http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544).

For small number of observations LOO and WAIC have large variance (also shown in the above mentioned paper and see also, e.g., Piironen and Vehtari (2016). Comparison of Bayesian predictive methods for model selection. Statistics and Computing, doi:10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y), and it is difficult to estimate this variance reliably for n<<100, which makes LOO and WAIC model comparison more difficult for n<<100. Currently I can't recommend using LOO or WAIC for your sequential decsiion making unless n>100. We are looking for n<100 case, too.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, November 2, 2016 at 6:19:19 PM UTC-4, Luca Campanelli wrote:
>
> I'm aware of some limitations of BF and that it’s not easy to compute. But, as you know, I can easily get the WAIC index from Stan outputs.
> My question is if you are aware of any method based on the WAIC index (or some other method) that I can use to quantify the degree of evidence of one model over another. That degree of evidence would then be used as stopping criterion.
>
> Thank you for any suggestion you may have.
> Luca

As WAIC/LOO are estimates on the same scale as A/DIC and are estimators of the same K-L distance, to the best of my understanding, perhaps you could use what Burnham and Anderson call 'Akaike weights'. Let d_i be the difference between the XAIC measure of model i from the minimal one (so D_i{min} = 0) then w_i = exp(-d_i / 2) / SUM{over models} ( exp(-d_i / 2). For example, if your WAIC (on deviance scale) for two models are 250 and 252, then weight for model 1 is ~73.1% (exp(0) / {exp{0} + exp{-1}). Their specific language (2002, pg. 75) is that a "given w_i is considered as the weight of evidence in favor of model i being the actual K-L best model for the situation at hand _given_ that one of the R models must be the K-L best model of that set of R models." Perhaps that will help you.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Two solutions come to my mind:

1. Represent your integral as the solution to an ODE problem and you get a probably slow, but very good answer

2. Run your Stan model with 25 approximation terms for, let's say, 5 chains and run it for 5 more chains with 50 approximation terms. Then you ensure that Rhat across the 10 chains is OK for your quantities. If the answer is yes, then this answer should be fine.

I can e.g. numerically integrate this using a composite Simpson’s rule with a fixed number of terms and for my one particular integral it is pretty easy to remove any singularities and to turn this into a very nice straightforward problem. However, I cannot easily get any certainty about the quality of the numerical integral, because it is one of those cases where I have trouble to find the maximum of the fourth derivative over the plausible parameter values. Thus, even if I pick some large number of terms (e.g. 50), I am not entirely sure whether the integral approximation is all that good. Normally, one might just use an adaptive Simpson’s rule, but if I understand correctly how Stan works, a choice of the number of integral terms that is conditional on the values in successive iterations would lead to a problem with the automatic differentiation (which some suitably chosen fixed number of terms would not).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stopping rule for sampling
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] stopping rule for sampling
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Aki — what you really want to do for any kind of adaptive
trial is stop based on some posterior expectation, not a posterior
predictive expectation.

In addition to the variability issues with WAIC and LOO that Aki notes,
there’s a deeper problem.  These measures do not have a natural
calibration, so it’s hard to assign any meaning to the explicit values
outside of their ordering.  In particular, while a larger difference between
WAIC or LOO of two models means that one is getting better than
the other, it doesn’t inform how much better one is than another.

Bayes factors are actually similar in that any threshold decision is
arbitrary.  The advantage of Bayes factors are that they are probabilities
(or at least proportional to probabilities) and that helps in informing that
decision.

On Nov 3, 2016, at 1:45 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:

> You could examine the posterior distribution of the effect directly without need for model comparison. For example, you could compute the probability that you can infer the sign of the effect (making type-S error small).
>
> WAIC and LOO are asymptotically equal (if n->infty while p_eff->finite). In finite case they mostly differ in the computational approximation PSIS-LOO being more reliable than WAIC (See Vehtari, Gelman and Gabry (2016). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. In Statistics and Computing, doi:10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4. Preprint http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544).
>
> For small number of observations LOO and WAIC have large variance (also shown in the above mentioned paper and see also, e.g., Piironen and Vehtari (2016). Comparison of Bayesian predictive methods for model selection. Statistics and Computing, doi:10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y), and it is difficult to estimate this variance reliably for n<<100, which makes LOO and WAIC model comparison more difficult for n<<100. Currently I can't recommend using LOO or WAIC for your sequential decsiion making unless n>100. We are looking for n<100 case, too.
>
> Aki
>
>
> On Thursday, November 3, 2016 at 12:19:19 AM UTC+2, Luca Campanelli wrote:
> > Hello all,
> > I'm planning to preregister an experiment and to use the "sequential Bayes Factor" approach as sampling plan. In a few words, for those who are not familiar with that, participants keep being recruited and tested till an a priori decided level of evidence is reached (e.g., BF 10 or 1/10).
> > I don’t know if it mattes, but the model that I will fit is a mixed-effects model with crossed random effects.
> >
> > I'm aware of some limitations of BF and that it’s not easy to compute. But, as you know, I can easily get the WAIC index from Stan outputs.
> > My question is if you are aware of any method based on the WAIC index (or some other method) that I can use to quantify the degree of evidence of one model over another. That degree of evidence would then be used as stopping criterion.
> >
> > Thank you for any suggestion you may have.
> > Luca
> >
>

> --

It is running. You can set stan()'s refresh argument to be some number smaller than 10 to see updates at intervals more frequent than 10%. I'm not sure what myglmer2stan is but you should probably be using stan_glmer in the rstanarm package.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot to Jonah and Bob for answering my questions. I have to apologize that I made a couple mistakes while checking the results and didn't do a good job explaining my questions.

The problem related to my first question actually was caused by not specifying the "thin" option in my stan function, though I did specify the thinning parameter to be relayed to the thinning option outside the stan function. So here my question is whether the stan object contains posterior after thinning or before thinning. I guess Jonah already gave me the answer. It is the post-thinning posterior. But what if I want to have all iterations, including those dumped? Relatedly, which was probably answered by Jonah, is thinning a good idea to reach convergence. I wasn't able to reach convergence with a total of 100,000 iterations for three chains with thin set to 1. Convergence was not reached. I might be able to re-parameterize the model, which is complex and should be hard to estimate in theory. It was frustrating. So I increase the chain length with a large thinning number. So it is consensus that thinning is never a good idea?

Let me try to explain my second problem. Say we are to estimate a binary regression, and I also want to calculate the predicted probability of y=1 when all independent variables are set to their respective means. To calculate the prediction is straightforward, but its credible interval is not. One method we can use is to use generated quantities and calculate p(y=1) for each iteration, and once I get the posterior, I can simply get the 2.5% and 97.5% of p(y=1). Alternatively, I can put the posterior of all parameter estimates (of course iteration by iteration or vector by vector of parameters) into the inverse logit function, viz, exp(xb)/(1+exp(xb)), where x is given, and b is from each iteration of the posterior to get the distribution of predicted probability. My question is whether results from these two methods are equivalent. I would assume they are. Thanks a lot for all your help and sorry for my remiss.

Jun

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] myglmer2stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] myglmer2stan
messages.body_plain:
Iterations are meaningless in and of themselves.  What
you want to do is set a threshold for the effective
sample size (an estimate is reported as n_eff by Stan;
don't know about RStanArm).  There can be orders of
magnitude or more differences in n_eff per iteration based
on algorithm.  In some cases, Stan can generate an n_eff
in 500 iterations larger than JAGS can generate in 200,000
iterations, and in other cases, the n_eff rate per iterations
will be close to each other.  It depends primarily on the
shape of the posterior.

Of course, I understand that by "my discipline" you may mean
reviewers won't accept a paper that doesn't have some
ridiculous number of draws in in it.  Usually it's not much
use to get n_eff >> 100 or so, because at that point, the
mean estimates have 1/10 the error of the posterior standard
deviation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
messages.body_plain:
> On Nov 3, 2016, at 3:05 PM, jun...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Thanks a lot to Jonah and Bob for answering my questions. I have to apologize that I made a couple mistakes while checking the results and didn't do a good job explaining my questions.
>
> The problem related to my first question actually was caused by not specifying the "thin" option in my stan function, though I did specify the thinning parameter to be relayed to the thinning option outside the stan function. So here my question is whether the stan object contains posterior after thinning or before thinning. I guess Jonah already gave me the answer. It is the post-thinning posterior. But what if I want to have all iterations, including those dumped?

If you have room to save them all, you should do that.
It'll give you better inferences (higher n_eff than
if you thin).

> Relatedly, which was probably answered by Jonah, is thinning a good idea to reach convergence.

No.  Completely unrelated.  We try to assess convergence by
running multiple chains and making sure they all get to
the same marginal means and standard deviations for each
parameter.  That's what the R-hat stat does.  Thinning won't
help with convergence.

> I wasn't able to reach convergence with a total of 100,000 iterations for three chains with thin set to 1. Convergence was not reached. I might be able to re-parameterize the model,

You will need to if you haven't converged.  I don't
know what your model is, but this can be caused by
chains getting stuck at the same value due to
geometry (rarely, lowering step size and increasing adapt_delta
will help) or by their being alternative modes in which chains
get stuck (as in some kinds of mixture models) or by lack
of identifiability.  See the manual chapter on problematic
posteriors.

> which is complex and should be hard to estimate in theory. It was frustrating. So I increase the chain length with a large thinning number. So it is consensus that thinning is never a good idea?

The only reason to thin is if you have long autocorrelations
and don't have enough memory to save all the draws.  It
loses information, but saves space.  If the autocorrelation gets
too long, then you need to reparameterize as all the estimates
of R-hat and n_eff may be off as they're very hard to estimate
at that range.  In some cases like that, thinning may give the
illusion of convergence without actually having convergence, so
again, it's a bad idea.

> Let me try to explain my second problem. Say we are to estimate a binary regression, and I also want to calculate the predicted probability of y=1 when all independent variables are set to their respective means.

I take it the "independent variables" are what we call
"predictors" or "covariates"?   And presumably they're
modeled if you're estimating population means?  Or are
you just using sample means without any uncertainty?

> To calculate the prediction is straightforward, but its credible interval is not.

> One method we can use is to use generated quantities and calculate p(y=1) for each iteration, and once I get the posterior, I can simply get the 2.5% and 97.5% of p(y=1).

That's the Bayesian approach.

> Alternatively, I can put the posterior of all parameter estimates (of course iteration by iteration or vector by vector of parameters) into the inverse logit function, viz, exp(xb)/(1+exp(xb)), where x is given, and b is from each iteration of the posterior to get the distribution of predicted probability. My question is whether results from these two methods are equivalent. I would assume they are. Thanks a lot for all your help and sorry for my remiss.

They'd only be equivalent if the parameters were independent
and all the functions were linear.

- Bob

>
> Jun
>
> On Monday, October 31, 2016 at 4:23:57 PM UTC-4, jun...@gmail.com wrote:
> Dear RStanians,
>
> Here is a problem I am not sure how to deal with after reading the post by the Stan team. I have a Stan model with simulation parameters set to the following:
>
> ######
> parameters = c("b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5", "b6", "b7", "thresh", "bmean", "bsigma", "log_lik")  # The parameter(s) to be monitored.
> adaptSteps = 5000              # Number of steps to "tune" the samplers.
> burnInSteps = 5000            # Number of steps to "burn-in" the samplers.
> nChains = 3                   # Number of chains to run.
>
> numSavedSteps=30000           # Total number of steps in chains to save.
> thinSteps=10                  # Number of steps to "thin" (1=keep every step).
> nPerChain = ceiling( ( numSavedSteps * thinSteps ) / nChains ) # Steps per chain.
> ######
>
> Because this is a complex model for estimation and using shorter chains have failed to reach convergence, I am using a rather long chain with a thinning step set to 10 (save one iteration out of ten). Here I request to have 100,000 iterations for one chain, and only save one out of ten iterations for a total of three chains. It converged. Now my questions are:
>
> 1) How I can access only those saved steps? It looks like the extract() extracts all iterations, not those after thinning. So when I was trying to compare the descriptive statistics produced by summarizing across all iterations with those using pring(stan_fit), it's not surprising that they are different.
>
> 2) We can use the "generated quantities { }" block in stan to produce some post-estimation statistics using those means of estimated parameters and their credible intervals. I would assume we should be able to get the same results using the simulated posterior distributions. In this case, it should be the posterior after thinning, right?
>
> Any thoughts? Thanks a lot!
>
> Jun Xu, PhD

> Muncie, IN

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Adaptive quadrature (or similar) numerical integration within Stan
messages.body_plain:
Not yet.  You can try to write your own quadrature algorithm,
which has sometimes worked.  Basing termination of an algorithm
on parameter values isn't always a disaster.

We're going to be adding some numerical intergrators with
built-in derivatives soon (maybe next year?).

- Bob

> On Nov 3, 2016, at 4:24 AM, Björn Holzhauer <bjoernh...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Dear all,
>
> I am using a model with a likelihood that involves transformed parameters that are obtained via an integral, for which I do not have an analytic expression (the integral is of the form integral from 0 to t of exp(-(ax)^b-(cx)^d) * x^(b-1) dx, where a, b, c and d are all >0). I can e.g. numerically integrate this using a composite Simpson’s rule with a fixed number of terms and for my one particular integral it is pretty easy to remove any singularities and to turn this into a very nice straightforward problem. However, I cannot easily get any certainty about the quality of the numerical integral, because it is one of those cases where I have trouble to find the maximum of the fourth derivative over the plausible parameter values. Thus, even if I pick some large number of terms (e.g. 50), I am not entirely sure whether the integral approximation is all that good. Normally, one might just use an adaptive Simpson’s rule, but if I understand correctly how Stan works, a choice of the number of integral terms that is conditional on the values in successive iterations would lead to a problem with the automatic differentiation (which some suitably chosen fixed number of terms would not).
>
> Is there some standard trick to deal with this (or a totally different approach that should work)?
>
> Many thanks,
> Björn

I was wondering if there are best practices for my user-defined probability probability functions.
>
> Should I add first the choice?
>
>  real race_lpmf(int winner, real rt, row_vector alpha, real sigma){
>    ...
>  }
>
> or reaction times?
>
>  real race_lpdf(real rt, int winner, row_vector alpha, real sigma){
>    ...
>  }

We don't have conventions for ordering real vs. int arguments
other than that

> And just to be sure, there's no way to move the | after the second argument, right?
> In the first case I'll need to do this:
>
> model{
>   winner ~ race(rt, alpha, sigma)
> }
>
>
> and it's not possible to do the following, right?
>
> model{
>   winner,rt ~ race(alpha, sigma)
> }

Not yet.  In these cases, I'd really recommend just defining
a function race() and using

  target += race(winner, rt, alpha, sigma);

because the _lpdf and _lpmf notations are really just for single
outcomes (which can be vectors or matrices, but can't mix integers
and reals yet).   It'll be confusing if you have two random
variables (winner and rt) but only one before the ~.

- Bob

> On Oct 26, 2016, at 8:50 PM, Tobias Schwoerer <tschw...@alaska.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi,
> I am new to STAN and relatively new to Bayesian stats, but very excited about its application.
> We have survey data from floatplane pilots showing 727 destination lakes (j = 1 ... 727). For each j- destination we have:
> - total number of pilots flying to j
> - total number of pilots arriving at j from infested source lakes
> - total number of flights arriving at j
> - total number of flights to j originating at infested source lakes
>
> I set up a beta-binomial hierarchical model adapted from the rat example in Carpenter et al. 2016 "Stan: A probabilistic programming language ...",  p.16
> The objective is to get a marginal probability distribution for a measure of risk for each of the 727 destination lakes. The code below works great with results as expected.
> To meet the assumption of independence in the binomial, I had to choose the proportion of pilots from source lakes as the measure of risk (tumor rate). However, a better measure of risk in my case would be the proportion of flights from source lakes. Risk of invasion is greater the larger the number of flights from source lakes. Yet flights violate the assumption of independence in the binomial.
>
> Question:
> Is anybody aware of a hierarchical approach that would estimate the credible intervals using the number of pilots as the sample size, while using the proportion of flights as the measure of risk (theta)?
>
> Thank you very much for your help!
>
> Tobias
>
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> J; // number of lakes
>   int<lower=0> y[J]; // number of pilots from elodea-infested sources into lake j
>   int<lower=0> n[J]; // number of total pilots that fly into lake j (number of trials)
> }
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> theta[J]; // chances of success: a pilot originating from an elodea-infested source destined for j
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> lambda; // prior mean chance of success
>   real<lower=0.1> kappa; // prior count
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   real<lower=0> alpha; // prior success count
>   real<lower=0> beta; // prior failure count
>   alpha = lambda* kappa;
>   beta =   (1 - lambda)* kappa;
> }
> model {
>   lambda ~ uniform(0,1); // hyperprior
>   kappa ~ uniform(0.1,5); // hyperprior
>   theta ~ beta(alpha,beta); // prior
>   y ~ binomial(n,theta); // likelihood
> }
> generated quantities {
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> avg; // avg success
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> above_avg[J]; // true if j is above avg
>   int<lower=1,upper=J> rnk[J]; // rank of j
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> highest[J]; // true if j is highest rank
>   avg = mean(theta);
>     for (j in 1:J)
>     above_avg[j] = (theta[j] > avg);
>     for (j in 1:J) {
>     rnk[j] = rank(theta,j) + 1;
>     highest[j] = rnk[j] == 1;
>   }
> }
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, November 3, 2016, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
> > One method we can use is to use generated quantities and calculate p(y=1) for each iteration, and once I get the posterior, I can simply get the 2.5% and 97.5% of p(y=1).
>
> That's the Bayesian approach.
>
> > Alternatively, I can put the posterior of all parameter estimates (of course iteration by iteration or vector by vector of parameters) into the inverse logit function, viz, exp(xb)/(1+exp(xb)), where x is given, and b is from each iteration of the posterior to get the distribution of predicted probability. My question is whether results from these two methods are equivalent. I would assume they are. Thanks a lot for all your help and sorry for my remiss.
>
> They'd only be equivalent if the parameters were independent
> and all the functions were linear.
>
> - Bob

I think I disagree with Bob here but it's probably because we're interpreting the question differently and not because there's an actual disagreement. You can always achieve the same thing you're doing in generated quantities after fitting the model using the full set of draws. Whether you compute P(y=1) inside generated quantities or after fitting the model shouldn't matter at all. What you don't want to do is to confuse computing intervals of a function with computing a function of the intervals. That doesn't give you the same thing except under strict conditions.

Jonah

but we will be adding a tuple type and expressions to build them
that way.  But then this mix of real and integer values defeats

work is:

and then you'll be able to write something like

  (m, v) ~ foo(theta);

messages.body_plain:
I felt compelled to reply to this, with regard to sequential BFs. In the psych methods (or psychMAP?) facebook group, someone explored whether terminating collection upon reaching a BF threshold would bias results just as it would using an NHST criterion would, and it does indeed bias results. This is *especially* true with a threshold of 3, but still occurs with BF thresholds of 10.
All that to say --- Using these thresholds as stopping rules, in the long term, can bias your inference. I would instead recommend using a stopping rule based on posterior credible interval width (analogous to using SE size as an NHST stopping criterion); it will still bias effect size estimates a bit, but not as much.

messages.subject: Dealing with multimodality and unconstrained parameter in Generic Confirmatory Factor Analysis model
messages.subject_clean: Dealing with multimodality and unconstrained parameter in Generic Confirmatory Factor Analysis model
messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

I'm working on a general confirmatory factor analysis model with Stan, inspired by the lavaan and blavaan packages (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.05604.pdf). My idea is to build a pre-compiled model, similar to the strategy used in rstanarm, to quickly fit CFA models with Stan (and general SEM models later on), using lavaan's simple syntax to define the model and generate the parameter matrices.

I have some questions about my implementation:

(1) Especially with standardized latent variables, there are at least two modes for some sets of parameters (loadings lambda and latent covariance matrix Phi) due to sign switching. I have visited many threads about this issue here, but some proposed solutions, like manual initialization and positivity constraints, are not working as expected. For example, when I constrain the loadings to be positive, some chains find the right mode, but other chains keep bouncing at zero. I suspect I should constrain more parameters, but I don't know exactly which. Could someone suggest how to deal with this multimodality issue without post-processing?

(2) I read in another thread that leaving free parameters (parameters not really constrained by any data or prior) can be harmful to HMC. Currently, I'm defining unconstrained parameters in the 'parameters' block (with cholesky correlation matrix and vector of standard deviations for the CFA model matrices), and constraining them in the 'transformed parameters' block -- e.g., fixing some elements of a matrix to zero or one. The likelihood is defined with the constrained parameters, of course, but that leaves some parameters without any true connection to the model. All unconstrained parameters are given somewhat weakly informative priors (like normal(0,1) for loadings, cauchy(0,1) for residual standard deviations, etc. etc.), so they are not completely unconstrained. When estimating the parameter of a CFA with one indicator loading fixed to one for each latent factor, HMC samples very quickly and with very good mixing. Should I be worried about the unconstrained parameters?

Thanks!
Erikson

messages.subject: Re: Dealing with multimodality and unconstrained parameter in Generic Confirmatory Factor Analysis model
messages.subject_clean: Dealing with multimodality and unconstrained parameter in Generic Confirmatory Factor Analysis model
messages.body_plain:
First, this is an excellent project that you're working on. I'll hopefully soon be releasing a DIF/measurement invariance procedure in stan, and may borrow implementation ideas from you so the user can specify general CFA models. Very cool.

As for your questions:
1) You could try first fitting the model via optimization and using the output as the initial values for the chains. This hasn't work great for me in the past, but you may give it a shot. When I've fit CFAs in stan, I typically use the standardized solution with positive loadings and haven't hit much multimodality; this also gives better control over the priors. That said, it looks to me like you are using the covariance and multivariate normal approach, which I don't use. Try leaving the normal covariance-based approach to CFA fits and instead try fitting it via regressions. E.g., y[i,1] ~ normal(lambda[1,1]*theta[i], residual[1]) if theta is latent ability, lambda is the factor loading for factor 1 on item 1, and residual[1] is the residual for item 1. Does that make sense? Don't bother estimating the covariance matrix, but estimate the factor loadings and individuals' latent abilities and use likelihoods for each item and case. If you want the covariance matrix for later processing, generate it via transformed parameters or generated quantities.

2) The issue with leaving free parameters totally free is that they are totally unbound and winds up screwing up the adaptation of HMC. It doesn't know how to adapt the stepsize or evaluate u-turns for a particle than can essentially go onto infinity in any direction. This is fixed by priors, in which case the posterior distribution of the unconstrained, unused values will just be the prior distribution (because they are independent, p(unused | D) = p(unused). Ideally, you would just remove those if possible and only estimate parameters you actually use, but this quickly becomes a programming nightmare. It will speed up adaptation and sampling though, as there are fewer parameters to sample and adapt for.

messages.subject_clean: How to handle this: Stan model for consumer choice data.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am seeking advice on how to implement the following hierarchical model in STAN.
Model description: consumers get individual level parameters (and error terms) from population level distributions and then choose quantities by maximizing utility. Using conditions for optimization, one is able to back out the implied error terms and form likelihood for quantity by change of variables. The likelihood for the data (quantity vectors of the type q=(q_1,..,q_m,0,...,0)) is fairly complex.
We are attempting to recover all individual level parameters and the hyperparameters.

I would really appreciate if you could give some pointers or answer the following questions:
1) how should I enter the "model part" in STAN for this kind of model? I have only seen examples where the probabilistic model for the data is very simple (a known distribution) like y~normal(theta,sigma).

2) Should HMCMC be done with block sampling or is it possible to sample all parameters (individual values and hyperparameters) in one iteration? What is the best practice?

I am actively learning and I would appreciate if you could point me to some references that deal with more complicated hierarchical models.
Thanks!

We don't have good general solutions to (1) of which I'm aware.
In most of the sign switching cases we have (like in IRT 3PL for
generally well-posed problems) it's enough to constrain a single
variable.

As for (2), it's not just HMC.  If you have a parameter with
unbounded support (not constrained above and below) and an improper
uniform prior, you get an improper uniform posterior.
But if you give them a proper prior (as you do), then you get
a proper posterior.  This isn't a problem other than for efficiency.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The likelihood the OP is using is y ~ multinormal(means, covariance), where the covariance matrix is constructed from factor loadings, factor variances, and residuals.
In covariance-based latent variable modeling, the goal is to estimate factor loadings/variances and residuals, then construct the implied covariance matrix from such loadings and minimize the difference between the implied and observed covariance matrix (and there are several ways of assessing the difference between the matrices, hence why there are ML, WLS, GLS, ADF, etc estimators for CFA and SEM).

All I'm saying is to try not using the multinormal likelihood with means and the implied covariance matrix.
Instead, model each response of each individual using latent regression. Not ~ multinormal(means, covariance), but response[i,j] ~ normal(predicted value, residual), where predicted value is factor-loadings * latent abilities.

messages.body_plain:
Just to clarify: Use the responses directly in the likelihood rather than use a multinormal likelihood on the entire dataset.
If you still want the implied covariance matrix, then you can construct it in generated quantities for later analysis (e.g., for reporting, for fit metrics that require covariance matrix comparisons).

On Friday, November 4, 2016 at 4:22:51 PM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
> The likelihood the OP is using is y ~ multinormal(means, covariance), where the covariance matrix is constructed from factor loadings, factor variances, and residuals.
> In covariance-based latent variable modeling, the goal is to estimate factor loadings/variances and residuals, then construct the implied covariance matrix from such loadings and minimize the difference between the implied and observed covariance matrix (and there are several ways of assessing the difference between the matrices, hence why there are ML, WLS, GLS, ADF, etc estimators for CFA and SEM).
>
> All I'm saying is to try not using the multinormal likelihood with means and the implied covariance matrix.
> Instead, model each response of each individual using latent regression. Not ~ multinormal(means, covariance), but response[i,j] ~ normal(predicted value, residual), where predicted value is factor-loadings * latent abilities.
>
> On Friday, November 4, 2016 at 4:17:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > I'm not exactly sure what you're suggesting because I'm
> > not familiar with this class of models described this way,
> > but there's a difference between a covariance prior and
> > comptuing covariance in the posterior if that's what you're
> > suggesting.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Nov 4, 2016, at 4:59 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > First, this is an excellent project that you're working on. I'll hopefully soon be releasing a DIF/measurement invariance procedure in stan, and may borrow implementation ideas from you so the user can specify general CFA models. Very cool.
> > >
> > > As for your questions:
> > > 1) You could try first fitting the model via optimization and using the output as the initial values for the chains. This hasn't work great for me in the past, but you may give it a shot. When I've fit CFAs in stan, I typically use the standardized solution with positive loadings and haven't hit much multimodality; this also gives better control over the priors. That said, it looks to me like you are using the covariance and multivariate normal approach, which I don't use. Try leaving the normal covariance-based approach to CFA fits and instead try fitting it via regressions. E.g., y[i,1] ~ normal(lambda[1,1]*theta[i], residual[1]) if theta is latent ability, lambda is the factor loading for factor 1 on item 1, and residual[1] is the residual for item 1. Does that make sense? Don't bother estimating the covariance matrix, but estimate the factor loadings and individuals' latent abilities and use likelihoods for each item and case. If you want the covariance matrix for later processing, generate it via transformed parameters or generated quantities.
> > >
> > > 2) The issue with leaving free parameters totally free is that they are totally unbound and winds up screwing up the adaptation of HMC. It doesn't know how to adapt the stepsize or evaluate u-turns for a particle than can essentially go onto infinity in any direction. This is fixed by priors, in which case the posterior distribution of the unconstrained, unused values will just be the prior distribution (because they are independent, p(unused | D) = p(unused). Ideally, you would just remove those if possible and only estimate parameters you actually use, but this quickly becomes a programming nightmare. It will speed up adaptation and sampling though, as there are fewer parameters to sample and adapt for.
> > >
> > > On Friday, November 4, 2016 at 3:27:05 PM UTC-5, Erikson Kaszubowski wrote:
> > >
> > > Greetings,
> > >
> > > I'm working on a general confirmatory factor analysis model with Stan, inspired by the lavaan and blavaan packages (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.05604.pdf). My idea is to build a pre-compiled model, similar to the strategy used in rstanarm, to quickly fit CFA models with Stan (and general SEM models later on), using lavaan's simple syntax to define the model and generate the parameter matrices.
> > >
> > > I have some questions about my implementation:
> > >
> > > (1) Especially with standardized latent variables, there are at least two modes for some sets of parameters (loadings lambda and latent covariance matrix Phi) due to sign switching. I have visited many threads about this issue here, but some proposed solutions, like manual initialization and positivity constraints, are not working as expected. For example, when I constrain the loadings to be positive, some chains find the right mode, but other chains keep bouncing at zero. I suspect I should constrain more parameters, but I don't know exactly which. Could someone suggest how to deal with this multimodality issue without post-processing?
> > >
> > > (2) I read in another thread that leaving free parameters (parameters not really constrained by any data or prior) can be harmful to HMC. Currently, I'm defining unconstrained parameters in the 'parameters' block (with cholesky correlation matrix and vector of standard deviations for the CFA model matrices), and constraining them in the 'transformed parameters' block -- e.g., fixing some elements of a matrix to zero or one. The likelihood is defined with the constrained parameters, of course, but that leaves some parameters without any true connection to the model. All unconstrained parameters are given somewhat weakly informative priors (like normal(0,1) for loadings, cauchy(0,1) for residual standard deviations, etc. etc.), so they are not completely unconstrained. When estimating the parameter of a CFA with one indicator loading fixed to one for each latent factor, HMC samples very quickly and with very good mixing. Should I be worried about the unconstrained parameters?
> > >
> > > Thanks!
> > > Erikson

> On Nov 4, 2016, at 6:03 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Yeah, I think the regression notation would take a bit more thoughtwork, but should still allow general models implemented via matrices. And I honestly have no idea whether it would help the multimodality,

The only way it's going to reduce multimodality is if
it defines a different density.  The only difference
between two different implementations of the same density will
be efficiency and arithmetic stability.

In general, scalars will be faster than matrices.
For example, you'd never want to use a diagonal matrix for a
multivariate normal.  A vectorized scalar normal would be
better.  That is,

  y[n] ~ normal(mu, sigma);

is better than

  y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu, diag_matrix(sigma));

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stopping rule for sampling
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] stopping rule for sampling
messages.body_plain:
>
> Michael, the "Akaike weights", mentioned by Avi, have some meaningful interpretation; in my understanding they range from 0 to 1 and can be interpreted as the probability that a model is the best model. Does this answer part of your question about the meaning of WAIC values?

No, they absolutely cannot be interpreted that way.  It’s easy to see why —
w_{n} \propto exp(- LOO_{n}) is a valid weight, but so is w_{n} \propto exp( - alpha LOO_{n}).
Everything choice of alpha yields a valid set of weights that admit each model
different influence.  This is just a manifestation of the scaling ambiguity I mentioned
before.

> Aki and Michael, thank you for your suggestion to examine directly the posterior distribution, instead of posterior predictive expectation. That would be easy to compute and interpret. Are you aware of any article that used that approach as stopping rule in sequential testing?

There is a huge literature on Bayesian adaptive clinical trials.  Just google
“adaptive clinical trial”.  The stuff from M. D. Anderson was particularly
influential.

Using conditions for optimization, one is able to back out the implied error terms and form likelihood for quantity by change of variables. The likelihood for the data (quantity vectors of the type q=(q_1,..,q_m,0,...,0)) is fairly complex.

There are more complex models in the manual and on the example models: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models

No need to specify this at all. Stan will perform MCMC over all the parameters jointly. The language doesn't have any specification of the algorithm.

There's a quick write up of the motivation and brief history at the start of the manual.

If you want to see the actual source history, it's all there in git. It starts at GitHub.com/stan-dev/stan <http://GitHub.com/stan-dev/stan>. I'm pretty sure when we migrated from Google code to GitHub, we were able to maintain our historical commits. (I could be wrong.)

If you have specific questions, ask (here, on the users list)! The Stan team, on our webpage and manual, is listed in order of joining the team (almost: the first names joined at the start together in a sense).

If you're willing to dig, our development emails were moved to the stan-dev email list fairly early and some of us were big proponents of having as much communication be open as possible, so you can flip through the archive of that list and this list.

Every release of Stan is on GitHub. We started CmdStan and RStan under one repo: look in the Stan releases. The manual was included in each and I believe full programs were in the manual starting pre-v1.

And some of our examples in the example models have a long history. For example, dogs: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/commits/master/bugs_examples/vol1/dogs/dogs.stan

I have tried some of the suggestions given here. Reparameterizing the model to the regression notation made it considerably slower than the earlier version, without any clear gain in terms of mixing chains or mode avoidance.

Surprisingly, 'optimizing' the model to obtain inits is not working very well: the point estimates are off the target, so I ended up using lavaan's point estimate for chain initialization. I also messed up with step size via higher adapt_delta parameter. Models with fixed loadings in one indicator variable seems to avoid other modes without a significant loss of performance. But models with standardized latent variables still suffer from sign switching, so I have to postprocess them.

>
> The only way it's going to reduce multimodality is if
> it defines a different density.  The only difference
> between two different implementations of the same density will
> be efficiency and arithmetic stability.
>
> In general, scalars will be faster than matrices.
> For example, you'd never want to use a diagonal matrix for a
> multivariate normal.  A vectorized scalar normal would be
> better.  That is,
>
>   y[n] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>
> is better than
>
>   y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu, diag_matrix(sigma));
>

messages.body_plain:
I don't see anything wrong with the model.  You could
make it more efficient computationally, but that's another matter.
With half-normal priors, you're allowing the standard deviations
have support at 0 and it may be that the model is just driving
the result toward complete pooling.

Have you tried simulating data from the model with non-zero standard
deviation parameters to see if that will fit?

You may want to try the non-centered parameterization (use normal(0, 1)
and then multiply by standard deviation) --- that can be much more efficient
with small group counts.

- Bob

P.S.  Rather than

 beta_AB ~ normal(0, beta_AB_hyper);

we'd write

  beta_AB ~ normal(0, sigma_beta_AB);

The "sigma" helps indicate it's a scale (though I
see you don't have means here, which is good given you
have an overall intercept).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Dealing with multimodality and unconstrained parameter in Generic Confirmatory Factor Analysis model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Dealing with multimodality and unconstrained parameter in Generic Confirmatory Factor Analysis model
messages.body_plain:
I e-mailed Edgar Merkle, author of the blavaan package, to ask about usual ways of dealing with those pesky multiple modes, especially the sign switching. Turns out that constraining just one loading per factor to be positive should suffice. I tried with a few models, but I occasionally got chains bumping at zero for those parameters. But, by using lavaan's point estimates for iniatizaliation, the chains explored just one mode. I still get divergent transition in some models, but the parameter estimates are quite close to lavaan's point estimates, and I'm getting very good mixing.

I'm planning to package it all up, but I attached the source files for those who might be interested!

I also messed up with step size via higher adapt_delta parameter. Models with fixed loadings in one indicator variable seems to avoid other modes without a significant loss of performance. In order to test Stan, I've tried to reproduce the marginal for a 3D simplex. First, to confirm that the beta is indeed the marginal of the Dirichlet, I marginalized the Dirichlet([1 1 1]) distribution in Mathematica with the following result:

parameters {

model {

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Array of reals vs Matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Juan,

On Mon, Nov 7, 2016 at 8:03 AM, Juan <juan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello.
>
> Is it better to use a bidimensional array of reals or a matrix?
> (Speed, memory, safety or any other interesting related issue).

Speed: it'll depend on your case. Often an array of vectors could be the fastest thing to do. The deep reason is that it has to do with memory locality.
Memory: matrix. There's just slightly less overhead using the matrix variable type over arrays of arrays. But it shouldn't be much.
Saftey: both are equally safe

The real key to the difference is the usability. When you need to do linear algebra, use matrix, vector, row_vector. These have shapes and sizes and operations are well defined. Treat arrays as collections. What does it mean to multiply a bidirectional array with another? That doesn't really have meaning. (And if you can come up with some sort of "natural" thing, I'm sure someone thinks something else is "natural" for that same operation.)

>
> And another question, why is not possible to assign an array to a matrix or viceversa?

That's easy: an array is not a matrix and a matrix is not an array.

There should be enough conversion functions in the library for this to be easy. See to_array(), etc. If there's something obvious that's missing, please let us know.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] positive_infinity()
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] positive_infinity()
messages.body_plain:
positive_infinity() is a function. It returns the value of \infty.

It really doesn't have much purpose. One place you can use it is in a variable declaration. Suppose you have scale variable, sigma, that's lower bounded by 0. This is how I'd write it:
parameters {
  real<lower = 0> sigma;
}

You could write this, which isn't recommended, but you could still do this:
parameters {
  real<lower = 0, upper = positive_infinity()> sigma;
}

Since Stan is a language, I'm sure there are many other use cases that I haven't thought about.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 7, 2016 at 2:26:51 AM UTC-5, Ole Petter Hansen wrote:
> a very brief question: what is the default prior for an ordered vector?
>
> Is it a flat prior (i.e. U(-inf,inf)) for the first element, and thereafter x_n~U(x_(n-1),inf) for the rest?

Not really, because all elements but the last are going to have a random upper bound too. I would simply say that all vectors satisfying the constraints are equally likely before seeing the data. I don't even really like the phrase "default prior". You define a space by declaring what the parameter type is (and its lower and upper bounds, which can be infinite). And then in the model block you can describe the shape of your beliefs over that space with an explicit prior. If you don't, then you are simply left with that space until you condition on the data.

Ben

Treat arrays as collections. What does it mean to multiply a bidirectional array with another? That doesn't really have meaning. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Prior for orderd vector
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Prior for orderd vector
messages.body_plain:
All of Stan's parameters work the same way.  The distribution
is uniform over all values satisfying the constraint.  If you
want to see how we do that, there's a chapter near the end of
the manual on the Jacobians for constrained parameters.

The uniformity assumption means that if you add your own prior
for a variable, that's the prior it has because the uniform doesn't
add anything (a log constant, which can be ignored in all of our
algorithms).

- Bob

> On Nov 7, 2016, at 1:13 PM, Ole Petter Hansen <olepetter...@outlook.com> wrote:
>
> Won't that depend on what we are conditioning on? I.e. x_n can take all values from x_(n-1) to infty before conditioning on x_(n+1). This seems to be the logic in section 58.5 in the manual, where the unconstrained transforms of an ordered vector are defined recursively. So it is at least not apparent to me that the last element of the vector is treated any differently than anyone in the middle (unless we are interested in the distribution of x_n | x_(n-1), x_(n+1) ).
>
> So just to clarify: If I would like to have an ordered vector where each element is defined recursively with support x_n~U(x_(n-1),infty), then I would have to define this myself using e.g. transformed parameters?
>
> E.g. if I want an ordered vector x of length 3, I should do this as follows:
>
> parameters{
> real x_first_element;
> real[2] x_inc;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> vector[3] x;
>
> x[1]=x_first_element[1];
> x[2]=x_inc[1]+x[1];
> x[3]+x_inc[2]+x[2];
> }
>
> Do I understand you correctly that defining ordered[3] x; directly would imply a different prior?
>
> Thank you for your response.
>
> Ole-Petter
>
> mandag 7. november 2016 16.08.58 UTC+1 skrev Ben Goodrich følgende:
> On Monday, November 7, 2016 at 2:26:51 AM UTC-5, Ole Petter Hansen wrote:
> a very brief question: what is the default prior for an ordered vector?
>
> Is it a flat prior (i.e. U(-inf,inf)) for the first element, and thereafter x_n~U(x_(n-1),inf) for the rest?
>
> Not really, because all elements but the last are going to have a random upper bound too. I would simply say that all vectors satisfying the constraints are equally likely before seeing the data. I don't even really like the phrase "default prior". You define a space by declaring what the parameter type is (and its lower and upper bounds, which can be infinite). And then in the model block you can describe the shape of your beliefs over that space with an explicit prior. If you don't, then you are simply left with that space until you condition on the data.
>
> Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Poisson log-linear model
messages.body_plain:
I should have looked in the manual, I guess. :-)

I did a bit more of searching, and read that the negative binomial distribution can also handle zero cases like this, so I decided to try it out before moving to the (in my eyes) more advanced (and maybe not so easy to interpret) zero-inflated model.

The model was straight forward to implement, and required only very few modifications to the original code (Go Stan!). I uploaded the model here: https://gist.github.com/demodw/457aaff455b99bd5a36fa8961fb3c8bb. I just put normal(0,5) on the intercept, and normal(0, 2.5) on the coefficients.  When I run the model without any priors on sigma for each regression coefficient, the model converges nicely (R-hat < 1, tree depth ~ 8.5, log-posterior looks unimodal). Step-size is about 0.01 in all chains, so quite low, which may be due to the relatively weak priors (I guess). The coefficients are approximately the same as  if I had run it in 4 separate rstanarm runs. So far so good.

However, when I try to add priors on the scale values, I run into trouble. I uploaded the model to https://gist.github.com/demodw/37a7bb1a8e4cb6769f3ee1cf45ad2a25. The intercept is modelled with a normal(0, 2.5) prior on the scale, and the coefficients are modelled with a normal(0, 1) prior on the scale. I would have thought this corresponded approximately to the scenario above, since normal(0, 2.5) has support for values in the range +-5.7, and normal(0, 1) has support for the values in the range +-2.2. The model does converge (R-hat < 1.1, tree-depth ~6.5). Step-size is is about four times at large, at 0.04, in all chains. However there are quite a few divergences. From the inspection of energy and log-posterior, it also seems that it is now multi-model (see attachments). Initially I thought that the model might be unidentified, but I cannot really see why. I have coded male/female as -1, 1. The other categorical variable, Adm, I have forced to have a zero entry.

When I inspect each of the coefficients, they all look to behave nicely. They are within the bounds, and look normally distributed. Similar with the scale values, except I start seeing some tails, especially on sigma_A and sigma_B. For these two it seems that Stan tried to explored beyond the bounds of the specified distribution. So, naturally, I tried to increase these a bit. The result was the same: lots of divergences, and Stan once again tried to explore beyond the bonds. I've tried with both double exponential, cauchy, and student_t with 3 and 7 df. Same result. Even increasing the acceptance rate to 0.95 did not change it. Am I missing something? Is there an unidentified component in my model?

Cheers,

David
