messages.subject: Varying-intercept & varying-slope model in rstan
messages.subject_clean: Varying-intercept & varying-slope model in rstan
messages.body_plain:
Dear stan users.

I have been thoroughly enjoying working my way through McElreath’s and Gelman&Hill’s books. I have a question concerning the varying-intercept, varying-slope model, discussed in the radon example in Gelman&Hill (chapter 13), and the coffee robot example in McElreath (chapter 13).

I consider both individual level and group-level predictors (e.g. per-house radon and per-county uranium measurements), see attached stan model.

McElreath and the Stan manual (section 5.12) provide a full hierarchical model with multivariate priors on the group-level coefficients. This involves a covariance matrix that accounts for the correlation between group-level intercepts and slopes, as given in my attached model. So far, so good.
Question 1: The rstan-transposed examples from Gelman&Hill give a much simpler model, with uncorrelated separate priors for the group-level intercepts and slopes (see the model here <https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/ARM/Ch.13/radon_inter_vary.stan>). Why the different modelling approaches? Intuitively I would assume that taking into account the correlation between intercepts and slopes allows for more efficient pooling of information across groups. So why the independent prior model in the stan examples for Gelman&Hill?
Question 2: As an extension to the radon example, I would like to consider multiple uranium measurements, measured both at basement and ground floor levels of houses. I would like to explore whether some counties are showing unusually high or low radon levels, corrected for county-level uranium levels (and by taking into account variability in uranium levels between the basement and ground floor). Houses are not matched, i.e. we have uranium measurements of some houses within a county (basement and ground floor), and we have radon measurements of other houses within the same county (basement and ground floor). I am unsure how to model this within a hierarchical model.
Every time I feel I'm beginning to understand the big picture, I seem to be taking two steps back when faced with a new question. Any insight and explanation would be greatly appreciated!

Maurits

You can definitely have multiple radon measurements in a house; then you just need to include varying intercepts for houses, also you'll need coefs for whether the measurement is in basement or 1st floor. A lot of it's in there, but can be translated better

>

> On Monday, November 7, 2016 at 3:08:37 PM UTC+1, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Hi Juan,
>
> On Mon, Nov 7, 2016 at 8:03 AM, Juan <juan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello.
>
> Is it better to use a bidimensional array of reals or a matrix?
> (Speed, memory, safety or any other interesting related issue).
>
> Speed: it'll depend on your case. Often an array of vectors could be the fastest thing to do. The deep reason is that it has to do with memory locality.
> Memory: matrix. There's just slightly less overhead using the matrix variable type over arrays of arrays. But it shouldn't be much.
> Saftey: both are equally safe
>
> The real key to the difference is the usability. When you need to do linear algebra, use matrix, vector, row_vector. These have shapes and sizes and operations are well defined. Treat arrays as collections. What does it mean to multiply a bidirectional array with another? That doesn't really have meaning. (And if you can come up with some sort of "natural" thing, I'm sure someone thinks something else is "natural" for that same operation.)
>
>
> And another question, why is not possible to assign an array to a matrix or viceversa?
>
> That's easy: an array is not a matrix and a matrix is not an array.
>
> There should be enough conversion functions in the library for this to be easy. See to_array(), etc. If there's something obvious that's missing, please let us know.
>

Hi Andrew.

Again, thanks for your quick response. I feel that we’re missing each other’s point. I am actually a nuclear physicist, so nuclear radiation measurements are something that I am very familiar with.

However, I may have been mis-using your radon example to explore a different model (and question). For the sake of the model’s theme, let’s assume that we have Polonium measurements (ignoring the uranium measurements entirely). Radon alpha-decays to polonium, and we have managed to measure the cumulative radiation of all polonium isotopes in different houses, at basement and ground floor levels, and in different counties.

My question is: How to model a floor-dependent effect of polonium radiation, whilst controlling for floor-dependent radon radiation; based on different per-house measurements, in different counties.

Here, j denote the county indices.

I am not sure how to model this in rstan. The first two lines essentially correspond to two independent linear models. So one could estimate intercepts and slopes separately in two independent stan models, and then estimate coefficients c,d,e,f? In which case we wouldn't really propagate county- and individual measurement-based uncertainties across the two models within a Bayesian framework, or would we?

Maurits

On Tuesday, November 8, 2016 at 9:13:26 AM UTC-5, Dupond Hughes wrote:
> The model fits pretty much OK except for ~200 divergent iterations

That is not OK. We've got to get that fixed before your other questions become relevant.

I would suggest starting with non-centered reparameterizations (also known as the Matt trick) where the lower-level coefficients are declared and defined in the transformed parameters block with something like

for (j in 1:J)
  beta[j] = Beta + sigma_species .* beta_raw[j];

which entails declaring things as vectors rather than real arrays and making beta_raw an array of vectors. If each element of beta_raw has a standard normal prior, then your prior beliefs about beta[j] are normal with mean Beta and standard deviations sigma_species.

Ben

You need a model for the missingness.  See the chapter on missing data
in the Stan manual.  In a typical Bayesian setting, you create a joint
model p(y, x, beta) and then turn the usual Bayesian crank to draw
from p(x | y, beta) just as you would draw from p(beta | x, y).
That is, declare y and beta as data and x as a parameter, code the
joint density in Stan and push the button.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Varying-intercept & varying-slope model in rstan
messages.body_plain:
If you write a joint model p(theta, phi, x, y) with
two sets of parameters theta and phi that factor as

  p(theta , phi | x, y) = p(theta | x, y) * p(phi | x, y)

then you'll get the same result fitting them together
as separately.  If they have overlapping parameters, on
the other hand, or one's conditional on the other, then the
info will flow both ways.  Your example does not look like
it'll factor because the a^polonium_j depends on a^radon_j.

I'd suggest generating fake data and fitting it to your
model to see if it beheaves as you expect.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Assuming the parameters make sense physically, it makes
sense statistically and should work the way you expect it to.
As long as you think generatively like this, building observed
and derived quantities bottom up from priors, you're in good
shape with Bayesian modeling.  The priors can be uniform if
the posteriors are proper, but we recommend at least weakly informative
priors defining the expected order/scale of the answer.

Yes, you can code it in Stan directly as written with loops
or you can do it more efficiently with vectorization.  Basically,
as long as you can write down a differentiable density (using
arithmetic and the functions we support), you can code it in Stan.

- Bob

You need to constrain your parameters to be positive
when they are declared---just applying lognormal won't
make everything behave properly (it'll just cause rejections
and the kinds of messages you see, which can lead to either
bias or just slow sampling).

On Wednesday, November 9, 2016 at 8:40:37 PM UTC-5, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> Is this expected behaviour?

Yes. If X * v = lambda * v, you can let w = -v and X * w = lambda * w. If necessary, one way to proceed is to multiply the j-th eigenvector by -1 iff V[1,j] < 0.

Ben

On Thursday, 10 November 2016 12:21:10 UTC+11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Assuming the parameters make sense physically, it makes
> sense statistically and should work the way you expect it to.
> As long as you think generatively like this, building observed
> and derived quantities bottom up from priors, you're in good
> shape with Bayesian modeling.  The priors can be uniform if
> the posteriors are proper, but we recommend at least weakly informative
> priors defining the expected order/scale of the answer.
>
> Yes, you can code it in Stan directly as written with loops
> or you can do it more efficiently with vectorization.  Basically,
> as long as you can write down a differentiable density (using
> arithmetic and the functions we support), you can code it in Stan.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reference. I just checked it. The paper has similar justification as other AIC weight references, ie
1) Bayes factor is ratio of marginal likelihoods
2) marginal likelihood can be approximated with BIC which has a form -2 log(L)+q (with q=p log(n))
3) AIC has a form -2 log(L) + q (with q=2p), and thus it is plausible to use AIC weights

I don't think this analogy between BIC and AIC is a sufficient theoretical justification.
The same problem holds for LOO weights. I haven't seen theoretical justification for replacing BMA with LOO weighting
(replacing Bayes factors with pseudo Bayes factors). LOO weighting may work, but it hasn't been studied sufficiently (even empirically).

Aki

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the confusion, trying to simplify my model as example was not the best idea.

#1 Let's take stan manual example for linear regression (alpha = 0, beta_1 and beta_2)

--------------------------------
data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] x_1;
vector[N] x_2;
vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
real beta_1;
real beta_2;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
y ~ normal(beta_1 * x_1 + beta_2 * x_2, sigma);
}
--------------------------------

#2 let's suppose I have many beta as data and one x as parameter. The model becomes

--------------------------------
data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] beta_1;
vector[N] beta_2;
vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
real x_1;
real x_2;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
y ~ normal(beta_1 * x_1 + beta_2 * x_2, sigma);
}
--------------------------------

#3 Now, let's suppose I don't want just the real x, but I want x_mean and x_sd. How do I do it?

--------------------------------
data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] beta_1;
vector[N] beta_2;
vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
real x_1_mean;
real x_2_mean;
real x_1_sd;
real x_2_sd;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
y ~ normal(beta_1 * ??? + beta_2 * ???, sigma);
}
--------------------------------

I hope this proof of principle is a bit clearer.

Thanks!
Stefano Mangiola

The problem is how to define such a program!
What we want is a parameter or transformed parameter

  vector[N] theta;

satisfying the following three constraints:

1.  SUM_{n in 1:N} theta[n] == 0

2.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n * theta[n] == 0

3.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n^2 * theta[n] == 0

I don't know how to do that or even if it's possible.  For
any one of the constraints, you let theta[1:(N-1)] be
free and set theta[N] accordingly.  I don't know how to
satisfy all three simultaneously or how you'd do the
Jacobian.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You can’t do a Jacobian because the transformation
isn’t an isomorphism (you’re trying to map the plane
into a sphere, which always leaves some points
messed up).  Alternatively, if you try to calculate a
Jacobian you’ll see that you end up with an infinite
number of terms that contribute.

Geometrically, this is trying to find the intersections
of multiple spheres with varying radii along the
principle directions.  As Bob notes, this might not
even be possible (but maybe at theta[1] = 1,
theta[\1] = 0?), and even if it were you’d end up
with a disjoint space.

But this also smells of a bad, non-generative model
that we probably don’t want to be messing with
anyways.  Like some optimization problem that’s
trying to be forced into an ill-posed probabilistic
problem, or some “measurements” that are assumed
to be infinitely informative.

Liang, if you can write out the constraint for a1, then a2 as a function of a1, etc. then it's straightforward.

> On Nov 11, 2016, at 2:42 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> You can’t do a Jacobian because the transformation
> isn’t an isomorphism (you’re trying to map the plane
> into a sphere, which always leaves some points
> messed up).  Alternatively, if you try to calculate a
> Jacobian you’ll see that you end up with an infinite
> number of terms that contribute.
>
> Geometrically, this is trying to find the intersections
> of multiple spheres with varying radii along the
> principle directions.  As Bob notes, this might not
> even be possible (but maybe at theta[1] = 1,
> theta[\1] = 0?), and even if it were you’d end up
> with a disjoint space.
>
> But this also smells of a bad, non-generative model
> that we probably don’t want to be messing with
> anyways.  Like some optimization problem that’s
> trying to be forced into an ill-posed probabilistic
> problem, or some “measurements” that are assumed
> to be infinitely informative.
>
>> On Nov 11, 2016, at 11:33 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> The problem is how to define such a program!
>> What we want is a parameter or transformed parameter
>>
>> vector[N] theta;
>>
>> satisfying the following three constraints:
>>
>> 1.  SUM_{n in 1:N} theta[n] == 0
>>
>> 2.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n * theta[n] == 0
>>
>> 3.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n^2 * theta[n] == 0
>>
>> I don't know how to do that or even if it's possible.  For
>> any one of the constraints, you let theta[1:(N-1)] be
>> free and set theta[N] accordingly.  I don't know how to
>> satisfy all three simultaneously or how you'd do the
>> Jacobian.
>>
>> - Bob
>>

>>>
>>> Thanks a million

On Friday, November 11, 2016 at 2:33:40 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The problem is how to define such a program!
> What we want is a parameter or transformed parameter
>
>   vector[N] theta;
>
> satisfying the following three constraints:
>
> 1.  SUM_{n in 1:N} theta[n] == 0
>
> 2.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n * theta[n] == 0
>
> 3.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n^2 * theta[n] == 0
>
> I don't know how to do that or even if it's possible.  For
> any one of the constraints, you let theta[1:(N-1)] be
> free and set theta[N] accordingly.  I don't know how to
> satisfy all three simultaneously or how you'd do the
> Jacobian.

If you declare in parameters

vector[N - 3] theta_free;

and then in in transformed parameters you start with

vector[N] theta;
theta[1:(N - 3)] = theta_free;

and then you have three equations that along with theta_free pin down the three remaining elements of theta.

Ben

Sorry for being dense here, but I'm still not sure I get it.

Is the generative process:

1.  draw parameters for components theta[1], theta[2], and theta[3]

2.  for data points n in 1:N

    a.  draw a simplex phi[n] from ???

    b.  draw from each component
           z[n, 1] ~ foo(theta[1])
           ...
           z[n, 3] ~ foo(theta[3])

    c.  set y[n] = sum(z[n, 1:3] .* phi[n])

In that last case, it's an elementwise product.

And then the inference problem is:

Given observations of phi[1:N] and y[1:N], estimate theta[1:3]?

In other words, it's not a traditional mixture, but rather
we're only observing the sum of three variables, each of which
has a distribution?  And did I get the way to produce y right?

theta1 drawn from ~ lognormal(mu1, sigma1)
  theta2 drawn from ~ lognormal(mu2, sigma2)
  theta3 drawn from ~ lognormal(mu3, sigma3)

  y[n] = (theta1 * phi[n,1]) + (theta2 * phi[n,2]) + (theta3 * phi[n,3])

If y and phi are both known, then it gets tricky.  You
only have two degrees of freedom, and given that the theta
are positive (they're lognormal), you have

  0  <  theta[n, 1] * phi[n, 1]  <  y[n]

and then

  0  < theta[n, 2] * phi[n, 2] < y[n] - theta[n, 1] * phi[n, 1]

and then

 theta3[n] = y[n] - (theta1[n] * phi[n, 1]) + (theta2[n] * phi[n, 2]);

You have to do those two constraints custom, define theta3 as
a transformed parameter, and then do the Jacobian adjustments.

Possible, but a pain to code.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Suggestion for manual
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I just thought I'd make a quick suggestion for the manual. One thing I really like about R's docs about the various distributions is that it includes the expected mean and variance of the distributions in terms of the parameters.

For the distributions where such a thing would make sense, would it be too much work to add the E(X) and Var(X) for each univariate distribution given the parameters in terms of Stan's parameterizations? This would be especially useful for, e.g., skew normal, gamma, beta.
Currently, I either keep an R manpage open for the distribution (where applicable) or the wiki page for the distribution up, or I even plot the distributions in R using manipulate/shiny with curve(d[distributionName](x,parameters,...), ...) to better grok the priors.

Hey all,

Yet another post by me. I thought I posted this last night but I don't think it actually sent.

I have a model that makes pretty extensive use of logistic (and multinomial/softmax logistic) regression, or parameterization in terms of log-odds that is transformed to probabilities. I've tried my best to use stan functions that are more efficient (e.g., log_inv_logit(pi_logit[n]) for cluster membership probabilities), but I'm curious whether the Stan developers would recommend using probit as opposed to logit? Is one more efficient than the other? I know Phi_approx() was created as an efficient probit function for this sort of thing. Reparameterizing in terms of probits would be a hefty task, so before I tried it out, I was just curious what the Stan devs (or other users) think about the efficiency of Phi() vs inv_logit link functions.

Thanks,
--Stephen

Hi,

I have a three-level, non-nested hierarchical model that I am interested in performing variable selection for. If I include interaction terms in my model, which I would like to do, the number of covariates becomes rather large, so I would like to find a  good way to perform selection. My only goal of this model is prediction, so there is no great need for simplicity, but I don't want to include everything for fear of overfitting.

I am aware of the Laplace, Horseshoe, and Projective Predictive technique put forth by Vehtari, et al; I just wanted to check if there are any other ideas out there since most of the posts on variable selection are several years old at this point.

This group has been a very valuable resource that I have referenced many times in the past. Thank you to everyone who contributes to this group, you have been extremely helpful!

bart

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Logit or Probit recommendation?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Logit or Probit recommendation?
messages.body_plain:
There's a discussion in the Gelman and Hill regression book and
the conclusion is that it's primarily a matter of convenience.
The primary difference is in the scale.

With Stan, the inv_logit() function is much more efficient than
Phi and also more robust to outliers.  The Phi_approx() function
is close to Phi() and more efficient.

The logistic distribution is easy to understand as a log-odds (logit)
transofrm of a uniform(0, 1) variable.

In some Gibbs applications, it was easier to do probit because
the conjugate structure of the latent normal structure could be
exploited to simplify some computations (at least I'm pretty sure
that's why Probit is so popular).

- Bob

There is no need to experiment when you can read the documentation. Phi_approx(x) is no faster because it simply calls inv_logit(0.07056 * x ^ 3 + 1.5976 * x) but is only slightly slower because it only has to evaluate that polynomial.

Ben

messages.subject: Number of latent factors in Exploratory Factor Analysis
messages.subject_clean: Number of latent factors in Exploratory Factor Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan folk,

Just thought I'd check my intuition against the crowd on this one. I have multivariate data and I'm doing exploratory factor analysis where I don't have strong theory guiding the number of latent factors, nor on which items said factors are expected to load. As I understand it, there are two ways to approach this:

1) for each choice of N (number of latent factors, up to a reasonable value for N, like 10, and N being less than the dimensionality of the outcome multivariate), code a model implementing that number of factors, sample against the data, and compare the resulting posterior samples using LOO to choose which choice of N fits best.

2) combine all the above models in a single mixture model that would then yield posterior samples for the mixing proportion of each choice of N.

I tend to prefer (2) as I'm more a fan of parameter estimation over model comparison these days, but anyone have any other thoughts?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

The data enters through the likelihood. Some background: In the model all consumers get individual level coefficients from population level distributions and make purchasing decisions. Likelihood for the quantity bought is somewhat complex but depends on things like prices and individual level coefficients.

The likelihood is basically gumbel_pdf(Va/sigmaeps) for quantities that were purchased and gumbel_cdf(Va/sigmaeps) for quantites that were not purchased, where Va is an expression that depends on data and individual level coefficients. In addition, there is the Jacobian.

I will double check everything but as it currently is, data should be playing a role.

messages.body_plain:
You can also do an approximate Dirichlet process, coding a
larger N with an appropriately near-zero Dirichlet prior.

If you only have N choices, then the mixture might run.  It's
one of those nifty mixture of mixtures models.  Making a mixture
model's another way to do model comparison.  You may find the overall
mixture model itself may work better than any of its components.

- Bob

> On Nov 14, 2016, at 11:13 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Stan folk,
>
> Just thought I'd check my intuition against the crowd on this one. I have multivariate data and I'm doing exploratory factor analysis where I don't have strong theory guiding the number of latent factors, nor on which items said factors are expected to load. As I understand it, there are two ways to approach this:
>
> 1) for each choice of N (number of latent factors, up to a reasonable value for N, like 10, and N being less than the dimensionality of the outcome multivariate), code a model implementing that number of factors, sample against the data, and compare the resulting posterior samples using LOO to choose which choice of N fits best.
>
> 2) combine all the above models in a single mixture model that would then yield posterior samples for the mixing proportion of each choice of N.
>
> I tend to prefer (2) as I'm more a fan of parameter estimation over model comparison these days, but anyone have any other thoughts?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] linear regression: infer points (mean, sd) instead of slopes
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] linear regression: infer points (mean, sd) instead of slopes
messages.body_plain:
Why do you want mean(theta) and sd(theta)?  If they come from
a hierarchical normal prior, why not use its mean and standard deviation?

If you really just want those quantities, Stan has functions mean(theta)
and sd(theta) for sample means and standard deviations.  So you can define
those as transformed parameters or generated quantities.  But I wouldn't
try to put a distribution on them as it will no longer be a clean generative
model.  And if you do insist on putting a distribution on them, then you
need to take care of the Jacobian adjustment manually by incrementing the
target log density.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Logit or Probit recommendation?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Logit or Probit recommendation?
messages.body_plain:
In decreasing order of speed:

  1.  y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha);

  2.  y ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(alpha));

  3.  y ~ bernoulli(Phi_approx(alpha));

The speed comes because

  1 >> 2:  build simpler expression graph and thus quicker chain rule
           propagation for autodiff

  2 >> 3:  inv_logit() is faster than Phi_approx()

We could build a

  4.  y ~ bernoulli_probit(alpha);

which would be faster than option 3 but slower than option 1.

- Bob

> On Nov 14, 2016, at 4:44 PM, bart <bart.bl...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Just wanted to make sure I completely understood your comment (sorry, I'm a little new to this). By hierarchical priors, are you referring to regularizers like the laplace prior and the horseshoe prior? I've implement both, and now am thinking of averaging my predictions from both of those as well as the unregularized model. Does this make sense?

You can do that, but what you normally want to do in Bayesian modeling
is think about the generative process. Is the generative process a mixture
where some observations come from one model and one from the other for some
reason?

What kind of prior to use should depend on your data.  What do you
know about the coefficients before you start?

And I mean a hierarchical model.  You might want to check out this
simple case study if you aren't familiar with hierarchical models
or Bayesian modeling in general, there are two case studies that
should help:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html

  * A Primer on Bayesian Multilevel Modeling using PyStan

  * Pooling with Hierarchical Models for Repeated Binary Trials

- Bob

messages.subject: New paper on HMC principles and Stan vs. JAGS
messages.subject_clean: New paper on HMC principles and Stan vs. JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

FYI I have a commentary paper out (here <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12681/full>) that is geared towards ecologists accustomed to JAGS but wanting to move to Stan. I explain the principles of HMC/NUTS using simple language, illustrative examples, and minimal mathematics. I hope it will make a good primer for a lot of applied folks in other fields who want to make the jump but are confused by the HMC terminology (divergences, tree depths, etc.) and intimidated by the Stan user manual. I also do some efficiency comparisons for some difficult models in population ecology, and Stan was consistently faster.

The Stan team may be particularly interested in Fig. 1 which shows citation patterns for the BUGS family and Stan. It seems pretty clear Stan will dominate within a few years. Recreating something like Fig. 3 in the manual may also be a good idea to help introduce some of the concepts that are talked about mathematically.

Below is the BibTex citation.

Thanks to the dev team and community for all the help along the way.

Cheers,
Cole

messages.subject: Hierarchical spatial model specification advice
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical spatial model specification advice
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

First, I should apologize for my ignorance. I have workable understanding of general bayesian approaches (glm and hierarchical models), but I am totally new to spatial modeling. I am also new to stan.

I am trying to figure out the best approach for modeling a specific problem and I can't let go of the idea of modeling the entire problem simultaneously. I am hoping someone might be able to tell me whether stan is a suitable framework for this model, and if stan is not, perhaps an alternative could be nominated. I would also very eagerly welcome any feedback on the model I have in mind.

My dependent variable is aggravated assault rates at the county level, so I will be using a negative binomial model. I am interested in investigating the association between county-level attitude measures. However, the attitude data is at the individual level and it is terribly distributed. Some counties have very low coverage, responses are clustered in urban areas, etc. I also would like to include a few measures that occur only at the state level.

Ideally (I think), I would like to estimate county-level means for my attitude variables within the same model that regresses assault rates on them. My thinking is that this will preserve the uncertainty that will necessarily be associated with the attitude estimates.

This means that I have individuals, nested in counties, nested in states. And, if I'm really honest, I'd also like to avoid collapsing items in my attitude measurements, so I would like to add an item level to the attitude measurements (i.e. I have three indicators for each dimension). So, this already seems like a pretty scary model, given that I have about 170,000 cases for the attitude measurements and about 3000 counties. On top of all of this, I need to control for spatial auto-correlation.

The other option would be to estimate a separate model for the attitude measures and then propagate estimates from this model to the aggravated assault model. I am concerned, though, about just using point estimates for the attitude measures; so I wonder what approach could be used to ensure that the uncertainty of these measures is also included in the model.

I should note that I read the tutorial on exact sparse CAR models in Stan. I am just unsure about how feasible it is to scale this up to the model I'm describing (remember, I'm ignorant). I've also been looking into R -INLA and, of course, I've come across WinBugs.

Ultimately, the issue I am running into is that I can't find examples of models similar to the one I want to estimate. I don't know if that is just a coincidence, if it is because it is not feasible, or if it is because there is a much better way to go about constructing the model.

Any and all thoughts would be welcome!

Best,
Joe Hoover

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for dredging this up, but I had been thinking about PCA recently.

I don't see the code above as performing any dimension reduction. It looks like just fitting a multivariate normal distribution, rather than PCA.

There was an earlier thread that looked at a probabilistic PCA approach last year. https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/DYofzSAz1sk/iBlTEWcgGn8J

There were several suggestions to improve performance, though the OP did not post a followup whether they were successful. It would be interesting to see if their suggestions work. I was a little confused at how to integrate out the factors. For instance, most of the PPCA papers have the covariance matrix as something like WW'+I*sigma^2. Wouldn't the determinant of the covariance matrix be zero? The log determinant would then go to infinity, no?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical spatial model specification advice
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical spatial model specification advice
messages.body_plain:
We code up hierarchical models for this kind of data all the time.
The key question is how you code correlations---you can do it
with either random effects for counties, groupings of counties, or
you can literally try to do it via spatial proximity using something
like a Gaussian process (I'm not up on all the variants like CAR
and ICAR and what not).  You might want to look at something like
the radon case study:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/radon.html

I'd suggest you start with simpler models and work up to a bigger
model a piece at a time.

- Bob

> On Nov 16, 2016, at 3:35 AM, Joe Hoover <joeho...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> First, I should apologize for my ignorance. I have workable understanding of general bayesian approaches (glm and hierarchical models), but I am totally new to spatial modeling. I am also new to stan.
>
> I am trying to figure out the best approach for modeling a specific problem and I can't let go of the idea of modeling the entire problem simultaneously. I am hoping someone might be able to tell me whether stan is a suitable framework for this model, and if stan is not, perhaps an alternative could be nominated. I would also very eagerly welcome any feedback on the model I have in mind.
>
> My dependent variable is aggravated assault rates at the county level, so I will be using a negative binomial model. I am interested in investigating the association between county-level attitude measures. However, the attitude data is at the individual level and it is terribly distributed. Some counties have very low coverage, responses are clustered in urban areas, etc. I also would like to include a few measures that occur only at the state level.
>
> Ideally (I think), I would like to estimate county-level means for my attitude variables within the same model that regresses assault rates on them. My thinking is that this will preserve the uncertainty that will necessarily be associated with the attitude estimates.
>
> This means that I have individuals, nested in counties, nested in states. And, if I'm really honest, I'd also like to avoid collapsing items in my attitude measurements, so I would like to add an item level to the attitude measurements (i.e. I have three indicators for each dimension). So, this already seems like a pretty scary model, given that I have about 170,000 cases for the attitude measurements and about 3000 counties. On top of all of this, I need to control for spatial auto-correlation.
>
> The other option would be to estimate a separate model for the attitude measures and then propagate estimates from this model to the aggravated assault model. I am concerned, though, about just using point estimates for the attitude measures; so I wonder what approach could be used to ensure that the uncertainty of these measures is also included in the model.
>
> I should note that I read the tutorial on exact sparse CAR models in Stan. I am just unsure about how feasible it is to scale this up to the model I'm describing (remember, I'm ignorant). I've also been looking into R -INLA and, of course, I've come across WinBugs.
>
> Ultimately, the issue I am running into is that I can't find examples of models similar to the one I want to estimate. I don't know if that is just a coincidence, if it is because it is not feasible, or if it is because there is a much better way to go about constructing the model.
>
> Any and all thoughts would be welcome!
>
> Best,

ODEs aren't any different than other parts of Stan for
missing data.

The first thing to do is think about what the model would look
like if you had all the data.  Then you take the missing data and
declare it as parameters.  It's a strategy that's outlined in
the missing data chapter of the manual and will work for any
Bayesian application.

If you give us some more specifics of your problem, we might be
able to provide more concrete advice---I didn't know what to make
of two lines of data with some missing elements---where does it

> >

On Sunday, April 12, 2015 at 4:54:02 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> What Betancourt said.
>
> > On Apr 12, 2015, at 6:21 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Markov Chain Monte Carlo 101:
> >
> > In general we contract a Markov chain that generates
> > a series of states, x_{n}, such that as the number of
> > states, N, goes to infinity,
> >
> > lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} 1/N \sum_{n = 0}^{N} f(x_{n})
> > = \int dx p(x) f(x),
> >
> > where p(x) is our posterior distribution and f(x) is any
> > sufficiently nice function.
> >
> > In practice we’re not interested in the N \rightarrow \infty
> > limit because we’ll never get there — we want to know
> > what happens for finite N.  Assuming that the Markov
> > chain and the posterior distribution play nicely with
> > each other (a property called geometry ergodicity)
> > then we have for some large enough but still finite N,
> >
> > 1/N \sum_{n = 0}^{N} f(x_{n}) ~ normal( \int dx p(x) f(x), Var[f] / N).
> >
> > In words, the Markov chain Monte Carlo estimator,
> > 1/N \sum_{n = 0}^{N} f(x_{n}), is distributed around the
> > true expectation,  \int dx p(x) f(x), with a variance that
> > shrinks with the number of samples generated.  We
> > say that the Markov chain Monte Carlo estimator
> > _converges in distribution_ towards the true value.
> >
> > But we can actually do better — although we have the
> > above property for a Markov chain started at _any_ initial
> > point, those chains started at points far off in the tails
> > away from the posterior mass will take a while to reach
> > the posterior mass.  Those initial samples bias Markov
> > chain Monte Carlo estimators away from their true values
> > and we need a pretty large N in order for the rest of
> > the samples to wash out that initial bias and recover
> > the convergence above.  But if we simply remove those
> > initial samples than we can dramatically improve the
> > precision of our Markov chain Monte Carlo estimator.
> >
> > Warmup is just the discarding of these initial samples
> > to yield better estimators.  It’s not necessary, but it
> > means that we can get better estimators in fewer
> > samples.  Why call it warmup and not burn in?  Well
> > burn in has a certain connotation to it — when you
> > burn a product in you stress test it, throwing away
> > items that fail and keep the ones that work.  Running
> > a bunch of Markov chains and then throwing the
> > ones that fail (get stuck, behave weird, etc) is very,
> > very bad (with Markov chains, if one chain fails then
> > they’ve all failed).  Warmup is more evocative of
> > what’s really going on, which is an equilibration process.
> >
> > Finally, what’s all this adaptation business about?
> > The above results all hold for a Markov chain that is
> > constant — if you start modifying the Markov chain
> > _while_ generating samples then you lose all of the
> > precious convergence results.  There are ways of
> > very carefully modifying Markov chains while maintaining
> > some results, but they are fragile and hard to implement
> > and you only get N \rightarrow \infty results, not finite
> > N results.  Because we discard warmup iterations,
> > however, we can screw with the Markov chain in that
> > stage without compromising the validity of the samples
> > that we keep.
> >

messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: Multiple 'chains' when optimizing?
messages.body_plain:
Would it be possible to allow several parallel optimizing runs, similar to how stan() can have multiple chains?

Some of my models can be multimodal, but it would be nice to, e.g., run 80 optimizing() all with different inits in parallel (4 at a time, for example) then look at the optimal points of each one.
I know I could do this manually using the parallel package, but having built-in support for optimizing(..., chains=4, iter=80) would be nice (even if they aren't actually 'chains' at all), where iter refers to number of desired optimizing() runs to make (*not* max.iters for each run) and chins refers to the number in parallel to run.

I know it's not exactly a goal of Stan, but some other programs offer the ability to run multiple optimizers on a model at once to either find multiple modes or to find the mode with the 'best' value (highest log posterior, in Stan's case).

But each factor is only on 3 items. There is no permutation of the factors. Because the variance is fixed to 1, there shouldn't be swapping of the factor loadings either for the three indicators either. A factor with variance 1 having a positive .3 loading is not the same as it having a positive .5 loading on the same item. This should be an identified model. The factors aren't arbitrary (because they have unique sets of indicators), and with a variance of 1 each, the factor loadings should be identified. I don't see how those loadings would be permuted. If those three factors all loaded on the same set of items then I see your point, but these three factors are separate and defined by unique sets of items.

messages.subject_clean: Difference between monitor means and get_posterior_mean?
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I am trying to make an R package that uses Stan as the backend (first package I've ever made, so hopefully the code isn't miserable).

Anyway, I noticed that when I get means for a parameter using, e.g.,:
monitor(extract(bDifOut,pars='parameterName',permuted=FALSE)[,1,,drop=FALSE])[,1], I get a different estimate than when I use get_posterior_mean(bDifOut, pars='parameterName') and look at chain 1's mean.

What's up with that?

Example output:

> monitor(extract(bDifOut,pars='pi_sigma',permuted=FALSE)[,1,,drop=FALSE],print=TRUE,digits=3) #monitor(chain1)
Inference for the input samples (1 chains: each with iter=500; warmup=250):

          mean se_mean    sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff  Rhat
pi_sigma 0.667   0.065 0.487 0.043 0.271 0.597 0.917 1.905    57 0.999

For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
convergence, Rhat=1).
> get_posterior_mean(bDifOut,pars='pi_sigma')
         mean-chain:1 mean-chain:2 mean-chain:3 mean-chain:4 mean-all chains
pi_sigma    0.7357284    0.6942247    0.6349823    0.7632244         0.70704

messages.subject: Re: Difference between monitor means and get_posterior_mean?
messages.subject_clean: Difference between monitor means and get_posterior_mean?
messages.body_plain:
Sorry, but it's necessary for some problems. In mixture models, there can be arbitrary between-chain label switching. You can tell it's arbitrary visibly in the trace plot. For cases like that, you *do* want to examine similar chains for your inference. It's not ideal, but it most certainly is the correct decision to make. Some parameters are invariant to the swapped labels, but many aren't, and for those that aren't invariant, examining similar chains will yield the correct inference.

This is theoretically the correct thing to do, too. The identical, but swapped modes do indeed exist (so of course, Stan is correct), but one's decision is not 'what is the expected value assuming that the labels will swap in my population', but 'taking one of the arbitrary labelling solutions, what should my inference be?'.

Other times, there can be authentic multimodality, or true multiple solutions, and the inferences *would* depend on which mode you picked, so to speak. Even in this case, you may want to pick apart the separate modes to better understand why so much density is in separate regions.
E.g., I have a model that predicts latent group membership from demographic data, these groups which differ in how certain items correlate to a latent ability estimate (literally, it's latent group DIF detection for 2PL models and others). Usually there are only label-swapped modes, and your inferences are essentially the same no matter the mode. However, sometimes the predictors can produce true multimodality, such that one predictor separates people into two groups that implicates set A of items to be DIF, and another mode finds that a second predictor separates people into two other groups that implicate set B to be DIF. It is useful to examine both of these modes as well as the full posterior, because it's not arbitrarily multimodal and the posterior is actually expressing real uncertainty about the generative model.

Making per-chain summaries harder to come by on principle doesn't discourage people from doing it, it just makes using Stan unnecessarily more difficult. Put up a big warning when people select chains about the potential issues with non-convergence and be done with it. Otherwise, trust that the user is picking apart chains for a justifiable or at *least* a diagnostic reason.

messages.body_plain:
This is a common misunderstanding.  When properly implementing full Bayes,
all of the chains would explore all of the modes in the right proportions and
they would indeed look the same.  ANY application of a Markov chain where
multiple chains behave differently, however, is formally not a “correct thing to
do” theoretically as it will necessarily be only an approximation to full Bayes.

For example, if you can’t isolate a unique labeling in the model specification
then you can’t guarantee that you can identify different labelings with different
chains.  Eventually some chains will transition between modes and you’ll be
left with a convolution of multiple labels that can’t be separated out so easily,
if at all.

This is even more important when the multi modality is not from a labeling
degeneracy.  In that case the modes will have different weights, but having
different chains explore different modes will tell you _nothing_ about what
those weights should be so you have no way of combining the individual
chains in a well-posed manner.

I have been studying Markov chains intensely for the past four years and
I still don’t really trust myself to pull off an approximate multimodal analysis
like this (the more you learn, the more you see what can go wrong).  I think
it’s fair not to expect most users to be able to pull it off, either.  Many of our
design choices have been motivated to facilitate good practices and
frustrate bad practices.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Difference between monitor means and get_posterior_mean?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Difference between monitor means and get_posterior_mean?
messages.body_plain:
I agree with everything you say, of course, and you know far more about markov chains than I do.

Until there is a better method to handle multimodality in mixture models though, basing one's inference on the full posterior (even *if* all chains explored all modes) would be pointless.
On the other hand, if there *is* true multimodality that would change one's decisions/inference, having all chains explore all modes in correct proportion would help you understand the probability of solutions; the expected value would be difficult, but examining the posteriors could still tell you something about the probability of certain generative models.

Currently, we don't have that, and the best we can do is to examine the multiple modes separately. They still tell you something about the solution, but nothing about the relative probability of each. Not sure if lp__ would be useful there though (2 chains hit one mode, 2 hit another, but the latter two have a greater lp__, so perhaps that is the 'more probable' solution? I'm not sure how useful that metric would be).

The good thing is that the model I'm implementing is really more an exploratory procedure. It finds combinations of items that latent groups seem to operate differently on, so it detects biased items among latent groups. Sometimes it can find two modal solutions and one doesn't necessarily need to pick one or the other, but to just see 1) which items seem to be detected for that mode and 2) what are the characteristics of that mode's latent groups?
For that purpose, I think it's fair to pick apart the modes. One may decide which solution is more *important* (say, if 12 items are detected as biased when male and female seem to be the latent groups, and the error in the latent assignment seems low, it may be more important than if 4 items are detected as biased when age seems to divide individuals into latent groups, but the assignment is error-prone).

Thoughts on this? Yes, it's not using the full marginal posterior, but it still seems to lead one to make the 'correct' decisions in the context of my model (verifiably so, because I'm generating the data).

Also, are there any plans for improving mixture modeling in Bayes, such that this multimodality isn't so much an issue? I know this is a relatively unsolved problem, even in ML estimation (EM has the same multiple-solution problem).

On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:58:10 AM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> This is a common misunderstanding.  When properly implementing full Bayes,
> all of the chains would explore all of the modes in the right proportions and
> they would indeed look the same.  ANY application of a Markov chain where
> multiple chains behave differently, however, is formally not a “correct thing to
> do” theoretically as it will necessarily be only an approximation to full Bayes.
>
> For example, if you can’t isolate a unique labeling in the model specification
> then you can’t guarantee that you can identify different labelings with different
> chains.  Eventually some chains will transition between modes and you’ll be
> left with a convolution of multiple labels that can’t be separated out so easily,
> if at all.
>
> This is even more important when the multi modality is not from a labeling
> degeneracy.  In that case the modes will have different weights, but having
> different chains explore different modes will tell you _nothing_ about what
> those weights should be so you have no way of combining the individual
> chains in a well-posed manner.
>
> I have been studying Markov chains intensely for the past four years and
> I still don’t really trust myself to pull off an approximate multimodal analysis
> like this (the more you learn, the more you see what can go wrong).  I think
> it’s fair not to expect most users to be able to pull it off, either.  Many of our
> design choices have been motivated to facilitate good practices and
> frustrate bad practices.
>
> On Nov 17, 2016, at 10:06 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Sorry, but it's necessary for some problems. In mixture models, there can be arbitrary between-chain label switching. You can tell it's arbitrary visibly in the trace plot. For cases like that, you *do* want to examine similar chains for your inference. It's not ideal, but it most certainly is the correct decision to make. Some parameters are invariant to the swapped labels, but many aren't, and for those that aren't invariant, examining similar chains will yield the correct inference.
> >
> > This is theoretically the correct thing to do, too. The identical, but swapped modes do indeed exist (so of course, Stan is correct), but one's decision is not 'what is the expected value assuming that the labels will swap in my population', but 'taking one of the arbitrary labelling solutions, what should my inference be?'.
> >
> > Other times, there can be authentic multimodality, or true multiple solutions, and the inferences *would* depend on which mode you picked, so to speak. Even in this case, you may want to pick apart the separate modes to better understand why so much density is in separate regions.
> > E.g., I have a model that predicts latent group membership from demographic data, these groups which differ in how certain items correlate to a latent ability estimate (literally, it's latent group DIF detection for 2PL models and others). Usually there are only label-swapped modes, and your inferences are essentially the same no matter the mode. However, sometimes the predictors can produce true multimodality, such that one predictor separates people into two groups that implicates set A of items to be DIF, and another mode finds that a second predictor separates people into two other groups that implicate set B to be DIF. It is useful to examine both of these modes as well as the full posterior, because it's not arbitrarily multimodal and the posterior is actually expressing real uncertainty about the generative model.
> >
> > Making per-chain summaries harder to come by on principle doesn't discourage people from doing it, it just makes using Stan unnecessarily more difficult. Put up a big warning when people select chains about the potential issues with non-convergence and be done with it. Otherwise, trust that the user is picking apart chains for a justifiable or at *least* a diagnostic reason.
> >
> > On Thursday, November 17, 2016 at 11:33:56 PM UTC-6, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > > On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:27:05 AM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
> > > > Really, I wish there were an easier way to get posterior summaries of one or multiple chains, by choice.
> > >
> > > We usually don't want people summarizing a subset of chains. Either all the chains have converged and it makes sense to summarize all of them or some of the chains haven't converged and it doesn't make sense to summarize any of them.
> > >
> >

> > To post to this group, send email to stan-...@googlegroups.com.

messages.body_plain:
Each iteration of an MCMC chain is dependent on the last iteration. This means that each *chain* cannot be parallelized (not sure what will happen if/when Stan implements multiple crawlers to find multimodality for each chain though).

This is unlike other monte carlo techniques, like bootstrapping, because each iteration is functionally independent on any other iteration. Markov chains are defined to have dependent sampling, so each iteration is dependent on the previous iteration to some degree.

If your code.rda file was originally derived from a code.stan file with <- as the assignment indicator and now it uses =, then there will be a hash mismatch. You just need to force a new code.rda file to be created once, by doing rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE) beforehand.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parallelization
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] parallelization
messages.body_plain:
Two things.

1.  In my experience, setting it to the number of physical
cores rather than "hyperthreaded" cores results in faster
code.

2.  While we can't literally parallelize chains because of
the Markov dependency, we can parallelize all the code to
compute the density and derivatives.  Often in big models that's
a big matrix operation or solutions to ODEs with random effects
so you need to run the solver a number of times proportional
to the data.  In general, if the density can be broken into
chunks where the partial derivatives can be computed, they can
be packed back together into an expression graph for which you
can do autodiff.  The autodiff itself, which is over 90% of
a Stan's program execution, can also be parallelized.

We're thinking about how to do all these things.  Stay tuned.
Most likely thing we'll get going next is Eigen matrix operations
with GPU (CUDA) and multithreading (OpenMP) support.  Sebastian
Weber's already done the latter successfully and it resulted
in the natural massive speedup---it's nearly embarassingly parallel
when most of the compute time is in the parallelizable operation.

- Bob

> On Nov 18, 2016, at 11:48 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Each iteration of an MCMC chain is dependent on the last iteration. This means that each *chain* cannot be parallelized (not sure what will happen if/when Stan implements multiple crawlers to find multimodality for each chain though).
>
> This is unlike other monte carlo techniques, like bootstrapping, because each iteration is functionally independent on any other iteration. Markov chains are defined to have dependent sampling, so each iteration is dependent on the previous iteration to some degree.
>
> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 9:25:09 AM UTC-6, Vishv Jeet wrote:
>
> You mean if I have access to a 64 cores machine I can massively parallelize STAN code even if I am using 4 chains?
>
>

> By the way, I suspect that while that machine has 4 physical cores, it can do 8 things in parallel thanks to hyperthreading. I'm not sure if parallel::detectCores() will return 4 or 8, but you could try 4, see if your cpu usage is maxed (use task manager), and if not bump it up to 8.
>
>
> --
> Mike Lawrence
> Graduate Student
> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> Dalhousie University
>
> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

> Yup, when you sample, just set the cores argument:
>
> post = rstan::sampling(
>     object = my_stan_model
>     , data = my_data_for_stan
>     , cores = parallel::detectCores() #if you want to use all your cores, else put a number
> )
>
>
> --
> Mike Lawrence
> Graduate Student

> Dalhousie University
>
> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Difference between monitor means and get_posterior_mean?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Difference between monitor means and get_posterior_mean?
messages.body_plain:
For the pure label switching problem in symmetric mixture models,
you want to concentrate on inferences that are not sensitive to label.
That is, inferences that are exchangeable under component index permutation.
So where you might want to say item i is in group k with some probability
and item j is in group k with some probability to try to tell which items
are in which groups, that's not well formulated because the group k isn't
identified in the model.  But what you can do is look at the probability
that i and j are in the same group---that event is exchangeable under
component re-indexing.

Having said that, I would sometimes like to be able to explore different chains
easily just to visualize what's going wrong in some cases.  So a wrapper
to make it easier to extract chains out of a fit object would be helpful for
that or a way to visualize or summarize with only some of the chains.

- Bob

> On Nov 18, 2016, at 11:24 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I agree with everything you say, of course, and you know far more about markov chains than I do.
>
> Until there is a better method to handle multimodality in mixture models though, basing one's inference on the full posterior (even *if* all chains explored all modes) would be pointless.
> On the other hand, if there *is* true multimodality that would change one's decisions/inference, having all chains explore all modes in correct proportion would help you understand the probability of solutions; the expected value would be difficult, but examining the posteriors could still tell you something about the probability of certain generative models.
>
> Currently, we don't have that, and the best we can do is to examine the multiple modes separately. They still tell you something about the solution, but nothing about the relative probability of each. Not sure if lp__ would be useful there though (2 chains hit one mode, 2 hit another, but the latter two have a greater lp__, so perhaps that is the 'more probable' solution? I'm not sure how useful that metric would be).
>
> The good thing is that the model I'm implementing is really more an exploratory procedure. It finds combinations of items that latent groups seem to operate differently on, so it detects biased items among latent groups. Sometimes it can find two modal solutions and one doesn't necessarily need to pick one or the other, but to just see 1) which items seem to be detected for that mode and 2) what are the characteristics of that mode's latent groups?
> For that purpose, I think it's fair to pick apart the modes. One may decide which solution is more *important* (say, if 12 items are detected as biased when male and female seem to be the latent groups, and the error in the latent assignment seems low, it may be more important than if 4 items are detected as biased when age seems to divide individuals into latent groups, but the assignment is error-prone).
>
> Thoughts on this? Yes, it's not using the full marginal posterior, but it still seems to lead one to make the 'correct' decisions in the context of my model (verifiably so, because I'm generating the data).
>
> Also, are there any plans for improving mixture modeling in Bayes, such that this multimodality isn't so much an issue? I know this is a relatively unsolved problem, even in ML estimation (EM has the same multiple-solution problem).
>
> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:58:10 AM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> This is a common misunderstanding.  When properly implementing full Bayes,
> all of the chains would explore all of the modes in the right proportions and
> they would indeed look the same.  ANY application of a Markov chain where
> multiple chains behave differently, however, is formally not a “correct thing to
> do” theoretically as it will necessarily be only an approximation to full Bayes.
>
> For example, if you can’t isolate a unique labeling in the model specification
> then you can’t guarantee that you can identify different labelings with different
> chains.  Eventually some chains will transition between modes and you’ll be
> left with a convolution of multiple labels that can’t be separated out so easily,
> if at all.
>
> This is even more important when the multi modality is not from a labeling
> degeneracy.  In that case the modes will have different weights, but having
> different chains explore different modes will tell you _nothing_ about what
> those weights should be so you have no way of combining the individual
> chains in a well-posed manner.
>
> I have been studying Markov chains intensely for the past four years and
> I still don’t really trust myself to pull off an approximate multimodal analysis
> like this (the more you learn, the more you see what can go wrong).  I think
> it’s fair not to expect most users to be able to pull it off, either.  Many of our
> design choices have been motivated to facilitate good practices and
> frustrate bad practices.
>
> On Nov 17, 2016, at 10:06 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Sorry, but it's necessary for some problems. In mixture models, there can be arbitrary between-chain label switching. You can tell it's arbitrary visibly in the trace plot. For cases like that, you *do* want to examine similar chains for your inference. It's not ideal, but it most certainly is the correct decision to make. Some parameters are invariant to the swapped labels, but many aren't, and for those that aren't invariant, examining similar chains will yield the correct inference.
>>
>> This is theoretically the correct thing to do, too. The identical, but swapped modes do indeed exist (so of course, Stan is correct), but one's decision is not 'what is the expected value assuming that the labels will swap in my population', but 'taking one of the arbitrary labelling solutions, what should my inference be?'.
>>
>> Other times, there can be authentic multimodality, or true multiple solutions, and the inferences *would* depend on which mode you picked, so to speak. Even in this case, you may want to pick apart the separate modes to better understand why so much density is in separate regions.
>> E.g., I have a model that predicts latent group membership from demographic data, these groups which differ in how certain items correlate to a latent ability estimate (literally, it's latent group DIF detection for 2PL models and others). Usually there are only label-swapped modes, and your inferences are essentially the same no matter the mode. However, sometimes the predictors can produce true multimodality, such that one predictor separates people into two groups that implicates set A of items to be DIF, and another mode finds that a second predictor separates people into two other groups that implicate set B to be DIF. It is useful to examine both of these modes as well as the full posterior, because it's not arbitrarily multimodal and the posterior is actually expressing real uncertainty about the generative model.
>>
>> Making per-chain summaries harder to come by on principle doesn't discourage people from doing it, it just makes using Stan unnecessarily more difficult. Put up a big warning when people select chains about the potential issues with non-convergence and be done with it. Otherwise, trust that the user is picking apart chains for a justifiable or at *least* a diagnostic reason.
>>
>> On Thursday, November 17, 2016 at 11:33:56 PM UTC-6, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:27:05 AM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
>> Really, I wish there were an easier way to get posterior summaries of one or multiple chains, by choice.
>>
>> We usually don't want people summarizing a subset of chains. Either all the chains have converged and it makes sense to summarize all of them or some of the chains haven't converged and it doesn't make sense to summarize any of them.
>>
>>

For the first paragraph -- Indeed, that's what is invariant.
Currently, the likelihood is a mixture (with one component itself being a mixture):

So in this case, \Delta_j is invariant to label switching and will simply tell you whether the item's parameters do indeed seem to differ between some latent groups.
However, we can also predict \pi_{ik} (on a log odds scale via softmax regression) from other characteristics about the individual. Because the labels can switch, the coefficients for that regression can also arbitrarily switch signs or labels. This is usually obvious, so this is why I just look at one mode or another for the inference, e.g., "what seems to predict membership to group k=2, in a set of groups that seem to differ on items with high \Delta_j values?"

I wound up just writing a wrapper around summary() called summary_chain() that takes the same arguments as summary() but with an additional chains argument (e.g., summary_chains(..., chains = c(1,2)) would give you the posterior summary over chains 1 and 2).

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] parallelization
messages.body_plain:
The short answer is yes. The Eigen library has parallelization.

It's tricky to configure. I've been meaning to write a blog post about how I set up my machine to make OpenMP work. Rob Trangucci and I were able to figure it out.

Once configured, it's simple getting it working with CmdStan.

But beware: in most situations, single core will be faster. (You didn't misread that: using the wrong number of cores or if the size of the problem isn't the right scale, I saw run times of 2-5x.) On the problem we were looking at, after a lot of experimentation, we got it to run faster by something like 15%. That was on a laptop, so with a large machine, I could see there being larger gains.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
There’s nothing special about the missing data here.  You just
solve the ODE for all measurement times, and then include a
measurement model only for those components that you do
measure at time point.  So sometimes you’d have a likelihood
contributes for each components, sometimes just a few.

If you want to impute those values then in generated quantities
you sample from the corresponding random number generator
(i.e. if your measurement model is Gaussian then use the
normal_rng) around the latent state.

@Daniel,

The first example does not relate to my program. I was trying to draw a smaller example of a two row matrix of data I was trying to fit that was missing data in certain entries. For my actual example, which I will not post, there are many observations at the same time. The two rows of my actual data matrix consist of soil respiration and microbial biomass measurements. I am trying to fit soil respiration and microbial biomass solved by the model to those outputs. So in my integrate_ode line, I need to feed the function the list of times that I want output for. I imagine I feed it all my times -- the union of the set of times for soil respiration and microbial biomass. In the missing data example given in the Stan manual, it shows all missing times being gathered into one vector. However, I am not sure I would create a two row matrix representing missing times, considering that the missing times are different.

@Michael,
So I think I'm starting to get it. I'm going to put my thoughts in words pseudocode, and you can let me know if I am on the right track.

So I import some two-row matrix of data into Stan with columns corresponding to measurement times that is missing different entries on each row.

Let's say I am missing data in Data[1,3] and Data[2,5]. I will represent the missing as parameters. So in the parameters block, I will have

real<lower=0> missing1;
real<lower=0> missing2;

In the transformed parameters block, I would then state

Data[1,3] = missing1;  Data[2,5] = missing2;

And finally in my model block, I would have

missing1 ~ normal(0,1);
missing2 ~ normal(0,1);

Or whichever the ranges of values are and then finally have the line

Data ~ multi_normal(model_output_matrix, sigma);

messages.body_plain:
Let’s go to a simpler example.  Let’s say that we have a two-dimensional
Gaussian with known covariance and we measure only the first component.
The corresponding Stan model would look something like

data {
  int N;
  vector[2] y[N];
  matrix[2, 2] Sigma;
}

parameters {
  real mu;
}

model {
  mu ~ normal(0, 1);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[1] ~ normal(mu, Sigma[1, 1]);
}

In other words, we marginalize out over the unobserved components which
in the Gaussian case reduces to dropping any terms that depend on the
second component.

The important statistical concept here is that you can’t learn from unobserved
data, all you can do it predict it.  So you want to build a model without the
unobserved components and if you really care about trying to figure out what
went on then you predict those components in the generated quantities block.

> On Nov 18, 2016, at 11:00 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ....

> In other words, we marginalize out over the unobserved components which
> in the Gaussian case reduces to dropping any terms that depend on the
> second component.
>
> The important statistical concept here is that you can’t learn from unobserved
> data, all you can do it predict it.  So you want to build a model without the
> unobserved components and if you really care about trying to figure out what
> went on then you predict those components in the generated quantities block.

You can't learn from completely unobserved data, but you can
learn a bit from partially observed data (e.g., one or more of many
predictors is missing, or the outcome is missing).    But like
Michael says, the trick is to provide a joint model for everything
as if it were all observed, then marginalize out what's missing.  Sometimes
the easiest way to do that is to declare the missing quantity as a parameter.
Then you get a posterior that includes it, but if you ignore it, it amounts
to marginalizing it out.  Sometimes the model is neatly formed and you
can marginalize analytically (this is common in multivariate normal models).

- Bob

Stan and I are, like, buddies.  Well, a few squabbles (first it was ~ and +=, then <- and =, and now | is not or ... really?  On top of reals cannot become integers?) but we work things out.  Worth pointing out is this important sentence regarding variable scope in Stan the Man 2.12.0, section 29.2, page 320: "to make a variable accessible in the model and generated quantities block, it must be declared as a transformed parameter."
    In Stan's model block, I defined and assigned a variable called "predicted," so that Stan could calculate the log likelihood of observed given predicted.  To calculate PSIS-LOO or WAIC (post Stan), I need to use "predicted" again to calculate the log likelihood for each observed, again, but this time in Stan's generated quantities block so that he can save the point-by-point log-likelihoods for each sample.   If the variable "predicted" is defined in Stan's model block, Stan will insist he cannot see it in his generated quantities block.  He's like that sometimes.   If I try to define "predicted" in Stan's transformed data block, thinking, "Obviously predicted data goes with observed data," then Stan tells me that it is illegal to redefine data in the model block, "attempt to assign variable in wrong block. left-hand-side variable origin=transformed data", transformed data is data, OK?  Fine, be like that.
    Upon resorting to RTFM, our squabble seems to be resolved.  I happily move the definition of "predicted" to Stan's transformed parameters block, ...  Stan looks at his model block and says "attempt to assign variable in wrong block. left-hand-side variable origin=transformed parameter."
    I have nowhere left to define "predicted."  Stan is telling me that I cannot make a prediction in Stan's model block and re-use that prediction in Stan's generated quantities block.  My prediction is from a user-defined function of the data that is slow (advection, diffusion, and mortality of a time-series salmon smolts between dams on the Columbia River, see attached).  I cannot pull the log-likelihood calculation into my user-defined function because Stan will not be able to see "target += normal_lpdf(observed | predicted, sigma)" inside there.  I think I have to re-run my user-defined function to generate "predicted_again" in Stan's generated quantities block.  But Stan is cooler than that, right?  What am I missing?

> On Nov 19, 2016, at 3:59 AM, Scott Akenhead <sc...@s4s.com> wrote:
>
>     Stan and I are, like, buddies.  Well, a few squabbles (first it was ~ and +=, then <- and =, and now | is not or ... really?  On top of reals cannot become integers?) but we work things out.

We don't anticipate more changes in the basic syntax other than
adding new operations and data types.

When we move to Stan 3, we'll take everything deprecated now and
remove it.

| is not overloaded in Stan, because Stan doesn't have bitwise OR.
Stan uses || for disjunction, like many programming languages.

> Worth pointing out is this important sentence regarding variable scope in Stan the Man 2.12.0, section 29.2, page 320: "to make a variable accessible in the model and generated quantities block, it must be declared as a transformed parameter."

This follows from the general principle that block variables are
only visible in their own block and later blocks and that
variables are only assignable in their own blocks.  The model
block doesn't have any block variables, only local variables.

We've been debating whether to loosen this requirement, perhaps
removing transformed parameters altogether and just having the
model block have block variables.  But then we're also thinking
of allowing Jacobians to be defined and incremented in the transformed
parameter block (so you could write a model that could be used
for both MLE and for MCMC).

We could also take variables declared at the top of the model block
and just treat them like transformed parameters.  Unlike Perl,
I don't like having multiple ways to do the same thing syntatically.

Stay tuned for what we decide---it's an ongoing discussion, and as
with all of our discussions, we're happy to get feedback.

>     In Stan's model block, I defined and assigned a variable called "predicted," so that Stan could calculate the log likelihood of observed given predicted.  To calculate PSIS-LOO or WAIC (post Stan), I need to use "predicted" again to calculate the log likelihood for each observed, again, but this time in Stan's generated quantities block so that he can save the point-by-point log-likelihoods for each sample.   If the variable "predicted" is defined in Stan's model block, Stan will insist he cannot see it in his generated quantities block.  He's like that sometimes.   If I try to define "predicted" in Stan's transformed data block, thinking, "Obviously predicted data goes with observed data," then Stan tells me that it is illegal to redefine data in the model block, "attempt to assign variable in wrong block. left-hand-side variable origin=transformed data", transformed data is data, OK?  Fine, be like that.

See above.

>     Upon resorting to RTFM, our squabble seems to be resolved.  I happily move the definition of "predicted" to Stan's transformed parameters block, ...  Stan looks at his model block and says "attempt to assign variable in wrong block. left-hand-side variable origin=transformed parameter."

You have to define it in the transformed parameters block.
Again, see the general rule above.

>     I have nowhere left to define "predicted."  Stan is telling me that I cannot make a prediction in Stan's model block and re-use that prediction in Stan's generated quantities block.  My prediction is from a user-defined function of the data that is slow (advection, diffusion, and mortality of a time-series salmon smolts between dams on the Columbia River, see attached).  I cannot pull the log-likelihood calculation into my user-defined function because Stan will not be able to see "target += normal_lpdf(observed | predicted, sigma)" inside there.  I think I have to re-run my user-defined function to generate "predicted_again" in Stan's generated quantities block.  But Stan is cooler than that, right?  What am I missing?

Stan's not very particular about types and scope (see above).
Blame me---I'm the one that imposed strict scoping and typing
in the first place.

So you either have to define a variable in the transformed
parameters block and use it in the model block, or define
it as a local variable in the model block and then redefine
it in the generated quantities block.

- Bob

P.S.  I saw a lot of that salmon and dam stuff at the fisheries meeting for
ADMB before the last quant ecology conference in Seattle.  They're
nifty models.

Thanks for the help, gentlemen.

So Googling the phrase "marginalizing out," I am led to the Wikipedia page about marginal distributions. So it appears that marginal distributions are univariate distributions of variables by themselves in a joint distribution. They are different from conditional distributions because there is no contingency on other variables. To get marginal distributions, we "marginalize out" the other variable(s) as unknown(s).

So in simple terms, it sounds like what I should do in my case is:
1) Generate 2-row matrix solution for all times.
2) "Marginalize out" the unknown entries in the data matrix as parameters following some distribution.
3) Fit as I would usually.

Alternatively, (and forgive me if this is an absolutely idiotic and heretical question), what would be the effect of setting the missing data matrix entries to 0 and setting the corresponding entries of the model output matrix to 0, so as to not fit them?

> > In other words, we marginalize out over the unobserved components which
> > in the Gaussian case reduces to dropping any terms that depend on the
> > second component.
> >
> > The important statistical concept here is that you can’t learn from unobserved
> > data, all you can do it predict it.  So you want to build a model without the
> > unobserved components and if you really care about trying to figure out what
> > went on then you predict those components in the generated quantities block.
>
> You can't learn from completely unobserved data, but you can
> learn a bit from partially observed data (e.g., one or more of many
> predictors is missing, or the outcome is missing).    But like
> Michael says, the trick is to provide a joint model for everything
> as if it were all observed, then marginalize out what's missing.  Sometimes
> the easiest way to do that is to declare the missing quantity as a parameter.
> Then you get a posterior that includes it, but if you ignore it, it amounts
> to marginalizing it out.  Sometimes the model is neatly formed and you
> can marginalize analytically (this is common in multivariate normal models).
>
> - Bob
>
