messages.body_plain:
- Bob

> On Nov 19, 2016, at 5:00 PM, H. X. <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the help, gentlemen.
>
> So Googling the phrase "marginalizing out," I am led to the Wikipedia page about marginal distributions. So it appears that marginal distributions are univariate distributions of variables by themselves in a joint distribution. They are different from conditional distributions because there is no contingency on other variables. To get marginal distributions, we "marginalize out" the other variable(s) as unknown(s).

Right---that's the marginalization we're talking about.
Though it's really more about removing one of the variables
than getting something down to univariate---that's just the
textbook examples.  It's a pretty fundamental thing to understand
for applied and computational stats.

There's a chapter in the manual on latent discrete parameters
that goes through how to marginalize those out.

> So in simple terms, it sounds like what I should do in my case is:
> 1) Generate 2-row matrix solution for all times.
> 2) "Marginalize out" the unknown entries in the data matrix as parameters following some distribution.
> 3) Fit as I would usually.
>
> Alternatively, (and forgive me if this is an absolutely idiotic and heretical question), what would be the effect of setting the missing data matrix entries to 0 and setting the corresponding entries of the model output matrix to 0, so as to not fit them?

What happens is that you get inferences as if the values
were 0---they won't be ignored.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: advi feedback from users
messages.body_plain:
I tried using it on a fairly weird model of mine.
The data are dichotomous responses assumed to be generated from a 2PL model.
However, the purpose of the model is not to just estimate a 2PL IRT model, but to detect latent groups which some items exhibit DIF between.
So it's a fairly convoluted model --- The likelihood for each item and case is a mixture of bernoulli likelihoods, one which assumes DIF one which does not; when it assumes DIF, it is another mixture model aiming to assign individuals to latent clusters.
Moreover, one can 'predict' latent cluster membership using softmax or logistic regression from other respondent data.

Needless to say, ADVI did not work well. Optimizing doesn't either, presumably because this sort of problem needs an EM approach, not a basic ML approach.

I wanted to try ADVI because the model takes about 1200 seconds for 300 cases and 24 items.
I did try the fullrank, it didn't work well either.

By 'didnt work well', I mean it completely fails to estimate the correct latent group memberships (which I know, because I generate the data) and fails to discern the DIF items from non-DIF items.

Long story short, I've coded up the models I need --- the main idea is to package them up and pre-compile them, so that modellers can use them in a kind of automated way and in a computational time that is not so long as to drive them to the default MLE-based estimates all the time.

We have a new R package to facilitate this

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstantools/index.html

See especially its rstan_package_skeleton() function (which used to just be in rstan).

We have noticed similar issues with Gamma likelihoods in the stan_glm() function in the rstanarm package. Also, gamma_lcdf() and gamma_lccdf() are a bit slow and fragile because of the numerical approximations. You might compare with the models mentioned in

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/ALIQnFy4b3g/MtgQnVMUAwAJ

to see if there is something about the implementation that makes a big difference.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thank you, Bob and Ben.

Ben: I have used rstantools to pre-compile the models --- it works really nicely, thanks! Also, I'll check out the models you suggest. On a *very* cursory look, they seem to have been parameterised in a slightly different way than I did --- but I'll have to check more closely.

Bob: thanks --- I have done some tests on varying the prior for the shape. I don't think the vague Gamma is responsible for much of the problem, in this case --- I know this prior is often not ideal, but it seems like changing it to a Uniform or a log-Normal doesn't change much both in terms of estimates or running time... Interestingly enough, the prior doesn't make much of a difference in terms of the estimates and, by and large, convergence (only marginally in terms of autocorrelation), when compared with the (intuitively) less efficient parameterisation (using the missing data approach). I guess Ben's point on  similar issues with Gamma likelihoods is kind of "consistent"?

BW

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
My current favored approach is to get rid of the aliasing using constraints on the parameters.  This does become more difficult in multiple dimensions, and there's more work to be done here.  I've been thinking about the general problem for many years, and it seems to me that some restriction is the way to go. Also, it's not necessary that the restriction be a hard constraint; a soft constraint could work too, maybe.
A

> On Nov 18, 2016, at 1:29 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> For the pure label switching problem in symmetric mixture models,
> you want to concentrate on inferences that are not sensitive to label.
> That is, inferences that are exchangeable under component index permutation.
> So where you might want to say item i is in group k with some probability
> and item j is in group k with some probability to try to tell which items
> are in which groups, that's not well formulated because the group k isn't
> identified in the model.  But what you can do is look at the probability
> that i and j are in the same group---that event is exchangeable under
> component re-indexing.
>
> Having said that, I would sometimes like to be able to explore different chains
> easily just to visualize what's going wrong in some cases.  So a wrapper
> to make it easier to extract chains out of a fit object would be helpful for
> that or a way to visualize or summarize with only some of the chains.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>> On Nov 18, 2016, at 11:24 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> I agree with everything you say, of course, and you know far more about markov chains than I do.
>>
>> Until there is a better method to handle multimodality in mixture models though, basing one's inference on the full posterior (even *if* all chains explored all modes) would be pointless.
>> On the other hand, if there *is* true multimodality that would change one's decisions/inference, having all chains explore all modes in correct proportion would help you understand the probability of solutions; the expected value would be difficult, but examining the posteriors could still tell you something about the probability of certain generative models.
>>
>> Currently, we don't have that, and the best we can do is to examine the multiple modes separately. They still tell you something about the solution, but nothing about the relative probability of each. Not sure if lp__ would be useful there though (2 chains hit one mode, 2 hit another, but the latter two have a greater lp__, so perhaps that is the 'more probable' solution? I'm not sure how useful that metric would be).
>>
>> The good thing is that the model I'm implementing is really more an exploratory procedure. It finds combinations of items that latent groups seem to operate differently on, so it detects biased items among latent groups. Sometimes it can find two modal solutions and one doesn't necessarily need to pick one or the other, but to just see 1) which items seem to be detected for that mode and 2) what are the characteristics of that mode's latent groups?
>> For that purpose, I think it's fair to pick apart the modes. One may decide which solution is more *important* (say, if 12 items are detected as biased when male and female seem to be the latent groups, and the error in the latent assignment seems low, it may be more important than if 4 items are detected as biased when age seems to divide individuals into latent groups, but the assignment is error-prone).
>>
>> Thoughts on this? Yes, it's not using the full marginal posterior, but it still seems to lead one to make the 'correct' decisions in the context of my model (verifiably so, because I'm generating the data).
>>
>> Also, are there any plans for improving mixture modeling in Bayes, such that this multimodality isn't so much an issue? I know this is a relatively unsolved problem, even in ML estimation (EM has the same multiple-solution problem).
>>
>> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:58:10 AM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> This is a common misunderstanding.  When properly implementing full Bayes,
>> all of the chains would explore all of the modes in the right proportions and
>> they would indeed look the same.  ANY application of a Markov chain where
>> multiple chains behave differently, however, is formally not a “correct thing to
>> do” theoretically as it will necessarily be only an approximation to full Bayes.
>>
>> For example, if you can’t isolate a unique labeling in the model specification
>> then you can’t guarantee that you can identify different labelings with different
>> chains.  Eventually some chains will transition between modes and you’ll be
>> left with a convolution of multiple labels that can’t be separated out so easily,
>> if at all.
>>
>> This is even more important when the multi modality is not from a labeling
>> degeneracy.  In that case the modes will have different weights, but having
>> different chains explore different modes will tell you _nothing_ about what
>> those weights should be so you have no way of combining the individual
>> chains in a well-posed manner.
>>
>> I have been studying Markov chains intensely for the past four years and
>> I still don’t really trust myself to pull off an approximate multimodal analysis
>> like this (the more you learn, the more you see what can go wrong).  I think
>> it’s fair not to expect most users to be able to pull it off, either.  Many of our
>> design choices have been motivated to facilitate good practices and
>> frustrate bad practices.
>>
>> On Nov 17, 2016, at 10:06 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> Sorry, but it's necessary for some problems. In mixture models, there can be arbitrary between-chain label switching. You can tell it's arbitrary visibly in the trace plot. For cases like that, you *do* want to examine similar chains for your inference. It's not ideal, but it most certainly is the correct decision to make. Some parameters are invariant to the swapped labels, but many aren't, and for those that aren't invariant, examining similar chains will yield the correct inference.
>>>
>>> This is theoretically the correct thing to do, too. The identical, but swapped modes do indeed exist (so of course, Stan is correct), but one's decision is not 'what is the expected value assuming that the labels will swap in my population', but 'taking one of the arbitrary labelling solutions, what should my inference be?'.
>>>
>>> Other times, there can be authentic multimodality, or true multiple solutions, and the inferences *would* depend on which mode you picked, so to speak. Even in this case, you may want to pick apart the separate modes to better understand why so much density is in separate regions.
>>> E.g., I have a model that predicts latent group membership from demographic data, these groups which differ in how certain items correlate to a latent ability estimate (literally, it's latent group DIF detection for 2PL models and others). Usually there are only label-swapped modes, and your inferences are essentially the same no matter the mode. However, sometimes the predictors can produce true multimodality, such that one predictor separates people into two groups that implicates set A of items to be DIF, and another mode finds that a second predictor separates people into two other groups that implicate set B to be DIF. It is useful to examine both of these modes as well as the full posterior, because it's not arbitrarily multimodal and the posterior is actually expressing real uncertainty about the generative model.
>>>
>>> Making per-chain summaries harder to come by on principle doesn't discourage people from doing it, it just makes using Stan unnecessarily more difficult. Put up a big warning when people select chains about the potential issues with non-convergence and be done with it. Otherwise, trust that the user is picking apart chains for a justifiable or at *least* a diagnostic reason.
>>>
>>> On Thursday, November 17, 2016 at 11:33:56 PM UTC-6, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>>> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:27:05 AM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
>>> Really, I wish there were an easier way to get posterior summaries of one or multiple chains, by choice.
>>>
>>> We usually don't want people summarizing a subset of chains. Either all the chains have converged and it makes sense to summarize all of them or some of the chains haven't converged and it doesn't make sense to summarize any of them.
>>>
>>>

messages.subject: Re: Example Stan converges but BUGS does not
messages.subject_clean: Example Stan converges but BUGS does not
messages.body_plain:
I've *never* seen a case where Stan takes longer than BUGS *in terms of effective samples*.
BUGS/JAGS may take much less time to cycle through 2000 iterations, and it may even say it converges.

However, and this is a *big* however:
1) BUGS/JAGS do not use random inits. This means the chains are more likely to converge to one mode of an inherently multimodal posterior.
Due to the problems of gibbs, random walk metropolis, and slice sampling, they will likely stay in the one mode.
The convergence diagnostics will say "hey, the gibbs sampler has converged across all chains", when in reality the problem is that gibbs found one mode and failed to escape it due to to the conditional sampling that it uses.
This means you can incorrectly conclude that you explored the full posterior, when in reality you only explored one mode of it, and it failed to escape the mode to find other high density areas of the posterior. Your inference will be potentially jeopardized as a result.

2) Stan will take longer than Gibbs. Period. Stan has to evaluate the gradient of the posterior in order to simulate a particle flowing across the multidimensional surface.
You may say "well, my problem is unimodal, so why not use Gibbs, since it's faster"?
The issue is that per-iteration, Gibbs is faster, but in terms of uncorrelated, representative samples, Stan is usually faster.
Gibbs has less to compute per iteration, so it can crawl through 2000 iterations quickly.
Stan has more to compute per iteration, so it will crawl through 2000 iterations slower.
Then you look at the output and see that Gibbs may only have 40 effective samples (relatively independent samples), because due to conditional sampling, Gibbs can get stuck in highly correlated areas of the posterior.
On the other hand, Stan may have 1800 effective samples, because it samples across the posterior in a joint, unconditional manner, naturally flowing across the surface. It doesn't have much of an issue with correlated areas, and won't get 'stuck' as often as Gibbs.

As a concrete example of this, I currently have a very high dimensional model.
It includes a series of mixture models and latent variables.
It takes Gibbs about 20 minutes to go through it, and Stan about 40 minutes to go through it (2000 iterations each, 1000 of them are warmup in my case).
After 20 minutes, Gibbs has about 30 effective samples (yes, you read that correctly, 30 out of 1000 post-adaptation draws are relatively independent).
After 40 minutes, Stan has about 900.
I'll take that 40 minutes: 900/40 >>> 30/20; roughly 15x 'faster' in terms of effective samples from the posterior.

messages.body_plain:
For my model, the best option is to set a positivity constraint (half-cauchy, half-normal) on the beta coefficient predicting latent group membership, but it's not generalizable (not everyone using my model would use latent regressors).

I've tried an ordering constraint on item coefficients (e.g., difficulty of item 1 is ordered across latent groups), but this seems to prevent within-chain switching moreso than between-chain modes. I'm guessing the issue is that the ordering constraint doesn't affect the overall likelihood enough to prevent two modes from occurring. One mode will just have a slightly higher lp__ than the other, since only one item has a constraint (out of, e.g., 20 items).

Ignoring that multimodality (which, again, is easy to detect either through trace plots, summary stats, or looking at the latent regressors' magnitude and signs), the model *can* have authentic multimodality, which I think I can fix by using a more informative prior on the latent regression 'error term' (categorization error). Rather than allow the error to be small or fairly large, I can put a gamma(1,1) or exp(1) prior on the error to favor models that use the latent regressors more for latent group assignment than allowing people to freely be assigned to each cluster. Testing this out now.

I hope to publish this model soon (along with an R package for fitting it), I'm just trying to figure out what the best 'default' priors might be on realistic datasets. The only 'problem' with this model is that it works great with MCMC, but optimizing fails miserably and vb does fairly poorly as well. But to be fair, it's a weird model --- If there are J items, then the model is fitting J + 1 mixture models, something that optimizing() should fail at, and it isn't remotely mvn, so vb fails too.

> My current favored approach is to get rid of the aliasing using constraints on the parameters.  This does become more difficult in multiple dimensions, and there's more work to be done here.  I've been thinking about the general problem for many years, and it seems to me that some restriction is the way to go. Also, it's not necessary that the restriction be a hard constraint; a soft constraint could work too, maybe.
> A
>
> > On Nov 18, 2016, at 1:29 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > For the pure label switching problem in symmetric mixture models,
> > you want to concentrate on inferences that are not sensitive to label.
> > That is, inferences that are exchangeable under component index permutation.
> > So where you might want to say item i is in group k with some probability
> > and item j is in group k with some probability to try to tell which items
> > are in which groups, that's not well formulated because the group k isn't
> > identified in the model.  But what you can do is look at the probability
> > that i and j are in the same group---that event is exchangeable under
> > component re-indexing.
> >
> > Having said that, I would sometimes like to be able to explore different chains
> > easily just to visualize what's going wrong in some cases.  So a wrapper
> > to make it easier to extract chains out of a fit object would be helpful for
> > that or a way to visualize or summarize with only some of the chains.

> >

> >> On Nov 18, 2016, at 11:24 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> I agree with everything you say, of course, and you know far more about markov chains than I do.
> >>
> >> Until there is a better method to handle multimodality in mixture models though, basing one's inference on the full posterior (even *if* all chains explored all modes) would be pointless.
> >> On the other hand, if there *is* true multimodality that would change one's decisions/inference, having all chains explore all modes in correct proportion would help you understand the probability of solutions; the expected value would be difficult, but examining the posteriors could still tell you something about the probability of certain generative models.
> >>
> >> Currently, we don't have that, and the best we can do is to examine the multiple modes separately. They still tell you something about the solution, but nothing about the relative probability of each. Not sure if lp__ would be useful there though (2 chains hit one mode, 2 hit another, but the latter two have a greater lp__, so perhaps that is the 'more probable' solution? I'm not sure how useful that metric would be).
> >>
> >> The good thing is that the model I'm implementing is really more an exploratory procedure. It finds combinations of items that latent groups seem to operate differently on, so it detects biased items among latent groups. Sometimes it can find two modal solutions and one doesn't necessarily need to pick one or the other, but to just see 1) which items seem to be detected for that mode and 2) what are the characteristics of that mode's latent groups?
> >> For that purpose, I think it's fair to pick apart the modes. One may decide which solution is more *important* (say, if 12 items are detected as biased when male and female seem to be the latent groups, and the error in the latent assignment seems low, it may be more important than if 4 items are detected as biased when age seems to divide individuals into latent groups, but the assignment is error-prone).
> >>
> >> Thoughts on this? Yes, it's not using the full marginal posterior, but it still seems to lead one to make the 'correct' decisions in the context of my model (verifiably so, because I'm generating the data).
> >>
> >> Also, are there any plans for improving mixture modeling in Bayes, such that this multimodality isn't so much an issue? I know this is a relatively unsolved problem, even in ML estimation (EM has the same multiple-solution problem).
> >>
> >> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:58:10 AM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >> This is a common misunderstanding.  When properly implementing full Bayes,
> >> all of the chains would explore all of the modes in the right proportions and
> >> they would indeed look the same.  ANY application of a Markov chain where
> >> multiple chains behave differently, however, is formally not a “correct thing to
> >> do” theoretically as it will necessarily be only an approximation to full Bayes.
> >>
> >> For example, if you can’t isolate a unique labeling in the model specification
> >> then you can’t guarantee that you can identify different labelings with different
> >> chains.  Eventually some chains will transition between modes and you’ll be
> >> left with a convolution of multiple labels that can’t be separated out so easily,
> >> if at all.
> >>
> >> This is even more important when the multi modality is not from a labeling
> >> degeneracy.  In that case the modes will have different weights, but having
> >> different chains explore different modes will tell you _nothing_ about what
> >> those weights should be so you have no way of combining the individual
> >> chains in a well-posed manner.
> >>
> >> I have been studying Markov chains intensely for the past four years and
> >> I still don’t really trust myself to pull off an approximate multimodal analysis
> >> like this (the more you learn, the more you see what can go wrong).  I think
> >> it’s fair not to expect most users to be able to pull it off, either.  Many of our
> >> design choices have been motivated to facilitate good practices and
> >> frustrate bad practices.
> >>
> >> On Nov 17, 2016, at 10:06 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >>> Sorry, but it's necessary for some problems. In mixture models, there can be arbitrary between-chain label switching. You can tell it's arbitrary visibly in the trace plot. For cases like that, you *do* want to examine similar chains for your inference. It's not ideal, but it most certainly is the correct decision to make. Some parameters are invariant to the swapped labels, but many aren't, and for those that aren't invariant, examining similar chains will yield the correct inference.
> >>>
> >>> This is theoretically the correct thing to do, too. The identical, but swapped modes do indeed exist (so of course, Stan is correct), but one's decision is not 'what is the expected value assuming that the labels will swap in my population', but 'taking one of the arbitrary labelling solutions, what should my inference be?'.
> >>>
> >>> Other times, there can be authentic multimodality, or true multiple solutions, and the inferences *would* depend on which mode you picked, so to speak. Even in this case, you may want to pick apart the separate modes to better understand why so much density is in separate regions.
> >>> E.g., I have a model that predicts latent group membership from demographic data, these groups which differ in how certain items correlate to a latent ability estimate (literally, it's latent group DIF detection for 2PL models and others). Usually there are only label-swapped modes, and your inferences are essentially the same no matter the mode. However, sometimes the predictors can produce true multimodality, such that one predictor separates people into two groups that implicates set A of items to be DIF, and another mode finds that a second predictor separates people into two other groups that implicate set B to be DIF. It is useful to examine both of these modes as well as the full posterior, because it's not arbitrarily multimodal and the posterior is actually expressing real uncertainty about the generative model.
> >>>
> >>> Making per-chain summaries harder to come by on principle doesn't discourage people from doing it, it just makes using Stan unnecessarily more difficult. Put up a big warning when people select chains about the potential issues with non-convergence and be done with it. Otherwise, trust that the user is picking apart chains for a justifiable or at *least* a diagnostic reason.
> >>>
> >>> On Thursday, November 17, 2016 at 11:33:56 PM UTC-6, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> >>> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 12:27:05 AM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
> >>> Really, I wish there were an easier way to get posterior summaries of one or multiple chains, by choice.
> >>>
> >>> We usually don't want people summarizing a subset of chains. Either all the chains have converged and it makes sense to summarize all of them or some of the chains haven't converged and it doesn't make sense to summarize any of them.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephen,

We're actually intentionally trying to avoid having anything like that in bayesplot to keep the code more modular and easier to maintain. But what you're asking about will definitely exist soon in the rstan package. bayesplot is intended to not have as many dependencies as rstan and to be usable by rstan, rstanarm, and other R packages that return different types of objects. The idea is that those packages can offer wrappers for bayesplot that make it work with the specific objects from those packages. This is what the plot method in rstanarm now does for stanreg objects in the new version of rstanarm and what the plot method in rstan will soon do for stanfit objects. So, for example, to get bayesplot's mcmc_violin plot with a stanfit object you'll be able to do something like plot(stanfit, "mcmc_violin") or just plot(stanfit, "violin") and it will get what bayesplot needs from the stanfit object and call bayesplot::mcmc_violin.

Jonah

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Example Stan converges but BUGS does not
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Example Stan converges but BUGS does not
messages.body_plain:
The punchline of (2) is why we built Stan in the first place.

I also wouldn't trust your estimate of a 30 effective sample
size (30 effective draws) if you had 1000 iterations --- that's too
much long-range autocorrelation for the estimators to be very
reliable.  (Also, Stan uses slightly more conservative estimates
than JAGS does in that it uses split R-hat and then uses that
to further adjust effective sample size based on R-hat-like properties;
it's described in the manual.)

HMC/NUTS is almost always slower than Gibbs per iteration because
we almost always evaluate more than a single log density and
gradient and the gradients are done with autodiff.
As Andrew was alluding to, Gibbs can get expensive
when you don't have conjugate forms in the conditionals because
you have to start doing things like slice sampling (JAGS) or
adaptive rejective sampling (BUGS).  But in everything we've
looked at, JAGS has been faster than Stan per iteration.

A lot of this comes down to implementation details, too.
JAGS can do some neat tricks with GLMs, Stan can do some
neat tricks with vectorization.  So all this relative speed
stuff is very model specific.  And can even depend on the
data---Stan's not very good with badly misspecified models.
(Goes back to Andrew's folk theorem.)

- Bob

> On Nov 20, 2016, at 9:39 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> I've *never* seen a case where Stan takes longer than BUGS *in terms of effective samples*.
> BUGS/JAGS may take much less time to cycle through 2000 iterations, and it may even say it converges.
>
> However, and this is a *big* however:
> 1) BUGS/JAGS do not use random inits. This means the chains are more likely to converge to one mode of an inherently multimodal posterior.
> Due to the problems of gibbs, random walk metropolis, and slice sampling, they will likely stay in the one mode.
> The convergence diagnostics will say "hey, the gibbs sampler has converged across all chains", when in reality the problem is that gibbs found one mode and failed to escape it due to to the conditional sampling that it uses.
> This means you can incorrectly conclude that you explored the full posterior, when in reality you only explored one mode of it, and it failed to escape the mode to find other high density areas of the posterior. Your inference will be potentially jeopardized as a result.
>
> 2) Stan will take longer than Gibbs. Period. Stan has to evaluate the gradient of the posterior in order to simulate a particle flowing across the multidimensional surface.
> You may say "well, my problem is unimodal, so why not use Gibbs, since it's faster"?
> The issue is that per-iteration, Gibbs is faster, but in terms of uncorrelated, representative samples, Stan is usually faster.
> Gibbs has less to compute per iteration, so it can crawl through 2000 iterations quickly.
> Stan has more to compute per iteration, so it will crawl through 2000 iterations slower.
> Then you look at the output and see that Gibbs may only have 40 effective samples (relatively independent samples), because due to conditional sampling, Gibbs can get stuck in highly correlated areas of the posterior.
> On the other hand, Stan may have 1800 effective samples, because it samples across the posterior in a joint, unconditional manner, naturally flowing across the surface. It doesn't have much of an issue with correlated areas, and won't get 'stuck' as often as Gibbs.
>
> As a concrete example of this, I currently have a very high dimensional model.
> It includes a series of mixture models and latent variables.
> It takes Gibbs about 20 minutes to go through it, and Stan about 40 minutes to go through it (2000 iterations each, 1000 of them are warmup in my case).
> After 20 minutes, Gibbs has about 30 effective samples (yes, you read that correctly, 30 out of 1000 post-adaptation draws are relatively independent).
> After 40 minutes, Stan has about 900.
> I'll take that 40 minutes: 900/40 >>> 30/20; roughly 15x 'faster' in terms of effective samples from the posterior.
>
> On Sunday, November 20, 2016 at 6:38:29 PM UTC-6, jt...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Are there any standard examples in Stan that does not work in BUGS (ie MCMC does not converge or take a miraculously long time to converge)?
>
>

messages.body_plain:
It's when the simulated Hamiltonian diverges from
the true Hamiltonian.  There's a section in the HMC
chapter of the manual about it.

I think RStan was overreporting divergences as being
after warmup that had actually occurred during
warmup.

- Bob

messages.subject: rstan too-many-dlls problem - are there sane solutions?
messages.subject_clean: rstan too-many-dlls problem - are there sane solutions?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm trying to run sensitivity analyses (e.g. hundreds of fits with varying priors). If I understand correctly, if the prior changes I DO need to recompile the model, so updating is not an option.

As has been pointed out, cleaning up the dll's would be desirable as default R has a dll maximum of 100: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24832030/exceeded-maximum-number-of-dlls-in-r

I have tried the solution by Frederic H. (last reply on the page) but this unpredictably and repeatedly crashes my rsession, at least if I run multiple instances of R.

My question is: are there any plans to include dll cleanup or even sensitivity analysis functions in rstan in the future and do you have any suggestions for how I could avoid 100+ dll's piling up?

I should mention that I run rstan via the brms package on Windows 7, using R64 & RStudio.

Regards and thanks,
Paul

messages.subject_clean: rstan too-many-dlls problem - are there sane solutions?
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 21, 2016 at 5:44:04 AM UTC-5, Paul Zerr wrote:
> I'm trying to run sensitivity analyses (e.g. hundreds of fits with varying priors). If I understand correctly, if the prior changes I DO need to recompile the model, so updating is not an option.

Hundreds of prior families or just different hyperparameter values? If the later, then you should be able to pass those values into the data block and not recompile.

> My question is: are there any plans to include dll cleanup or even sensitivity analysis functions in rstan in the future and do you have any suggestions for how I could avoid 100+ dll's piling up?

No plans to remove the dlls (they are needed for some post-estimation functions). You could call Stan (via brm) in a separate R processes using the makePSOCKcluster() function in the parallel library and then kill that process with stopCluster(). But you would need to avoid returning an object to the parent process that contains the stanfit object, possibly by calling as.array() or something.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan users and friendly Stan developers.
Could any one help to give a hint what should I do to improve my model?

I have a model built in Stan where there is a recursive relationship between latent quantities S, I, R.
So:
S[t] = S[t-1] - Inew[t]
      I[t] = I[t-1] + Inew[t] - Rnew[t]
      R[t] = R[t-1] + Rnew[t]

and
      Rnew[t] ~ sampling from a binomial distribution with total = I[t-1] and rate = 1-exp(-sigma) where sigma >0 to assume that 0 < rate <1.
      Inew[t]  ~ sampling from a binomial distribution with total = S[t-1] and rate[i] = 1-exp(-lambda[i]) where lambda[i] = p1+p2*age[i].
I can not sample from a binomial distribution in the transformed parameters block so I need to code them like:

    Inew[i]   <- rate[i]*S[i-1] ;
     Rnew[i]   <- rateRecover*I[i-1];

 Then at each iteration, I calculate: p[i] <- (I[i] + R[i]) / (S[i] + I[i] + R[i]) but I only extract 83 of them based on the index ind <- 365*c(1:83) + 1: prob <- p[ind]. This will be used later in the model block.
Since there is only 83 values of age, but it is more of interest to run the above recursing process longer so I create an index ind with length = 83 but the loop for running the above procedure is much longer.
I have the data on Pos and Tot so in the model block, I have:
model {
  for (k in 1:n){
    Pos[k] ~ binomial(Tot[k], prob[k]);
  }

However, when running the program, I got some errors like:

[505] "Rejecting initial value:"
[506] "  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity."
[507] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value."
[508] "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:"
[509] "validate transformed params: lambda[k0__] is -0.00015359, but must be greater than or equal to 0"
[510] "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,"
[511] "but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."
[512] "Rejecting initial value:"
[513] "  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value."
[514] "Rejecting initial value:"
[515] "  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity."
[516] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value."
[517] "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:"
[518] "validate transformed params: lambda[k0__] is -0.614633, but must be greater than or equal to 0"
[519] "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,"
[520] "but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."
[521] "Rejecting initial value:"
[522] "  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value."
[523] "Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts. "
[524] " Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."
[525] "Error : "
[1] "error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done"

In the attachment is my complete program and data.

Merci :D

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for that answer. I certainly got a lot of insight from that. Perhaps, I should be more specific to my question. Is there a standard example in the Stan Documentation or the Case Studies that show  an example that Stan would be able to but BUGS cannot. For instance, I know Gibbs Sampling performs poorly when your parameters are correlated such as the x and y variable inside a multivariate normal. I am aiming to re-create or duplicate a simple  example where BUGS cannot solve the problem but STAN can, especially in this case for correlated samples.

On Monday, 21 November 2016 02:39:11 UTC, Stephen Martin wrote:
> I've *never* seen a case where Stan takes longer than BUGS *in terms of effective samples*.
> BUGS/JAGS may take much less time to cycle through 2000 iterations, and it may even say it converges.
>
> However, and this is a *big* however:
> 1) BUGS/JAGS do not use random inits. This means the chains are more likely to converge to one mode of an inherently multimodal posterior.
> Due to the problems of gibbs, random walk metropolis, and slice sampling, they will likely stay in the one mode.
> The convergence diagnostics will say "hey, the gibbs sampler has converged across all chains", when in reality the problem is that gibbs found one mode and failed to escape it due to to the conditional sampling that it uses.
> This means you can incorrectly conclude that you explored the full posterior, when in reality you only explored one mode of it, and it failed to escape the mode to find other high density areas of the posterior. Your inference will be potentially jeopardized as a result.
>
> 2) Stan will take longer than Gibbs. Period. Stan has to evaluate the gradient of the posterior in order to simulate a particle flowing across the multidimensional surface.
> You may say "well, my problem is unimodal, so why not use Gibbs, since it's faster"?
> The issue is that per-iteration, Gibbs is faster, but in terms of uncorrelated, representative samples, Stan is usually faster.
> Gibbs has less to compute per iteration, so it can crawl through 2000 iterations quickly.
> Stan has more to compute per iteration, so it will crawl through 2000 iterations slower.
> Then you look at the output and see that Gibbs may only have 40 effective samples (relatively independent samples), because due to conditional sampling, Gibbs can get stuck in highly correlated areas of the posterior.
> On the other hand, Stan may have 1800 effective samples, because it samples across the posterior in a joint, unconditional manner, naturally flowing across the surface. It doesn't have much of an issue with correlated areas, and won't get 'stuck' as often as Gibbs.
>
> As a concrete example of this, I currently have a very high dimensional model.
> It includes a series of mixture models and latent variables.
> It takes Gibbs about 20 minutes to go through it, and Stan about 40 minutes to go through it (2000 iterations each, 1000 of them are warmup in my case).
> After 20 minutes, Gibbs has about 30 effective samples (yes, you read that correctly, 30 out of 1000 post-adaptation draws are relatively independent).
> After 40 minutes, Stan has about 900.
> I'll take that 40 minutes: 900/40 >>> 30/20; roughly 15x 'faster' in terms of effective samples from the posterior.
>
> On Sunday, November 20, 2016 at 6:38:29 PM UTC-6, jt...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > Are there any standard examples in Stan that does not work in BUGS (ie MCMC does not converge or take a miraculously long time to converge)?
> >
> >

messages.subject: Multivariate logistic approximation?
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate logistic approximation?
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I'm just curious what you all think about this.
I know that the logistic distribution is approximately N(0,1.6).
I'm curious whether one could then use a multivariate normal ([zeroes],1.6^2*Sigma) as an approximation to a 'multivariate' logistic distribution? Is this mathematically sound?
The idea of allowing for correlated errors in multinomial probit models makes me wonder if my latent regression for latent categories would benefit from this. Currently, for K latent groups, each individual's multinomial logit values are estimated from covariates, then converted to a simplex using softmax.
So, for(k in 2:K, n in 1:N) { //k = 1 is fixed to 1 for scale in the softmax function
lambda[n,k] ~ logistic(X*Beta, 1)
}
for(n in 1:N){
pi[n] = softmax(lambda[n])
}

This means the categorization error is assumed independent, and allowing a covariance would loosen that assumption.
I can't wrap my head around multinomial probits, or how to convert them to probabilities of membership to latent groups, so I'm wondering if using a multivariate normal that's scaled to be like a logistic would suffice?

Thanks as always for your input.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Example Stan converges but BUGS does not
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Example Stan converges but BUGS does not
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately this is a somewhat ill-posed question.

MCMC will always get the right answer asymptotically, but we might
not be able to reach that asymptotic regime in practice.  In other
words, our MCMC estimators will converge to the right answer as
the number of iterations goes to infinity, but they will only become
useful if they converge fast enough.

Consequently there are two stages of questions to ask:

1 - Will my sampler be able to explore the target distribution well
enough to be able to reach this asymptotic regime in a finite
amount of time?  Formally the sufficient and usually necessary
condition for this to happen is called geometric ergodicity.

2 - Assuming these nice enough properties, will the convergence
time be fast enough that I can get sufficiently precise estimators
in practice?

Most people focus on (2), but (1) is an extremely important condition
in practice.  The problem is that (1) is really, really hard to verify in theory,
and still tricky to verify in practice.  We know that HMC is geometrically
ergodic over a larger class of models  than many other algorithms, but
it’s hard to construct a nontrivial example of something that is unequivocally
fine for HMC but unequivocally bad for another algorithm.

So if you want to do a proper comparison you need to follow these steps:

1 - Simulate data from a model with known parameters.

2 - Ensure that all diagnosis are good, including general diagnostics
like Rhat and sampler-specific diagnostics like those we have for
HMC in Stan.

3 - Ensure that your MCMC algorithm recovers the exact parameters within
a few MCMC standard errors.

Any samplers passing these conditions have not demonstrated any
failures of (1), although that is not a guarantee that (1) holds so be careful.
Now we can continue on to focus on (2).

4 - Compute effective sample sizes.  If effective sample size / iteration < 1e-3
then your sampler probably isn’t converging fast enough to even quantify
its precision well enough to compare.

5 - Finally, rank the samplers by effective sample size / time.  You can
set a target effective sample size and maximum time so that if

(effective sample size / time) * target effect sample size > maximum time

then the sampler is considered impractical

Any samplers failing (5) can be considered to fail (2).

Anyways, the reason that we don’t have a bunch of examples that we can
quote off the top of our head is that doing these comparisons correctly is
subtle and requires lots of time and we haven’t been able to test everything.
You can see some hierarchical models that I used a few years ago in
https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, although even those tests weren’t as
careful as we now know that they should have been!

>>>> On Monday, 21 November 2016 02:39:11 UTC, Stephen Martin wrote:
>>>> I've *never* seen a case where Stan takes longer than BUGS *in terms of effective samples*.
>>>> BUGS/JAGS may take much less time to cycle through 2000 iterations, and it may even say it converges.
>>>>
>>>> However, and this is a *big* however:
>>>> 1) BUGS/JAGS do not use random inits. This means the chains are more likely to converge to one mode of an inherently multimodal posterior.
>>>> Due to the problems of gibbs, random walk metropolis, and slice sampling, they will likely stay in the one mode.
>>>> The convergence diagnostics will say "hey, the gibbs sampler has converged across all chains", when in reality the problem is that gibbs found one mode and failed to escape it due to to the conditional sampling that it uses.
>>>> This means you can incorrectly conclude that you explored the full posterior, when in reality you only explored one mode of it, and it failed to escape the mode to find other high density areas of the posterior. Your inference will be potentially jeopardized as a result.
>>>>
>>>> 2) Stan will take longer than Gibbs. Period. Stan has to evaluate the gradient of the posterior in order to simulate a particle flowing across the multidimensional surface.
>>>> You may say "well, my problem is unimodal, so why not use Gibbs, since it's faster"?
>>>> The issue is that per-iteration, Gibbs is faster, but in terms of uncorrelated, representative samples, Stan is usually faster.
>>>> Gibbs has less to compute per iteration, so it can crawl through 2000 iterations quickly.
>>>> Stan has more to compute per iteration, so it will crawl through 2000 iterations slower.
>>>> Then you look at the output and see that Gibbs may only have 40 effective samples (relatively independent samples), because due to conditional sampling, Gibbs can get stuck in highly correlated areas of the posterior.
>>>> On the other hand, Stan may have 1800 effective samples, because it samples across the posterior in a joint, unconditional manner, naturally flowing across the surface. It doesn't have much of an issue with correlated areas, and won't get 'stuck' as often as Gibbs.
>>>>
>>>> As a concrete example of this, I currently have a very high dimensional model.
>>>> It includes a series of mixture models and latent variables.
>>>> It takes Gibbs about 20 minutes to go through it, and Stan about 40 minutes to go through it (2000 iterations each, 1000 of them are warmup in my case).
>>>> After 20 minutes, Gibbs has about 30 effective samples (yes, you read that correctly, 30 out of 1000 post-adaptation draws are relatively independent).
>>>> After 40 minutes, Stan has about 900.
>>>> I'll take that 40 minutes: 900/40 >>> 30/20; roughly 15x 'faster' in terms of effective samples from the posterior.

Hello Andrew,
yes it works in the NON vectorized version

=======================================
data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
real alpha[N]; // predictor (covariate)
real alpha_2[N]; // predictor (covariate)
real alpha_3[N]; // predictor (covariate)

real y[N]; // outcome (variate)
}
parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma; // outcome noise

real<lower=0> x[N]; // unknown true value
real<lower=0> mu_x; // prior location
real<lower=0> sigma_x; // prior scale

real<lower=0> x_2[N]; // unknown true value
real<lower=0> mu_x_2; // prior location
real<lower=0> sigma_x_2; // prior scale

real<lower=0> x_3[N]; // unknown true value
real<lower=0> mu_x_3; // prior location
real<lower=0> sigma_x_3; // prior scale

}
model {
x ~ normal(mu_x, sigma_x); // prior

x_2 ~ normal(mu_x_2, sigma_x_2); // prior
x_3 ~ normal(mu_x_3, sigma_x_3); // prior

for(n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal( (alpha[n] * x[n]) + (alpha_2[n] * x_2[n]) + (alpha_3[n] * x_3[n]), sigma);
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}
=======================================

But it does not work in the vectorized form (it's obviously possible I'm missing something..)

=======================================
data {
    int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
    int<lower=0> K; // number of cases
    vector[K] alpha[N]; // predictor (covariate)
    real y[N]; // outcome (variate)
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma; // outcome noise

    vector<lower=0>[K] x[N]; // unknown true value
    vector<lower=0>[K] mu_x; // prior location
    vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_x; // prior scale

}
model {
    vector[K] temp;
    for(k in 1:K) x[k] ~ normal(mu_x[k], sigma_x[k]); // prior

    for(n in 1:N) {
        for(k in 1:K)  temp[k] = alpha[n,k] * x[n,k];
        y[n] ~ normal( sum(temp), sigma);

    }
    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}
=======================================

Thanks!

messages.subject: JAGs better than Stan for estimating parameters of Bayesian Network CPDs?
messages.subject_clean: JAGs better than Stan for estimating parameters of Bayesian Network CPDs?
messages.body_plain:
I have a Bayesian network DAG structure, and a conditional probability distribution (CPD) for each node.  I want to fit the parameters of the CPDs with a Bayesian method, since I have some prior knowledge on the parameters.  I implemented my procedure in Stan.  But I wonder, would it not be preferable to fit the procedure in JAGS?

My thinking is that the joint distribution in a Bayesian network can be decomposed into the product of conditional probabilities of each node given its parents in the graph.  The parameters of the CPDs for all the child-parents are independent (usual assumption in graphical models).  So you can have a separate posterior for the parameters of each CPD, conditional on the child and parent nodes.

I'm thinking the Hamiltonian MCMC wouldn't make use of this parameter independence while a Gibbs sampler could.  This might make JAGs preferable to Stan when fitting a BN with more nodes.  Anyone have any insight?

messages.body_plain:
Let’s say you’re even luckier and you can exactly sample from each
of those conditional distributions.  How well will a Gibbs sampler do?

Well, conditioned on the values of the parents you can very quickly
generate new values for the child.  But then you have to generate
new values for the parents based on the children’s values.  Not only
is p(parent | child) not something you have in closed form, any
numerical approximation will require communicating with all of the
children.  So this will probably be slow.

Then you repeat, but because the parents are moving only very
slowly you explore the _joint_ distribution only very slowly.  It can
still take a very long time to generate a nearly independent sample
from the parents, which is the same time it takes for the conditional
distributions of the children to convolve together to generate a nearly
independent sample from their _marginal_ distributions.

In other words, conditional samples aren’t that informative when you
want to sample the entire model.  Especially when you have lots of
parameters.  This is a fundamental weakness of Gibbs sampling
that in some real respects can never be avoided (there are sort of
exceptions, but they tend to be subtle and can be argued to be
different problems entirely).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to create some triangular matrix ?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to create some triangular matrix ?
messages.body_plain:
I'm guessing you want to do some kind of mixture of mixtures
and the M here are the mixing probabilities.  Sadly, we don't
have a clean way to code that.

So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
are both dense and rectangular.  So there's no way to
create a single data structure of the kind you want.  If
you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
can be folded into a function).

My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
and ragged structures.  So hopefully some time later in 2017.  But
even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
simplexes.

- Bob

What the ereror message is saying is that there's a bug
in your model evaluating the log density.  Maybe a variable
isn't being defined or a parameter isn't being declared with
the right constraints.

Also, not clear why you're doing 1 - exp(-sigma) regression
rather than the more standard logistic regression, which
doesn't require that p1 + p2 * age[i] > 0 for it to make sense.
If you really want to keep doing what you're doing, then you need
to constraint p1 and p2 appropriately so that p1 + p2 * age[i] > 0
(e.g., p1 declared with <lower = -fmin(p2 * age)>  --- I think that's
right).

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to create some triangular matrix ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,

Le mardi 22 novembre 2016 à 16:44 -0500, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> I'm guessing you want to do some kind of mixture of mixtures
> and the M here are the mixing probabilities.

Close, but no cigar :-). (A lollipop ?)

Sorry to be so imprecise : the idea does belong to me, but this is (as
always in science) a collaboration, and I do not (yet) have the
approval of all the participants to share it : some of them fear undue
competition.

> Sadly, we don't
> have a clean way to code that.

The ability to use structures of types specified at runtime is one of
the key points of C++'s intricacies (as well as a strong point of
"weakly typed" languages such as Lisp, R or, to some degree, Python).

That's one feature of C++ that Stan should keep or emulate. The
obsession of statisticians with vectors, matrices and arrays is
somewhat unhealthy : it is difficult and "unnatural" to use them to
represent "sparse" or "irregular" suructures, such as the graphs that
are a "natural" representation of correlation (or causality)
structures.

>
> So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
> are both dense and rectangular.  So there's no way to
> create a single data structure of the kind you want.  If
> you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
> and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
> do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
> can be folded into a function).

That's what I was afraid of. Sigh...

>
> My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
> and ragged structures.  So hopefully some time later in 2017.  But
> even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
> simplexes.

A Lisp-like list type with unspecified (or run-time specified) content,
or even a vector of unspecified (or runtime-specified) content (à la
Python list) would be a good start.

After all, C manages that quite efficiently (and sloppily) with
pointers, pointers to pointers, pointers to pointers to... You know the
drill. And Lisp is even more parsimonious (and elegant (and sloppy))
with exactly one data structure to do all of this.

(And yes, I know the drill of debugging the messes so easily created.
Memory allocation and management is not fun... At least, Lisp manages
*that*).

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Nov 22, 2016, at 6:29 PM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob,
>
> Le mardi 22 novembre 2016 à 16:44 -0500, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
>> I'm guessing you want to do some kind of mixture of mixtures
>> and the M here are the mixing probabilities.
>
> Close, but no cigar :-). (A lollipop ?)
>
> Sorry to be so imprecise : the idea does belong to me, but this is (as
> always in science) a collaboration, and I do not (yet) have the
> approval of all the participants to share it : some of them fear undue
> competition.
>
>> Sadly, we don't
>> have a clean way to code that.
>
> The ability to use structures of types specified at runtime is one of
> the key points of C++'s intricacies (as well as a strong point of
> "weakly typed" languages such as Lisp, R or, to some degree, Python).
>
> That's one feature of C++ that Stan should keep or emulate.

I'm not sure what you mean by feature of C++.

If you define an array in C++ (or in C), it's rectangular.

If you use the Eigen matrix library in C++, the matrices
and vectors are dense.  They have a sparse matrix library,
but it's not as complete and it's *much* slower.  The obsession
computer scientists have with rectangular structures is that
it allows us to control memory locality and blocking in order
to write these efficient matrix operations.

If you use the vector class in the standard C++ library,
you do get ragged structures, but you don't get efficient,
low-memory structures with guaranteed memory locality.

So it's all a tradeoff, as usual.

> The
> obsession of statisticians with vectors, matrices and arrays is
> somewhat unhealthy : it is difficult and "unnatural" to use them to
> represent "sparse" or "irregular" suructures, such as the graphs that
> are a "natural" representation of correlation (or causality)
> structures.

I only play a statistician on this list.

As you may have noticed in my last message, I said I'd be
working on adding sparse and ragged structures.  They're
also much harder to work with on the code side, which is why
I can't bang them out in a weekend.

>> So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
>> are both dense and rectangular.  So there's no way to
>> create a single data structure of the kind you want.  If
>> you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
>> and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
>> do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
>> can be folded into a function).
>
> That's what I was afraid of. Sigh...
>
>>
>> My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
>> and ragged structures.  So hopefully some time later in 2017.  But
>> even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
>> simplexes.
>
> A Lisp-like list type with unspecified (or run-time specified) content,
> or even a vector of unspecified (or runtime-specified) content (à la
> Python list) would be a good start.

Not going to happen on my watch.

> After all, C manages that quite efficiently (and sloppily) with
> pointers, pointers to pointers, pointers to pointers to...

No!  It's not efficient at all.  It might seem that way compared
to R or python, but it's terrible from a CPU perspective.
Specifically, it destroys memory locality, introducing "pointer chasing",
which can take an order of magnitude longer than an arithmetic operation
even on a machine with fast memory.  Wherever possible, optimizing
compilers will unfold this chase statically at compile time (inlining,
etc.), but if you make it dynamic, you're hosed.  And making it
really dynamic in terms of type is what makes R and Python so slow
in their interpreted forms.

It also loses type safety because a pointer is just a pointer to
memory.

> You know the
> drill.

Sadly, I do.

> And Lisp is even more parsimonious (and elegant (and sloppy))
> with exactly one data structure to do all of this.

And even less efficient.

> (And yes, I know the drill of debugging the messes so easily created.
> Memory allocation and management is not fun... At least, Lisp manages
> *that*).

Memory allocation isn't the issue (it's an issue, but that's not why
pointers are avoided in modern C++ libraries like Boost and Eigen---it's
the fact that they require pointer-chasing at run time---it's the same
reason templates are preferred over OO).

We're managing dynamic memory  in C++ through operator new abstractions
for reverse-mode autodiff and RAII patterns for other memory (following
both the std::vector and Eigen::Matrix pattern).

And we take code contributions and are happy to welcome new contributors!

- Bob

>
> I've been looking at this code for hours. Can someone help me.
> I am trying to find parameters(tau and mu) of a data generating process of a multivariate normal.
> I am attempting to turn this BUGS code from this link  https://people.orie.cornell.edu/davidr/or678/r2winbugs/MultiNormalBug.pdf
> into stan code
>
>   data {
>     int N;
>     vector[2] mu0;
>     cov_matrix[2] S2;
>     cov_matrix[2] S3;
>     real y[N,2];
>   }
>
> parameters {
>   cov_matrix[2] tau ;
>   vector[2] mu;
> }
>
>
> model {
>
>   mu ~ multi_normal_prec(mu0,S2);
>   tau ~ wishart(3,S3);
>
>
>
>   for(i in 1:N)
>   {
>       y[i,1:2]~multi_normal_prec(mu,tau);   // I have a good feeling that the problem is here

This is also going to fail, because y[i, 1:2] is a real array,
and multi-normal requires a vector.  So you need to declare

  matrix[N, 2] y;

instead.

>

>   }
>
> }
>
> Why do I get the error?
>
> SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
>
>
> ERROR at line 31
>
>  29:        for(j in 1:2){
>  30:          y[i,j] ~normal(0,1) //multi_normal_prec(mu,tau);
>  31:        }
>             ^
>  32:
>
> PARSER EXPECTED: ";"

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

What the parser says.  It expects a semicolon after statements.
The semicolon on line 30 is in a comment.

> Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
>   failed to parse Stan model 'multivar2' due to the above error.
>
> In addition, I would also like to trace the covariance as oppose to the precision but when I insert  this chunk
>
> transformed parameters{
>   Sigma<-inverse(tau)
> }
>
> I also get an error.

Presumably an error that Sigma doesn't exist.  You need to declare Sigma
before you can define it.

This will all work, but we strongly recommend LKJ priors on
correlation matrices coded with Cholesky factors and then scaled
with whatever prior you think makes sense on the scales.  Details
in the regression chapter of the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: R package ctsem - now with hierarchical continuous time dynamic models via Stan
messages.subject_clean: R package ctsem - now with hierarchical continuous time dynamic models via Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hey folks, I put this up on CRAN just a few days ago, some here may be interested. Essentially, hierarchical multivariate carmax (continuous time autoregressive moving average with exogenous variables) models with just a few lines of code.
Feedback or questions on any aspect is welcome.

There is a pre-print of an 'in submission' article on the topic here: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/310747801_Hierarchical_Bayesian_Continuous_Time_Dynamic_Modeling
A quick intro to the software here: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/310747987_Introduction_to_Hierarchical_Continuous_Time_Dynamic_Modelling_With_ctsem

The super quick intro to the software: data with one subject and 1 time point per row, ctModel, ctStanFit, summary, plot

Abstract from the introduction:

 ctsem allows for specification and fitting of a range of continuous and discrete time dynamic models with stochastic system noise. The models may include multiple indicators (dynamic factor analysis), multiple, interrelated, potentially higher order processes, and time dependent (varying within subject) and time independent (not varying within subject) covariates. Classic longitudinal models like latent growth curves and latent change score models are also possible.  Version 1 of ctsem provided structural equation model based functionality by linking to the OpenMx software, allowing mixed effects models (random means but fixed regression and variance parameters) for multiple subjects. For version 2 of the R package ctsem, we include a Bayesian specification and fitting routine that uses the Stan probabilistic programming language, via the rstan package in R. This allows for all parameters of the dynamic model to individually vary, using an estimated population mean and variance, and any time independent covariate effects, as a prior. Frequentist approaches with ctsem are documented in a forthcoming JSS publication (Driver, Voelkle, Oud, in press), and in R vignette form at https://cran.r-project.org/package=ctsem/vignettes/ctsem.pdf , here we provide the basics for getting started with the Bayesian approach included in version 2.

Some of the plots:

Based on suggestions, here are portions of my updated code.

data {
...
  matrix[N,N] I_N;                  // Identity_N
}
parameters {
...

  vector[N] Z;                      // location mean random effect
}
model {
  matrix[N, N] Sigma;

  vector[N] Z_mod;

  Sigma = cov_exp_quad(px_pz, sig, l);                // Squared exponential cov matrix

  for (n in 1:N)

    Sigma[n, n] = Sigma[n, n] + 1e-6;                     // add noise to diagonal
  Sigma = cholesky_decompose(Sigma);

  Z_mod = Sigma * Z;                                            // Transform Standard MVN to Correlated MVN

  l ~ gamma(0.5,1);

  Z ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zero, I_N);               // Standard MVN
  hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + X*beta + Z_mod);
}

Chris

> On Nov 23, 2016, at 11:39 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hey folks, I put this up on CRAN just a few days ago, some here may be interested. Essentially, hierarchical multivariate carmax (continuous time autoregressive moving average with exogenous variables) models with just a few lines of code.
> Feedback or questions on any aspect is welcome.
>
> There is a pre-print of an 'in submission' article on the topic here: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/310747801_Hierarchical_Bayesian_Continuous_Time_Dynamic_Modeling
> A quick intro to the software here: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/310747987_Introduction_to_Hierarchical_Continuous_Time_Dynamic_Modelling_With_ctsem
>
> The super quick intro to the software: data with one subject and 1 time point per row, ctModel, ctStanFit, summary, plot
>
> Abstract from the introduction:
>
>  ctsem allows for specification and fitting of a range of continuous and discrete time dynamic models with stochastic system noise. The models may include multiple indicators (dynamic factor analysis), multiple, interrelated, potentially higher order processes, and time dependent (varying within subject) and time independent (not varying within subject) covariates. Classic longitudinal models like latent growth curves and latent change score models are also possible.  Version 1 of ctsem provided structural equation model based functionality by linking to the OpenMx software, allowing mixed effects models (random means but fixed regression and variance parameters) for multiple subjects. For version 2 of the R package ctsem, we include a Bayesian specification and fitting routine that uses the Stan probabilistic programming language, via the rstan package in R. This allows for all parameters of the dynamic model to individually vary, using an estimated population mean and variance, and any time independent covariate effects, as a prior. Frequentist approaches with ctsem are documented in a forthcoming JSS publication (Driver, Voelkle, Oud, in press), and in R vignette form at https://cran.r-project.org/package=ctsem/vignettes/ctsem.pdf , here we provide the basics for getting started with the Bayesian approach included in version 2.

messages.body_plain:
On your question about length-scale: I would suggest using a distribution for l with a sharper tail, maybe a log-normal or a normal. If the data isn't informative about your length-scale, you'll need to pin it down with a prior. See if you can come up with plausible upper and lower bounds on your length-scale, and then use a distribution to put soft constraints on l. Without specifying stronger priors on l, you can run into trouble where your GP can act as a second constant term in your regression for large draws of length-scale and large draws of alpha. You should also put priors on sig for this reason.

It'll also be good beta, and beta0. Make sure your x, y coordinates and your X variables are standardized, as it'll ensure that your parameters are all on the N(0, 1) scale. If you still have trouble, running a QR decomposition on your X variables and changing your likelihood to:

hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);

can also help the sampler run more efficiently. See here for more info: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/p5vILNIgOYY/MPjb6foPBQAJ

In general, it's hard to run complex models in Stan without specifying proper priors (rather than uniform, as you have here) for all your coefficients, especially if your coefficients are on different scales.

Rob

messages.body_plain:
Assuming your installation is up-to-date with the github version, it looks like a Windows bug in rstan:::find_rtools and/or a configuration error. For some reason, the following code is returning either a 0-length vector or NULL:

system2(file.path(Sys.getenv("R_HOME"), "bin",
                  Sys.getenv("R_ARCH_BIN"), "R"),
                  args = "CMD config CXX", stdout = TRUE)

A good way to debug would be to execute (from the console, or ideally directly into the Rmd):

print(execPath <- file.path(Sys.getenv("R_HOME"), "bin", Sys.getenv("R_ARCH_BIN"), "R"))
print(CXX <- system2(execPath, args = "CMD config CXX", stdout = TRUE))

In my Windows R session R_ARCH_BIN isn't defined, but it looks like it maybe should refer to R_ARCH. A workaround would be to define those environment variables:

if (nchar(Sys.getenv("R_HOME")) == 0) Sys.setenv(R_HOME = R.home())
if (nchar(Sys.getenv("R_ARCH_BIN")) == 0) Sys.setenv(R_ARCH_BIN = .Platform$r_arch)

Presumably, an upstream fix is to check for the NULL result and instead find R by using file.path(R.home("bin"), "R").

After I verified it worked for a linear combination of normally distributed variables

e.g., y = normal(..,..) * 0.5 + normal(..,..) * 0.1 + normal(..,..) * 0.4

I tried to solve the same problem for LOGnormally distributed variables

e.g., y = LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.5 + LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.1 + LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.4

Code, below. However the inference does not have the same performances. Why(?):

1) The problem might itself be harder
2) I have a bug in the code

==================================================
library(MCMCpack)
alpha = rdirichlet(100, c(10,4,1))

x = exp(rnorm(100, 5,0.5))
x_2 = exp(rnorm(100, 2,0.5))
x_3 = exp(rnorm(100, 8,1))

y = (alpha[,1] * x) + (alpha[,2] * x_2) + (alpha[,3] * x_3)

m = "

data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
int<lower=0> K; // number of cases
vector[K] alpha[N]; // predictor (covariate)
real y[N]; // outcome (variate)
}
parameters {

real<lower=0.00001> sigma; // outcome noise
vector<lower=0.00001>[K] sigma_x; // prior scale

vector<lower=0>[K] x[N]; // unknown true value
vector<lower=0>[K] mu_x; // prior location

}

model {
vector[K] temp;
for(n in 1:N) x[n] ~ lognormal(mu_x, sigma_x); // prior

for(n in 1:N) {
for(k in 1:K)  temp[k] = log(alpha[n,k]) + log(x[n,k]);
y[n] ~ lognormal( log_sum_exp(temp), sigma);
}
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2);
sigma_x ~ normal(0.75, 0.3);  //test values
mu_x ~ normal(5,2);  //test values
}
"

fit <- rstan:::stan(
    model_code =m,
    data=list(y=y, alpha = alpha, K = 3, N=100),
    control=list(adapt_delta=0.999, stepsize = 0.01, max_treedepth =15)
)

==================================================

Thanks!

Stefano Mangiola

Data analyst (MSc, MPhil, PhD candidate)
@ Melbourne University
Hovens lab - Papenfuss lab
Royal Melbourne Hospital - WEHI

The real culprit looks like the call to system2. Normally, the output from system2 should be a character string even if an error is generated. Since the result appears to be empty, it might be worth trying to executing the call from the Windows command line (Windows menu -> type "cmd" -> copy/paste "C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-33~1.1/bin/x64/R" CMD config CXX). From what I can see, exit status 2 means that the child R process crashed horribly, which I guess might make sense for it to have a completely empty message.

By "upstream", I meant that it might make sense to modify Rstan's find_rtools function to catch the error and print an informative error message, although so far this seems a little obscure.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Bob.
The data are: Age2, Pos2 and Tot2.
And I think I could not move everything into the generated quantities block because Inew, Rnew are intermediate variables that are involved in the calculation of p (is the probability of being infected: Pos2 ~ binomial(p, Tot2)).
And the idea of marginalization out the discrete paramter is quite complicated in this case???

On Wednesday, 23 November 2016 21:58:46 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It's impossible to tell how to interpret a JAGs
> program without your telling us which variables are
> given as data and which are defined by the model.
>
> But I'm also not sure what you mean by monitor.  You
> mean save in the output for RStan or one of the other
> interfaces?
>
> If Inew and Rnew are discrete parameters (not given as
> data), then you can't translate this directly into Stan.
> You have to marginalize out Inew and Rnew (which might be
> computationally intractable if the counts are high).  Or if nothing
> that depends on Inew or Rnew is used in the rest of the model,
> you can move everything that does depend on them into the
> generated quantities block and make draws from discrete distributions
> like this using binomial_rng.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Nov 23, 2016, at 8:02 AM, Thao Tran <thao...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi everybody,
> > I have one question: How to monitor an intermediate variables?
> > I have some model in Jags and want to translate it into Stan. However, I faced the difficulty to moninor an intermediate variables:
> > The model in Jags has some parts like:
> > model {
> >   # Initial condition: At the lowest age
> >   S[1] <- S1;  I[1] <- I1;  R[1] <- R1
> >   rateRecover     <- 1-exp(-sigma)
> >   # From the 2nd age-group
> >   for (i in 2:84)
> >   {
> >     # lambda[i] = age-dependent-FOI.
> >     lambda[i] <-  beta1 + 2*beta2*age[i]
> >     # Newly infecteds, recovers, susceptible again.
> >     rate[i]   <- 1-exp(-lambda[i])
> >     Inew[i]   ~ dbin(rate[i], S[i-1])                            # New infected
> >     Rnew[i]   ~ dbin(rateRecover, I[i-1])                        # New recovers
> >     # Transition process
> >     S[i]  <- S[i-1]  - Inew[i] ;    I[i]  <- I[i-1]  + Inew[i] - Rnew[i];    R[i]  <- R[i-1]  + Rnew[i]
> >     # Probability to be infected
> >     p[i]  <- (I[i] + R[i])/ (I[i] + R[i] + S[i])
> >     # Put in a logistic regression
> >     Pos[i] ~ dbin(p[i], Tot[i])
> >   }
> >    # Low information prior for parameters
> >    beta1 ~ dnorm(0,.0001);   beta2 ~ dnorm(0,.0001);   sigma ~ dnorm(8,0.0001)
> > }
> >
> >
> >
> > The important part that I could not do the same thing in Stan is:
> >   Inew[i]   ~ dbin(rate[i], S[i-1])                            # New infected
> >   Rnew[i]   ~ dbin(rateRecover, I[i-1])                        # New recovers
> >
> > I was thinking to do something like this for the model in Stan like this:
> > model {
> >   real rateRecover;
> >   real lambda[n];
> >   real rate[n];
> >   int S[n]; int Inew[n];
> >   int I[n]; int Rnew[n];
> >   int R[n]; real p[n];
> >   real prob[n];
> >
> >   rateRecover <- 1-exp(-sigma);
> >   S[1] <- S1; Inew[1] <- 0;
> >   I[1] <- I1; Rnew[1] <- 0;
> >   R[1] <- R1; p[1]    <- (I1+R1)/(I1+R1+S1);
> >   lambda[1] <- p1+p2*0.5;
> >   rate[1]   <- 1-exp(-lambda[1]);
> >   for (i in 2:n) {
> >     lambda[i] <- p1+p2*age2[i];
> >     rate[i]   <- 1 - exp(-lambda[i]);
> >     Inew[i]   ~ binomial(S[i-1] , rate[i])  ;                  # New infected
> >     Rnew[i]   ~ binomial(I[i-1] , rateRecover) ;               # New recovers# Transition process
> >     S[i]  <- S[i-1]  - Inew[i];
> >     I[i]  <- I[i-1]  + Inew[i] - Rnew[i];
> >     R[i]  <- R[i-1]  + Rnew[i]           ;                       # Probability to be infected
> >     p[i]  <- (I[i] + R[i])/ (I[i] + R[i] + S[i]);                # Put in a logistic regression
> >   }
> >
> >
> >   Pos2 ~ binomial(Tot2, p);
> >   # Low information prior for parameters
> >   p1 ~ normal(0,1000);
> >   p2 ~ normal(0,1000);
> >   sigma ~ normal(8,10)   ;                                      # Prior for recovery rates
> >   # Duration in infected class
> > }
> >
> >
> > However, when I ran this model in Stan, I ran into the following error:
> >
> > [459] "  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value."
> > [460] "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:"
> > [461] "Exception thrown at line 39: stan::math::binomial_log: Probability parameter is -0.0480671, but must be between (0, 1)"
> > [462] "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,"

> > [464] "Rejecting initial value:"
> > [465] "  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value."
> > [466] "Rejecting initial value:"
> > [467] "  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity."
> > [468] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value."
> > [469] "Rejecting initial value:"
> > [470] "  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity."
> > [471] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value."
> > [472] "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:"
> >
> >
> > I tried to specify "good" starting values but the sampling could not be initialized.
> > I also tried move verything else into the transformed parameters block like:
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >   real<lower = 0, upper = 1> rateRecover;
> >   real<lower = 0> lambda[n];
> >   real<lower = 0, upper = 1> rate[n];
> >   real<lower = 0, upper = 1> p[n];
> >   rateRecover <- 1-exp(-sigma);
> >   lambda[1] <- p1+p2*0.5;
> >   rate[1]   <- 1-exp(-lambda[1]);
> >
> >   {int S[n]; int Inew[n];
> >   int I[n]; int Rnew[n];
> >   int R[n];
> >   S[1] <- S1; Inew[1] <- 0;
> >   I[1] <- I1; Rnew[1] <- 0;
> >   R[1] <- R1; p[1]    <- (I1+R1)/(I1+R1+S1);
> >   for (i in 2:n) {
> >     lambda[i] <- p1+p2*age2[i];
> >     rate[i]   <- 1 - exp(-lambda[i]);
> >     Inew[i]   <- binomial_rng(S[i-1], rate[i]) ;                 # New infected
> >     Rnew[i]   <-  binomial_rng(I[i-1] , rateRecover);            # New recovers# Transition process
> >     S[i]  <- S[i-1]  - Inew[i];
> >     I[i]  <- I[i-1]  + Inew[i] - Rnew[i];
> >     R[i]  <- R[i-1]  + Rnew[i]           ;                       # Probability to be infected
> >     p[i]  <- (I[i] + R[i])/ (I[i] + R[i] + S[i]);                # Put in a logistic regression

> >
> > }

> >
> >
> > But now I got this error:

> >
> >
> > ERROR at line 35
> >
> >
