> >
> >  34:        rate[i]   <- 1 - exp(-lambda[i]);
> >
> >  35:        Inew[i]   <- binomial_rng(S[i-1], rate[i]) ;                 # New infected
> >
> >                                                       ^
> >
> > Does any one know how I can improve what I was doing?
> > In the attachment is the model I have run.
> > Thank you a lot.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks! Just checking this out now. When you're generating fake data, your procedure for generating the Betas ends up always yielding 0 for Beta[1,2]; is this intentional?

Oh, and instead of:

    m_init <- stan("stan/leung_drton_factor_analysis.stan",
                   iter = 2, chains = 1, data = stan_d)
    m_fit <- stan(fit = m_init, chains = 3, iter = 2000,
                  pars = c("Sigma", "sigma_L", "y_miss"),
                  init_r = .1)

You should do (ignore my linebreaks):

    m_mod <- rstan::stan_model("stan/leung_drton_factor_analysis.stan")
    m_fit <- rstan::sampling(
        object = m_mod
        , data = stan_d
        , chains = 3
        , iter = 2000
        , pars = c("Sigma", "sigma_L", "y_miss")
        , init_r = .1
    )

On Mon, Nov 21, 2016 at 12:39 PM, Maxwell Joseph <maxwell...@gmail.com> wrote:

> You might check out this recent paper by Leung & Drton, who devise priors for the loading matrix that they claim leads to an identified model: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1409.7672
>
> Here's a little simulation and a rough translation to Stan syntax (though some of my priors are different): https://gist.github.com/mbjoseph/952b807bf5aad4a72a9d865f84d67afa
>
> It's a little more complicated than a typical EFA because I have coded it to accommodate and estimate missing observations.
>
> Maybe useful?
>
>
>
>
> On Sunday, November 20, 2016 at 5:35:20 PM UTC-7, Stephen Martin wrote:
> > Under this formulation, I don't think there is a way to address the multimodality. Honestly, I don't think EFA is generally identified. It extracts factors and labels them in descending order of eigenvalue. It then just applies a transform to the eigenvectors to produce a simple structure. I'm also willing to bet that if you ran an EFA multiple times, you may get similar loadings, but with permuted latent variable names.
> >
> > One could try imposing prior constraints where, e.g., loading from 'factor 1' to item 1 puts most of the probability above 0, centered, e.g., at 1, whereas the loading to the same item to the other factors is spiked at 0 with some probability above and below. However, I'm guessing this would only identify one factor and its loadings with other items; the other K-1 factors would probably swap arbitrarily.
> >
> > I'd be interested in solutions to this too, but I'm guessing there isn't one.
> >
> > I *have* tried using Stan to estimate the *number* of latent factors for EFA, but it didn't really work. One could do a mixture-of-K models to determine p(k=K|D), but I opted for something more EFA-flavored, and it failed:
> > 1) use multi_normal as likelihood, estimate Sigma
> > 2) On each iteration, find eigenvalues of Sigma
> > 3) Determine the distribution of eigenvalues to see the posterior probability distributions of eigenvalues in order to assess plausible number of factors to extract. This didn't work well; eigenvalue decomposition was too expensive.
> >
> > On Sunday, November 20, 2016 at 4:28:21 PM UTC-6, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > > As a build-up to the full exploratory factor analysis that we talked about earlier (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/KlwFwrsCBZs), I thought I'd code up a version that takes the number of latent factors as data. Below is my attempt, but I fear I've run into identifiability issues since my posterior samples are multimodal. To test my code, I'm using the same data as in the confirmatory factor analysis version the list helped with earlier (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/vkv_-9qW2IQ), but I the solution suggested there (positively constrain all factor loadings) won't work since in EFA you let each factor potentially load on all outcomes. Thoughts?
> > >
> > > Here's the model:
> > >
> > > data{
> > >
> > >   #N: number of subjects
> > >   int N ;
> > >
> > >   #K: number of outcomes per subject
> > >   int K ;
> > >
> > >   #Y: matrix of outcomes
> > >   matrix[N,K] Y ;
> > >
> > >   #F: number of latent factors
> > >   int F ;
> > >
> > > }
> > > transformed data{
> > >
> > >   # zeroesForFacMeans: vector of zeroes for factor means
> > >   vector[F] zeroesForFacMeans ;
> > >   zeroesForFacMeans = rep_vector(0,F) ;
> > >
> > > }
> > > parameters{
> > >
> > >   # facCor: correlations amongst the F latent factors
> > >   corr_matrix[F] facCor ;
> > >
> > >   # subjFacs: matrix of values for each factor associated with each subject
> > >   matrix[N,F] subjFacs ;
> > >
> > >   # outcomeMeans: means for each outcome
> > >   vector[K] outcomeMeans ;
> > >
> > >   # outcomeSds: SDs for each outcome
> > >   vector<lower=0>[K] outcomeSds ;
> > >
> > >   # betas: how each factor loads on to each outcome.
> > >   matrix[K,F] betas ;
> > >
> > > }
> > > model{
> > >
> > >   #priors, assumes data have been scale()ed
> > >   facCor ~ lkj_corr(1) ;
> > >   outcomeMeans ~ normal(0,1) ;
> > >   outcomeSds ~ weibull(2,1) ;
> > >   to_vector(betas) ~ normal(0,1) ;
> > >
> > >   #generative model:
> > >   for(n in 1:N){ #loop over subjects
> > >     subjFacs[n,] ~ multi_normal(zeroesForFacMeans,facCor) ;
> > >     for(k in 1:K){ #loop over outcomes
> > >       Y[n,k] ~ normal( subjFacs[n,] * betas[k,]' + outcomeMeans[k] , outcomeSds[k] ) ;
> > >     }
> > >   }
> > >
> > > }
> > >

messages.body_plain:
For mysterious reasons, it seems as if R cannot find itself. Reinstalling is probably a good idea, as is confirming that R actually exists in that directory. I'm not a Windows expert, but it sounds like there is some incorrect information in the registry somewhere.

On Thu, Nov 24, 2016 at 12:00 PM, <jt...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

> Somehow I managed to get the error on R now(not just R markdown) when I  call stan() procedure
>
> 1: running command '"C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-33~1.1/bin//R" CMD config CXX' had status 2
> 2: In if (nchar(CXX) > 0) return(TRUE) :
>   the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
>
>
> Am I better off uninstalling and re-installing?
>
> On Thursday, 24 November 2016 11:23:01 UTC, jt...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:
> > So I tried using the command line and it returns, "no such file or directory"
> > When I run devtools::find_rtools() I get  both in console and Rmarkdown I get
> > Rmarkdown
> > Error in if (!file.exists(path)) { : argument is of length zero
> > Calls: <Anonymous> ... eval -> <Anonymous> -> scan_path_for_rtools -> find_gcc49
> > Execution halted
> >
> > Console
> > Error: running command '"C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-33~1.1/bin/x64/R" --no-site-file --no-environ --no-save --no-restore --quiet CMD config CC' had status 2
> >
> > On Thursday, 24 November 2016 04:54:26 UTC, Vincent Dorie wrote:
> > > The real culprit looks like the call to system2. Normally, the output from system2 should be a character string even if an error is generated. Since the result appears to be empty, it might be worth trying to executing the call from the Windows command line (Windows menu -> type "cmd" -> copy/paste "C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-33~1.1/bin/x64/R" CMD config CXX). From what I can see, exit status 2 means that the child R process crashed horribly, which I guess might make sense for it to have a completely empty message.
> > >
> > > By "upstream", I meant that it might make sense to modify Rstan's find_rtools function to catch the error and print an informative error message, although so far this seems a little obscure.
> > >

> > > > devtools::find_rtools()
> > > > ```

> > > > This seems to be some sort of bug in the find_rtools function on Windows, and that should confirm it.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to create some triangular matrix ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,

I agree that there is a tradeoff between expressivity and efficiency (which is, of course, a special aspect of the general tradeoff between competence and performance).

I also agree that the nature of MCMC computations tips the scales very heavily in favor of performance. (and, yes, I understand that a general-purpose Lisp-like list isn't efficient (linear access time...)). In my case, the scale has just been tipped a bit too far...

But a vector-of-vectors *can* be accessed efficiently : it "just" needs a *different* accessor, that offsets its index. *That* should be implemented.

As for implementing it myself : Heavens ! My performance in C++ is abysmal.

For my problem : I think that, in current Stan, I can neglect that M[1,1]==1 constant create auxilliary functions translating (row-column) adresses in M to linear adresses in a vector and back, and declare a vector of parameters :
vector<min=0,max=1>[n*(n+1)/2] p_raw;
and making
 p[suitable_adresses]<-p_raw[same_adresses)/sum(p_raw[same_adresses]).
That should induce Stan to take care of the jacobians. Finding the prior distribution on p_raw giving the "right" Dirichlet prior to p is probably somewhere in the literature, but, in my case, I can also go with a
p_raw~uniform(0,1)
without being far from the truth... which spares me to add anything to the log-posterior for these priors. Yay !
Only problem : force initialization to non-zero values, to avoid sum(p_raw[<suitable_adresses])==0, which would cause a division by 0 exception...

What do you think ?

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

Le mercredi 23 novembre 2016 01:23:59 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
>
> > On Nov 22, 2016, at 6:29 PM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear Bob,
> >
> > Le mardi 22 novembre 2016 à 16:44 -0500, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> >> I'm guessing you want to do some kind of mixture of mixtures
> >> and the M here are the mixing probabilities.
> >
> > Close, but no cigar :-). (A lollipop ?)
> >
> > Sorry to be so imprecise : the idea does belong to me, but this is (as
> > always in science) a collaboration, and I do not (yet) have the
> > approval of all the participants to share it : some of them fear undue
> > competition.
> >
> >> Sadly, we don't
> >> have a clean way to code that.
> >
> > The ability to use structures of types specified at runtime is one of
> > the key points of C++'s intricacies (as well as a strong point of
> > "weakly typed" languages such as Lisp, R or, to some degree, Python).
> >
> > That's one feature of C++ that Stan should keep or emulate.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by feature of C++.
>
> If you define an array in C++ (or in C), it's rectangular.
>
> If you use the Eigen matrix library in C++, the matrices
> and vectors are dense.  They have a sparse matrix library,
> but it's not as complete and it's *much* slower.  The obsession
> computer scientists have with rectangular structures is that
> it allows us to control memory locality and blocking in order
> to write these efficient matrix operations.
>
> If you use the vector class in the standard C++ library,
> you do get ragged structures, but you don't get efficient,
> low-memory structures with guaranteed memory locality.
>
> So it's all a tradeoff, as usual.
>
> > The
> > obsession of statisticians with vectors, matrices and arrays is
> > somewhat unhealthy : it is difficult and "unnatural" to use them to
> > represent "sparse" or "irregular" suructures, such as the graphs that
> > are a "natural" representation of correlation (or causality)
> > structures.
>
> I only play a statistician on this list.
>
> As you may have noticed in my last message, I said I'd be
> working on adding sparse and ragged structures.  They're
> also much harder to work with on the code side, which is why
> I can't bang them out in a weekend.
>
> >> So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
> >> are both dense and rectangular.  So there's no way to
> >> create a single data structure of the kind you want.  If
> >> you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
> >> and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
> >> do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
> >> can be folded into a function).
> >
> > That's what I was afraid of. Sigh...
> >
> >>
> >> My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
> >> and ragged structures.  So hopefully some time later in 2017.  But
> >> even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
> >> simplexes.
> >
> > A Lisp-like list type with unspecified (or run-time specified) content,
> > or even a vector of unspecified (or runtime-specified) content (à la
> > Python list) would be a good start.
>
> Not going to happen on my watch.
>
> > After all, C manages that quite efficiently (and sloppily) with
> > pointers, pointers to pointers, pointers to pointers to...
>
> No!  It's not efficient at all.  It might seem that way compared
> to R or python, but it's terrible from a CPU perspective.
> Specifically, it destroys memory locality, introducing "pointer chasing",
> which can take an order of magnitude longer than an arithmetic operation
> even on a machine with fast memory.  Wherever possible, optimizing
> compilers will unfold this chase statically at compile time (inlining,
> etc.), but if you make it dynamic, you're hosed.  And making it
> really dynamic in terms of type is what makes R and Python so slow
> in their interpreted forms.
>
> It also loses type safety because a pointer is just a pointer to
> memory.
>
> > You know the
> > drill.
>
> Sadly, I do.
>
> > And Lisp is even more parsimonious (and elegant (and sloppy))
> > with exactly one data structure to do all of this.
>
> And even less efficient.
>
> > (And yes, I know the drill of debugging the messes so easily created.
> > Memory allocation and management is not fun... At least, Lisp manages
> > *that*).
>
> Memory allocation isn't the issue (it's an issue, but that's not why
> pointers are avoided in modern C++ libraries like Boost and Eigen---it's
> the fact that they require pointer-chasing at run time---it's the same
> reason templates are preferred over OO).
>
> We're managing dynamic memory  in C++ through operator new abstractions
> for reverse-mode autodiff and RAII patterns for other memory (following
> both the std::vector and Eigen::Matrix pattern).
>
> And we take code contributions and are happy to welcome new contributors!
>
> - Bob
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Looks like you're doing censoring here and I'm going
to guess that Q and W are integers (in which case they
should be arrays, not matrices).

If you need to compute lik_mat rather than just
summing, you can't really do any better than this.

But if you only need the lik_mat to do that sum, then
it's much more efficient to collect the values together
and vectorize.

Most efficiently, you'd pack declare a new (m * n) variable
v that is V packed into an array (you can use to_array to
define it).

Then in transformed data, collect two integer arrays of idxs1.

  idxs1:  indexes of v where you want to use lpdf
  idxs2:  indexes of v where you want to use lcdf

then replace that whole code block with this:

  target += gumbel_lpdf(v[idxs1], 0, sigmaeps);
  target += gumbel_lcdf(v[idxs2], 0, sigmaeps);

It won't be particularly transparent, but you can probably
do something like rename idxs1 as cases_observed and
idxs2 as cases_censored or something like that if that's
what you're coding.

- Bob

> On Nov 24, 2016, at 2:00 PM, Rudolf-Harri Oberg <rudolf...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The problem is the following. You have a matrix V and matrices Q,W. All have dimension nxm. You want to select certain elements from V and use them to increase the log-likelihood. The elements are selected based on the corresponding values from the "condition matrices" Q and W.
>
> The basic (non-vectorized) code looks like this
>
> matrix[n,m] lik_mat;
> lik_mat=rep_mat(0,n,m); //collects likelihood values
>
> for (i in 1:n){
>      for (j in 1:m){
>
> 	 if (Q[i,j]==1){  //condition 1
>
> 	   if (W[i,j]>0) { //condition 2
> 	   lik_mat[i,j]=gumbel_lpdf(log(V[i,j]])|0,sigmaeps);}
>
> 	   if (W[i,j]==0){
> 	   lik_mat[i,j]=gumbel_lcdf(log([V[i,j])|0,sigmaeps);}
> 	 }
> 	 }
> }
> target+=sum(lik_mat)
>
>
> The problem is making the selection, taking the log from the selected values and then either applying gumbel_lpdf or gumbel_lcdf. I am not sure how to improve from the basic loop-case.
>
> I would appreciate any ideas or tips you may have in making this faster.
>
>
>

Hi Bob,

So I want to try both approaches in terms of declaring the missing data elements as parameters or ignoring them. When I ignore the missing data, I need to get rid of the corresponding the matrix entries of my ODE solution. This is easy in a row vector, when I can just eliminate elements and shrink the length of the ODE solution vector. However, for a bivariate matrix in which different elements and different numbers of elements are missing on each row, I can't just delete elements, since it is obviously impossible to have a matrix with different sized rows. What would be the protocol for ignoring elements in this multivariate case? This is a question I was trying to get at earlier, but could not mentally phrase.

>
> No, but I'll try to fix it before rstan 2.13.x goes onto CRAN.

This is an odd error, but you don't need to do parallel chains to trigger it. Simply doing

library(bDif)
saveRDS(bDif:::stanmodels$difSimplex3, file = "/tmp/bDif_object.rda")
q("no")

and then in a new R session

obj <- readRDS("/tmp/bDif_object.rda") # same warning

So, something about the way your stanmodels are being created causes R to look for something in the bDif namespace (which is not yet available). This does not happen with the stanmodels in other R packages, such as rstanarm:::stanmodels$polr.

Ben

Hi everyone,

Anyone have idea if the Von Mises-Fisher distribution is expected to be available in the future at rstan?

I saw at the Stan user manual just the Von Mises distribution, which is restricted for only two dimensions. I am developing a AMMI Bayesian model that is a nice model to get insights into Genotype by enviroment interactions of plants under genetic breeding. A restriction of these models is the need to sample orthomal set of vectors, which can be trivially achieved with the Von Mises-Fisher distribution (can be extended beyond two dimentions).

Thank you!
Best,
Jhonathan Pedroso
Ph.D candidate in Genetics and Plant Breeding at University of São Paulo, Brazil.

On Saturday, November 26, 2016 at 1:05:58 PM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
> Thanks so much for looking at this. It seems that you *have* to import Rcpp into the namespace. That's the only necessary change (So I cherry picked from your PR).
>
> Apparently methods isn't required for imports, and I think recent R versions assume methods as part of base; maybe cran has a separate policy though.

We have had endless headaches over the years every time we have tried to avoid putting methods into the Depends field. At a minimum, your package won't work if called via Rscript unless the --default-packages=methods argument is specified.

> What is the preference of rstan devs about importing or depending on rstan? I chose to depend (not import) on rstan so that the rstan package is attached upon loading bDif, so all the rstan plotting and summary functions are also available. Is there a particular reason why I should choose to import instead of depend on stan (in the Description)?

CRAN has a stronger opinion that we do. The print and summary functions should work for a stanfit object even if rstan is only in the Imports field. If there are particular rstan functions you think your users will need, you can always import them and reexport them. For plotting, it is now better to use the bayesplot package directly (the rstanarm package does so now and rstan will follow).

Ben

messages.subject: Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.subject_clean: Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
I am working with time series data. The actual application (to electricity consumption in large buildings) involves time series that have a regular daily pattern (low at night, high during the day) that is sometimes changed; for instance, lights might be scheduled to turn on at 6 a.m. daily until,  they are changed to turn on at 5 a.m. instead for a few weeks, then set back to 6 a.m.

The model I really want to fit is quite a bit more complicated than this, but let's start here.

I have tried an implementation of this that "should work" but doesn't. The problem seems to be with convergence rather than with the model per se.

I have attached a file called "CreateData.R". Sourcing this file in R will create a time series y, as well as some ancillary parameter values (such as the number of data points per day, and their time-of-day indices).  This fake data set is very unrealistic: it is flat at y=1 every hour of every day for three weeks, then goes up to y=2 for the next three weeks, then back to y=1. Then some iid normal noise is added.

The model writes
ypred[ t ] = betaTOD[ iWeek[t], iTOD[t]]
where iWeek[t] is the week number ( = 1 for every hour of the first week, 2 for the second week, etc.)
and iTOD[t] is the time of day for time t.

the betaTOD values are themselves written as a sum:
betaTOD[jWeek, jTOD] = betaTOD[1, jTOD] + phiTOD[jWeek, jTOD]

That is, betaTOD in a given week is whatever it was in week 1 at that time of day, plus a change.
The change is itself a sum over "changes", where each change has a start time, a duration, and a magnitude delta:

 phiTOD[week, jTOD] = phiTOD[week, jTOD] + deltaTOD[iChangeTOD, jTOD];

 In the test example given, there is only one change for each hour of the day as determined  with nChangesTOD = 1. For the test data, this is the right number.

SimpleModel.Stan.txt contains a Stan model that fits the data. You can run it with a command like:
res = stan("./SimpleModel.Stan.txt", iter=400, chains=3, data=c("cooked", "nN", "nChangesTOD", "nTOD", "nWeeks", "iTOD", "iWeek", "sigmaMax", "y"))

The parameter "cooked" chooses between two models:
If cooked = 1, very tight prior distributions are set, for instance:
 if ( cooked==1 ) {
        weekStartTOD[iChangeTOD, jTOD] ~ normal(3.1,0.01);
        tauTOD[iChangeTOD, jTOD] ~ normal(3.1, 0.01);
        deltaTOD[iChangeTOD, jTOD] ~ normal(1.0, 0.1);
}

If cooked is not 1, then more real-world priors are used.

So here's the problem: if you use cooked = 0, you don't get the right answer...or, rather, maybe you can but you would need to set the number of iterations to some very very large number.

But if you set cooked=1, you do get the right answer. (For this test problem, with only a small amount of noise added, the 'right answer' is quite tightly defiined, with distant parameter values being very unlikely.

What's happening is this: the "start time" and the "duration" are effectively quantized with units of weeks. They are defined as continuous variables, but whether the value of the start time is 2.1 or 2.9 or 2.99 makes no difference: all of these define the start time to be in "week 2". This makes it easy for the system to get trapped in a local likelihood maximum and unable to find the global one.

Suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Phil Price

messages.subject: Is there a good way of hierarchically modeling correlation matrices?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a good way of hierarchically modeling correlation matrices?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Could anyone recommend some reading on hierarchically modeling correlation
matrices?

My problem looks like this. I have a multi-dimensional unbounded outcome Y.
You could think of each observation as being a vector of GDP growth, investment
growth and consumption growth. I have repeated observations for many countries.
If I had a single country, I would just build a vector autoregression, which Stan
handles nicely. Seeing as I have many countries, I want to build a hierarchical
VAR. Something like

Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu[country[n]], quad_form_diag(Omega[country[n]], tau[country[n]]))

but where I have a model for each country's mu.

The question is, I can easily specify hierarchical priors for mu and tau, but I don't
know what I should be using for Omega. At the moment I'm modeling

Omega[country] ~ lkj(nu)

nu ~ half cauchy(0, 5)

But this gives away mountains of information; might as well not be doing partial pooling.

Any thoughts on approaches to take?

Jim

messages.body_plain:
The most natural thing to do is a hierarchical model
on the latent, unconstrained space.  For a correlation
matrix that reduces to the N(N-1)/2 lower diagonal
elements of the Cholesky factor.  In other words,
have N(N-1)/2 independent univariate hierarchical
models then fill in a the lower diagonal elements
with those values, ones on the diagonal, and then
construct Omega.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is there a good way of hierarchically modeling correlation matrices?
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, November 26, 2016 at 10:34:28 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> The most natural thing to do is a hierarchical model
> on the latent, unconstrained space.  For a correlation
> matrix that reduces to the N(N-1)/2 lower diagonal
> elements of the Cholesky factor.  In other words,
> have N(N-1)/2 independent univariate hierarchical
> models then fill in a the lower diagonal elements
> with those values, ones on the diagonal, and then
> construct Omega.

This would be easier if the transformation from

real numbers -> canonical partial correlations -> Cholesky factors -> correlation matrices

were exposed in the Stan language. You could look at the implementations (yes, there are two for reasons I don't understand) in Stan or you could access them yourself with a little C++ in version 2.13.

But perhaps a more fundamental issue is that I don't think anyone knows what hierarchical prior to put on the real numbers in the unconstrained space. The LKJ thing is derived from a symmetric beta priors over the (-1,1) interval on the canonical partial correlations, but those have mean zero and so their derivation wouldn't go through in a hierarchical setting. The onion method is more promising since it is derived from unit vectors to the left of the diagonal on the Cholesky factor of a KxK correlation matrix, but there is no easy way in the Stan language to get as many unit vectors as there are countries for each value of k between 2 and K.

An alternative would be to set in transformed parameters

for (c in 1:N_countries) Omega[c] = alpha * Omega_global + (1 - alpha) * Omega_local[c];

where Omega_global is a correlation matrix with a LKJ(1) (i.e. joint uniform) prior, each Omega_local[c] is a correlation matrix with a LKJ(eta) prior for eta >> 1, and alpha is a weight over the [0,1] interval with a beta or Kumaraswamy prior. Or maybe set eta = alpha / (1 - alpha).

Ben

Hi Stan Developers,

Thank you again for your very patient help in the last thread. I learned a lot from it and profusely apologize for the amount of time I've taken from you guys. A few more issues have been cropping up as I've been coding. I will break them up into parts.

1) I tried returning a real[N,2] derived from my ODE solutions and found that to be impossible, so right now I am jamming my solutions into a real[2*N] and then converting to a vector[N,2] in another block. Would it be possible to return a multi-dimensional array from a function and avoid the "Mismatched array dimensions. Returned expression does not match return type LHS type = real[]; RHS type = real[,]" error?

2) On a related note, is there a vectorized way of doing the operation

for (n in 1:N_t) {
  ratios_hat_vector[n,1] = ratios_hat[n];
  ratios_hat_vector[n,2] = ratios_hat[N_t+n];
}

with a single function? I tried doing the to_vector operation and got the error message, "dimension mismatch in assignment; variable name = ratios_hat_vector, num dimensions given = 1; right-hand side dimensions = 0."

3) I left missing data elements blank on my CSV file, and R fills the those elements with "NA." I thought I could leave that alone, but Stan does not seem to like that and gives me the error message "Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : Stan does not support NA (in CO2_flux_ratios) in data failed to preprocess the data; sampling not done." What should I fill in then for missing data elements in my CSV file? I thought I could simply ignore the NA's previously.

4) Per our last discussion, I took Bob and Michael's advice and "ignore" rather than impute the missing data such that sometimes likelihood incorporates both measurements, and other times only uses the one available measurement. In my code which I've attached, I have the following lines based on Bob's example code in the previous thread:

//likelihood
ratios_vector[obs12] ~ multi_normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs12], Sigma); // Fit elements with both entries
ratios_vector[obs1,1] ~ normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs1,1], Sigma[1,1]); // Fit elements with only flux ratio entries
ratios_vector[obs2,2] ~ normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs2,2], Sigma[2,2]); // Fit elements with only microbial ratio entries

(I am not sure I can use this notation, since obs12, obs1, obs2 are arrays of ints that list the indices for which ratios_vector has both elements, is missing one element, and is missing the other element, respectively. I just have it in there for now in the hopes that this will work for vectorization.) Sigma[1,1] and Sigma[2,2] represent measurement error/misprediction for each measurement. Can I assume the covariance as 0 for the Sigma matrix just to have slightly fewer varying parameters?

---------

Again, many thanks for all your help. As someone who came from a biology background and fell into a computational PhD topic, I've been struggling a lot with the pedagogy of the stats courses at my institution, and would be utterly lost without help from this Google Group. I've been relying heavily on reading Bob's code examples and rewatching Michael's videos on Youtube. I would gladly order a pizza for all of you guys in appreciation if you weren't geographically spread out.

No.  See the manual chapter on missing data.  Stan doesn't
accept NA values in any form under any coding.  You either
need to use a sparse encoding of the variables that are there
(see the ragged and sparse structure) or you need to do as
I suggested last time and pass in dummy values and then a separate
indexing of where values show up.

things work the way you expect.

But I think the answer is that yes, what you have here

you're better off storing away the results in transformed
data so you only have to compute it once.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is there a good way of hierarchically modeling correlation matrices?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is there a good way of hierarchically modeling correlation matrices?
messages.body_plain:
Ben, this is very helpful.

A question about the partial pooling weights. In this specification, alpha is common across countries. My panel is very imbalanced, so I don't know that is the best assumption (it might be, I'm just not sure). Are you aware of any methods that would allow me to set/estimate these weights, taking into account the relative noisiness of the local and global correlations?

Or is that implicitly set by the relative degrees of freedom of the local correlation prior?

On Saturday, November 26, 2016 at 11:53:48 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Saturday, November 26, 2016 at 10:34:28 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > The most natural thing to do is a hierarchical model
> > on the latent, unconstrained space.  For a correlation
> > matrix that reduces to the N(N-1)/2 lower diagonal
> > elements of the Cholesky factor.  In other words,
> > have N(N-1)/2 independent univariate hierarchical
> > models then fill in a the lower diagonal elements
> > with those values, ones on the diagonal, and then
> > construct Omega.
>
> This would be easier if the transformation from
>
> real numbers -> canonical partial correlations -> Cholesky factors -> correlation matrices
>
> were exposed in the Stan language. You could look at the implementations (yes, there are two for reasons I don't understand) in Stan or you could access them yourself with a little C++ in version 2.13.
>
> But perhaps a more fundamental issue is that I don't think anyone knows what hierarchical prior to put on the real numbers in the unconstrained space. The LKJ thing is derived from a symmetric beta priors over the (-1,1) interval on the canonical partial correlations, but those have mean zero and so their derivation wouldn't go through in a hierarchical setting. The onion method is more promising since it is derived from unit vectors to the left of the diagonal on the Cholesky factor of a KxK correlation matrix, but there is no easy way in the Stan language to get as many unit vectors as there are countries for each value of k between 2 and K.
>
> An alternative would be to set in transformed parameters
>
> for (c in 1:N_countries) Omega[c] = alpha * Omega_global + (1 - alpha) * Omega_local[c];
>
> where Omega_global is a correlation matrix with a LKJ(1) (i.e. joint uniform) prior, each Omega_local[c] is a correlation matrix with a LKJ(eta) prior for eta >> 1, and alpha is a weight over the [0,1] interval with a beta or Kumaraswamy prior. Or maybe set eta = alpha / (1 - alpha).
>
> Ben
>

You could allow alpha and / or eta to vary by country. Certainly, if you have fewer observations on some countries than others, then the posterior distribution of the parameters for those countries will tend to be less concentrated. But I don't really see how that would affect your prior beliefs about alpha and / or eta prior to observing the data (and thus which countries have more observations).

Hi Charles,

On Nov 28, 2016, at 6:25 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I understand this is already somewhat implemented in Stan, but not available due to limitations with the autodiff?

Michael already implemented RHMC in the Stan (github.com/stan-dev/stan <http://github.com/stan-dev/stan>) code base. It has not been enabled in any of the interfaces for 2 good reasons related to higher order autodiff.

1. For any expression in the Stan language, reverse mode autodiff works. That's what Stan currently needs. For forward mode autodiff, not only does everything not compile, we're uncertain about which functions have bugs. We could use help with both implementation and testing of higher order autodiff.

2. Builds. It won't work on Windows using the g++ distributed with RTools. (It might with the latest version; I haven't checked in a while.) Builds will take something like 5x longer (don't quote me on time). And that's all conditional on #1.

> Just wondering if there is any sort of expected time frame on this, or any way to make use of it as is?

If you're comfortable with C++, it's straightforward getting it working. Just a couple tweaks necessary.

You're on your own for results, though. I don't think any of the dev team is ready to take on users pushing higher order autodiff when we know it's untested.

> I think it would be helpful for the sorts of models I'm interested in.

Just curious: what makes you think that? Are gradients at different points of the lpdf in the typical set varying wildly? Are there any reparameterizations you can do? I think even recognizing that issue probably means you can do something to solve it.

> If it's still a long way away I might put a more concerted effort into getting a rough implementation of http://www2.warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/statistics/staff/academic-research/lan/publication/lmc.pdf , just to see how things go...

messages.body_plain:
I have tried ADVI lately on three different kinds of models:

- Small negative binomial regressions, just out of curiosity. Full rank, didn't always estimate the theta parameter well. Not many replications to estimate it, so I'm not surprised ADVI has problems.

- A simple non-negative regression model with fairly big count data (~ 100000, seven covariates), where I needed only point estimates for a recommender system. Full rank, works as expected.

- A nonnegative component model for count data, with some hierarchy in the model. 240k counts, 10k parameters. Mean field, works well and is surprisingly fast with the new indexing notation (4 minutes). Our goal is not to make exact inference, but to find descriptive components. Goes to local minima etc., but this is not ADVI's fault. Sometimes throws an overflow, don't remember which function it comes from.

A colleague has tested mean-field ADVI for a Poisson Factorisation model, with about 3M lines of data and at least the same number of parameters. (log-)Gaussian may not fit well with the posterior, or maybe the default gamma parametrisation was bad for mean field.

All these are quick tests made in the context of commercial projects or theses, so we don't have definite reports or papers to show.

> Thank you for reading this email! I plan to fit a model as follows:
>
> E(y)=b0+b1*(w1*x1+w2*x2+(1-w1-w2)*x3)
>
> where b0 and b1 are coefficients, w1, w2 and (1-w1-w2) are weights for x1, x2, and x3. I write a stan code for it. But I am not sure whether it is efficient or not. Could you give some suggestions on how to correct or improve the code? Thank you!

Presuming that you want w1 > 0, w2 > 0, and w3 = 1 - w1 - w2 > 0, then you need to do in the parameters block

simplex[3] w;

instead of

real<lower=0,upper=1> w1;
real<lower=0,upper=1> w2;

and then get rid of the uniform priors on w1 and w2. Use w[1] for w1, etc.

Ben

> On your question about length-scale: I would suggest using a distribution for l with a sharper tail, maybe a log-normal or a normal. If the data isn't informative about your length-scale, you'll need to pin it down with a prior. See if you can come up with plausible upper and lower bounds on your length-scale, and then use a distribution to put soft constraints on l. Without specifying stronger priors on l, you can run into trouble where your GP can act as a second constant term in your regression for large draws of length-scale and large draws of alpha. You should also put priors on sig for this reason.
>
> It'll also be good beta, and beta0. Make sure your x, y coordinates and your X variables are standardized, as it'll ensure that your parameters are all on the N(0, 1) scale. If you still have trouble, running a QR decomposition on your X variables and changing your likelihood to:
>
> hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);
>
> can also help the sampler run more efficiently. See here for more info: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/p5vILNIgOYY/MPjb6foPBQAJ
>
>
> In general, it's hard to run complex models in Stan without specifying proper priors (rather than uniform, as you have here) for all your coefficients, especially if your coefficients are on different scales.

>
>
> Rob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
On Nov 26, 2016, at 9:03 PM, Phil Price <pnp...@creekcats.com> wrote:
>
>
> I am working with time series data. The actual application (to electricity consumption in large buildings) involves time series that have a regular daily pattern (low at night, high during the day) that is sometimes changed; for instance, lights might be scheduled to turn on at 6 a.m. daily until,  they are changed to turn on at 5 a.m. instead for a few weeks, then set back to 6 a.m.
>
> The model I really want to fit is quite a bit more complicated than this, but let's start here.
>
> I have tried an implementation of this that "should work" but doesn't. The problem seems to be with convergence rather than with the model per se.

...

> What's happening is this: the "start time" and the "duration" are effectively quantized with units of weeks. They are defined as continuous variables, but whether the value of the start time is 2.1 or 2.9 or 2.99 makes no difference: all of these define the start time to be in "week 2". This makes it easy for the system to get trapped in a local likelihood maximum and unable to find the global one.

In general, that approach shouldn't work.  The assumption built into
Stan's algorithms is that the log density function is continuously
differentiable.  By hacking in discrete variables the way you do, you break
that property.

We see a lot of people try to do things like sample a Bernoulli(theta) by

parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> u1;

...

transformed parameters {
  int z1 = u1 < theta;

This won't work.   I think the impression people get is that Stan is
somehow sampling u1 first uniform(0, 1) and then assigning z1.  But
that's not how it works.  Instead, the algorithm feeds in values of
the parameters to evaluate, and Stan follows the gradients.  Here there
are no gradients to follow.

The only thing that'll work well in Stan is marginalizing out the
discrete parameter.  As we discussed when you're in town, this can be
combinatorially prohibitive.  If it is, then you're just out of luck with
the model as formulated in Stan.  Andrew or others may have ways to reformulate
to get the same effect, but I don't have any ideas.

- Bob

Rob,

Everything helped, but I think proper priors on all parameters was the golden ticket. It sampled MUCH faster after that change. I really appreciate your help.

Thanks,

Chris

On Wednesday, November 23, 2016 at 1:10:57 PM UTC-8, Rob Trangucci wrote:

> On your question about length-scale: I would suggest using a distribution for l with a sharper tail, maybe a log-normal or a normal. If the data isn't informative about your length-scale, you'll need to pin it down with a prior. See if you can come up with plausible upper and lower bounds on your length-scale, and then use a distribution to put soft constraints on l. Without specifying stronger priors on l, you can run into trouble where your GP can act as a second constant term in your regression for large draws of length-scale and large draws of alpha. You should also put priors on sig for this reason.
>
> It'll also be good beta, and beta0. Make sure your x, y coordinates and your X variables are standardized, as it'll ensure that your parameters are all on the N(0, 1) scale. If you still have trouble, running a QR decomposition on your X variables and changing your likelihood to:
>
> hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);
>
> can also help the sampler run more efficiently. See here for more info: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/p5vILNIgOYY/MPjb6foPBQAJ
>
>
> In general, it's hard to run complex models in Stan without specifying proper priors (rather than uniform, as you have here) for all your coefficients, especially if your coefficients are on different scales.

>
>
> Rob
>

messages.subject: Why is rstan so much slower in a docker container
messages.subject_clean: Why is rstan so much slower in a docker container
messages.body_plain:
I know I've asked a variant of this before. But I have worked on a couple of projects now that use run rstan in docker containers and every time I've noticed the runs within a docker container are about 4 times slower relative to what I get from running it on the host machine.

For example, the current project I am working on has the following dockerfile which loads the environment and data for an entire project:

FROM rocker/tidyverse:3.3.2
MAINTAINER James Camac <james...@gmail.com>

RUN    apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
         libcurl4-openssl-dev \
         texlive-latex-recommended \
         texlive-latex-extra \
         texlive-humanities \
         texlive-fonts-recommended \
         texlive-science \
         lmodern \
         git \
    && apt-get clean \
    && apt-get autoremove \
    && rm -rf var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN install2.r -r "https://mran.revolutionanalytics.com/snapshot/2016-11-25/" --error \
    --deps "TRUE" \
    rstan reshape2 cowplot lubridate

RUN installGithub.r \
    --deps "TRUE" \
    richfitz/remake

RUN rm -rf /tmp/downloaded_packages/ /tmp/*.rds

RUN git clone https://github.com/jscamac/Alpine_Shrub_Experiment /home/Alpine_Shrub_Experiment

This project can then be made reproducible (from data analysis through to compiling the pdf of the manuscript) in an interactive docker container by building the image and then running an interactive container, where you can move to the folder home/Alpine_Shrub_Experiment and run `remake::make()`.
On my host computer (Macbook Pro, OSX 10.11.6, 16 GB RAM, i7 2.8 GHz) the whole process takes about 50 minutes (it compiles the data, runs 11 stan models, builds figures and compiles the manuscript). However, using a docker container (allowing it full use of my machine) it takes 195 minutes.

Am I missing something with linux and some stan optimisation?

Dear Ben,

Thanks so much for the help. I removed the "transformed parameters" block and followed your instructions in the "parameters" block. domain error in lub_constrain;  lower bound = inf must be strictly less than upper bound = inf                     1
When a numerical problem occurs, the Metropolis proposal gets rejected.
However, by design Metropolis proposals sometimes get rejected even when there are no numerical problems.
Thus, if the number in the 'count' column is small, do not ask about this message on stan-users."

I understand that it happens for the change I made in the "parameters" block. So this is not actually an error but it indicates a more accurately specified model. And it occurs for very few number of cases (I got count=1 for most of the chains). But, when the true parameter k is greater than 1, I think, this code will not work. I took an exponential with rate 0.1 for the parameter "alpha". Everything else is same.  Among the 6 parameters, the code recovered:

2) mu; k; p; c in model 2

3)mu, beta     in model 3

.  How can I make a STAN code that will recover parameters for all sets of parameters?

Tas

The earthquake magnitudes follow a left-truncated exponential distribution with parameter "beta". I am estimating "beta" together with the 5 parameters of the ETAS model . This "joint estimation" is necessary because to avoid explosive simulation (for later use), the parameters have to satisfy two conditions:
> >
> > 1) beta> alpha;
> > 2) k*beta/ (beta-alpha) <1.
>
> In the parameters block, do something like
>
> real<lower = 0, upper = 1> k;
> real<lower = 0> alpha;
> real<lower = alpha, upper = -alpha / (k - 1)> beta;
>
> The restriction that k < 1 may be scientifically wrong. But you need some way of specifying lower and upper bounds on the parameters that can always be satisfied (i.e. lower is always less than upper). And you need a good approximation to that integral in the log-likelihood.
>
> Ben

Hi James,

I have found through experimentation (and Bob has mentioned earlier) that Stan is often bottlenecked by memory. I have found dramatic decreases in run-times moving to machines with faster memory, even with slower CPUs. There are a handful of reports of slow IO/memory performance on Docker images. For example:

https://github.com/docker/docker/issues/21485

I am no expert, but I would guess that could be the culprit.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
> > What's happening is this: the "start time" and the "duration" are effectively quantized with units of weeks. They are defined as continuous variables, but whether the value of the start time is 2.1 or 2.9 or 2.99 makes no difference: all of these define the start time to be in "week 2". This makes it easy for the system to get trapped in a local likelihood maximum and unable to find the global one.
>
> In general, that approach shouldn't work.  The assumption built into
> Stan's algorithms is that the log density function is continuously
> differentiable.  By hacking in discrete variables the way you do, you break
> that property.

I'm not surprised, indeed this is sort of what I expected...except that at the Stan meeting I attended a few weeks ago, I thought this was the model the Stan experts said I should fit.

I thought it seemed possible that the prior distributions could provide a sort of tug in one direction or another: even though the predictions are exactly the same for any start times that have the same integer week number, the likelihood will not be the same. But you're right that it will be discontinuous across the boundary, so I guess that is the problem.

Did I misunderstand what Andrew and Michael were suggesting?

> The only thing that'll work well in Stan is marginalizing out the
> discrete parameter.  As we discussed when you're in town, this can be
> combinatorially prohibitive.  If it is, then you're just out of luck with
> the model as formulated in Stan.  Andrew or others may have ways to reformulate
> to get the same effect, but I don't have any ideas.
>
>

If I have to try every combination of start time and duration, that would be combinatorially prohibitive. With 100 weeks of data, there are 100 possible start times, and, uh...let's see, duration has to be less than or equal to the number of remaining weeks, so... that's (100*99) + (99*98) + (98*97) + ... different possibilities, which is 1 million. And each time of day could have a different start time and duration, so if I do hours that's 24 million (and in fact it would be more convenient to work with 15-minute data, so that's 100 million)...and this all assumes just one "impulse" per time of day, over a two-year period. A more common real-world case would be 10 or more.  10 would not be 10x as much computation, since we could set a constraint that the next impulse has to be after the first one has ended, but I would still be in the hundreds of millions of combinations. This is not an appealing approach.

However, it seems like there should be a way to greatly reduce the amount of computation because it shouldn't be necessary to test every possible start time and duration:  Although p(y | start time, duration, magnitude ) is not a _continuous_ function of start time and duration, it is monotonic. If I were writing a search algorithm rather than a statistical model, I could find the week that is most different from the average and set the start time at the start of that week and the duration to 1 week. Then try increasing the duration to 2 weeks. Keep increasing the duration until things stop getting better. Then try stepping the start time back one week while increasing the duration one week (so the end time stays the same). Keep doing this until things stop getting better. I'm done. Then, to do another impulse, do the same thing with the residuals from the first one. And so on. Repeat until I'm happy with how well things fit.

Perhaps there are other approaches too.

Hmm. I would love to be able to do all of this in Stan, but perhaps I will need to try some kind of ping pong approach: use one system to come up with the first set of impulse start times and durations, then have Stan fit all of the continuous parameters, then pop back to system 1 to come up with the next impulse times, etc. Ugh.

Thanks for your help, Bob.

messages.body_plain:
Interesting. Stan doesn't "draw" random variables from distributions--the particle needs
to be able to transition from one part of the density to another. At a guess, the issue here
is might be that there is so little probability mass between the mixtures that it has difficulty
making its way around.

If you use a larger scale (say, 1 rather than .01) it should work. If what you are trying to do is
approximate a dirac delta function, then you'll have a bit of trouble. This thread might help
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/rachael$20dirac%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/BkVJanzue4U/eN4CmGHtAAAJ

Jim

Yes.

Set up data in R:
library(rstan)
stan_data <- list(mu = array(1:30, c(10, 3)))
fit <- stan("test.stan", data = stan_data, algorithm="Fixed_param")

test.stan:
data {
  vector[3] mu[10];

}
transformed data {
  simplex[3] p;
  p[1] = 0.25;
  p[2] = 0.5;
  p[3] = 0.25;
}
model {
}
generated quantities {
  real theta;

  int index;
  int mixture_component;

  index = categorical_rng(rep_vector(0.1, 10));
  mixture_component = categorical_rng(p);
  theta = normal_rng(mu[index, mixture_component], 0.01);
}

Does that make sense?

messages.subject: Inference in Stan about a distribution using data informative of E(X|X>a & X<b)
messages.subject_clean: Inference in Stan about a distribution using data informative of E(X|X>a & X<b)
messages.body_plain:
As a simple motivating example, consider a normally distributed variable X, and a dataset that contains the count and average value of X within different ranges from a sample of X-values.

For instance, we might have a dataset of ranges and averages as follows:

      category count   average
1: (73.9,89.6]    58  84.97311
2:  (89.6,105]   235  98.10409
3:   (105,121]    96 111.14513
4:   (121,137]    11 125.60737

We know the underlying variable X comes from a normal distribution (in this case - the data were simulated with mean 100 and sd 10) and we want to estimate the mean and sd of the distribution.

Can anyone help point me towards some way of coding the model block in Stan to use data of this form to infer the parameters of the distribution generating the X-values?

Although the illustration uses a normal distribution, I am curious as to whether there is a way of doing this that would work more generally than just in the case of a normal distribution. I've come across several related inference problems that I hope to find a way to code in Stan, where the key is to use information that speaks to the expected value of a distribution conditional on the values being in some specific range, and where I want to use this information to infer the underlying parameters of the distribution involved. Mathematically, I would express this by stating that some observed value is equal to some definite integral - but I haven't found a way to express such relationships in the Stan model block. Is it possible, or is there a "trick" that can be used to reformulate the problem and make it easier to code in Stan?

Sincerely,
Ole

messages.body_plain:
As with any model it is best to reason about your problem _generatively_.
Right now the problem you propose has gaping holes which is why it is
so confusing.

The first thing you need is a model for the latent value of x.  Let’s follow
your example and say that it’s Gaussian with unknown mean and standard
deviation,

mu ~ some_prior;
sigma ~ some_prior;
x ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Now you have a censoring process where you get only imitated information
about this distribution.  The binning part is straightforward: the relative
weight of each category is given by integrating the latent distribution between
the boundaries,

p_{i} = normal_cdf(right_bundary | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(left_boundary | mu, sigma);

The likelihood is then naturally a multinomial process,

n ~ multinomial(p, sum(N));

Which you can also approximate with individual Poisson distributions if N is
big enough,

n_{i} ~ poisson(sum(N) * p_{i});

And for the average?  Well, that’s going to be awkward no matter what given
that it’s hard to come up with a measurement model for “averages”.  Given
the latent distribution for x and the boundaries you can conceivably compute
the true mean in each category, although it won’t be analytic for event this
simple example (unless I’m missing some clever trick).  But even then, if
you knew the exact category means, mu_{i}, how would you define a
measurement model for “average” data, \bar{x}_{i}?  One immediate issue is that
any reasonable measurement model would corrupt the measured value of
x, causing measurements to move into different categories from which they
were generated.

In any case, all of that awkwardness is a sure sign that the model you’re trying
to build is not actually representative of a reasonable data generating process.
It may be an awkward approximation of one, but to really understand the
validity of that approximation you’ll want to figure out the proper data generating
process first and then approximate as necessary.

> The first thing you need is a model for the latent value of x.  Let’s follow

>
> mu ~ some_prior;
> sigma ~ some_prior;
> x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>
> Now you have a censoring process where you get only imitated information
> about this distribution.  The binning part is straightforward: the relative
> weight of each category is given by integrating the latent distribution between
> the boundaries,
>
> p_{i} = normal_cdf(right_bundary | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(left_boundary | mu, sigma);
>
> The likelihood is then naturally a multinomial process,
>
> n ~ multinomial(p, sum(N));
>
> Which you can also approximate with individual Poisson distributions if N is
> big enough,
>
> n_{i} ~ poisson(sum(N) * p_{i});
>

> that it’s hard to come up with a measurement model for “averages”.  Given
> the latent distribution for x and the boundaries you can conceivably compute

> simple example (unless I’m missing some clever trick).  But even then, if

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
> On Nov 29, 2016, at 6:58 PM, Phil Price <pnp...@creekcats.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> > What's happening is this: the "start time" and the "duration" are effectively quantized with units of weeks. They are defined as continuous variables, but whether the value of the start time is 2.1 or 2.9 or 2.99 makes no difference: all of these define the start time to be in "week 2". This makes it easy for the system to get trapped in a local likelihood maximum and unable to find the global one.
>
> In general, that approach shouldn't work.  The assumption built into
> Stan's algorithms is that the log density function is continuously
> differentiable.  By hacking in discrete variables the way you do, you break
> that property.
>
>
> I'm not surprised, indeed this is sort of what I expected...except that at the Stan meeting I attended a few weeks ago, I thought this was the model the Stan experts said I should fit.

> I thought it seemed possible that the prior distributions could provide a sort of tug in one direction or another: even though the predictions are exactly the same for any start times that have the same integer week number, the likelihood will not be the same. But you're right that it will be discontinuous across the boundary, so I guess that is the problem.
>
> Did I misunderstand what Andrew and Michael were suggesting?

Perhaps --- I'd ask them.  I have a hard time imagining Michael
would've recommended this kind of discontinuous approach since
he's been arguing we take out the means to do it from the language
altogether (conditioning on parameters).

> The only thing that'll work well in Stan is marginalizing out the
> discrete parameter.  As we discussed when you're in town, this can be
> combinatorially prohibitive.  If it is, then you're just out of luck with
> the model as formulated in Stan.  Andrew or others may have ways to reformulate
> to get the same effect, but I don't have any ideas.
>
>
>
> If I have to try every combination of start time and duration, that would be combinatorially prohibitive. With 100 weeks of data, there are 100 possible start times, and, uh...let's see, duration has to be less than or equal to the number of remaining weeks, so... that's (100*99) + (99*98) + (98*97) + ... different possibilities, which is 1 million.

That's what I was trying to say over lunch.  Yes, that is
a problem.

> And each time of day could have a different start time and duration, so if I do hours that's 24 million (and in fact it would be more convenient to work with 15-minute data, so that's 100 million)...and this all assumes just one "impulse" per time of day, over a two-year period. A more common real-world case would be 10 or more.  10 would not be 10x as much computation, since we could set a constraint that the next impulse has to be after the first one has ended, but I would still be in the hundreds of millions of combinations. This is not an appealing approach.

Agreed.

> However, it seems like there should be a way to greatly reduce the amount of computation because it shouldn't be necessary to test every possible start time and duration:  Although p(y | start time, duration, magnitude ) is not a _continuous_ function of start time and duration, it is monotonic. If I were writing a search algorithm rather than a statistical model, I could find the week that is most different from the average and set the start time at the start of that week and the duration to 1 week. Then try increasing the duration to 2 weeks. Keep increasing the duration until things stop getting better. Then try stepping the start time back one week while increasing the duration one week (so the end time stays the same). Keep doing this until things stop getting better. I'm done. Then, to do another impulse, do the same thing with the residuals from the first one. And so on. Repeat until I'm happy with how well things fit.

You could try to do something like Metropolis with a custom proposal
for the discrete parameters.  We haven't played with this kind of
thing and don't know how changing the discrete parameters will
affect the sampling for the continuous parameters (the log density of
the continous parameters and hence the potential energy for HMC,
changes with the discrete parameters).

> Perhaps there are other approaches too.
>
> Hmm. I would love to be able to do all of this in Stan, but perhaps I will need to try some kind of ping pong approach: use one system to come up with the first set of impulse start times and durations, then have Stan fit all of the continuous parameters, then pop back to system 1 to come up with the next impulse times, etc. Ugh.

It's called "blocked" sampling and that's what PyMC3 does.
And NIMBLE's also set up to do that but I don't think they
give you HMC for the continuous parameters.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The co-linearities aren't a problem if the scales are similar.
The biggest issue that RHMC can overcome is if the curvature
varies dramatically, as in some hierarchical models.

And if the reparameterization comes with compromises, it's
not a reparameterization in the sense we're talking about.  We
reparameterize to fit exactly the same models with a different
basis of parameters (e.g., you can reparameterize a lognormal variate
as an exponentiated normal variable [plus Jacobian if you give it
a distribution, which gets you back to the lognormal distribution]).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
This isn't a bug.

lower_truncated_normal_lpdf_vector(...) is just a function, like if I called it foo(...). To use it, you'd want to call:

    target += lower_truncated_normal_lpdf_vector(x, mu, sigma, 0);

Notice, the use of comma and not vertical bar.

If you called it lower_truncated_normal_vector_lpdf(...), then it's treated as a log probability distribution function. Notice the suffix is "_lpdf" -- now you can do something like:
       target += lower_truncated_normal_vector_lpdf(x | mu, sigma, 0);

Hope that makes sense.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Spatial Logistic GLMM - Optimization
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Spatial Logistic GLMM - Optimization
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I decided to try the QR factorization. Does this look right to you?

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                        // Number of observations
  int<lower=0> p;                         // number of predictors

  matrix[N,p] Q;                           // QR decomp - Q ***********************
  matrix[p,p] R;                            // QR decomp - R ***********************
  int<lower=0, upper=1> hit[N];   // 0/1 outcomes; array of integers
  vector[2] px_pz[N];                   // N-dim array of 2-dim vectors
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> l;                  // length-scale parameter
  real<lower = 0> sigma;       // scale parameter
  real beta0;                          // intercept
  vector[p] theta;                   // ***********************
  vector[N] Z;                        // location random effect
}

transformed parameters {      // ***********************
      vector[p] beta;                 // ***********************
      beta = inverse(R)*theta;  // ***********************

}

model {
  matrix[N, N] Sigma;
  vector[N] Z_mod;

      l ~ lognormal(-2,1);
      sigma ~ lognormal(-1.5, 1.5);
      beta0 ~ normal(0,5);
      beta ~ normal(0,5);                  // N(0,5) priors on all beta

      Sigma = cov_exp_quad(px_pz, sigma, l);

      for (n in 1:N)
        Sigma[n, n] = Sigma[n, n] + 1e-6;

      Sigma = cholesky_decompose(Sigma);

      Z ~ normal(0, 1);  // Each element is N(0,1)
      Z_mod = Sigma * Z; // (Cov matrix Cholesky)*MVN(0,1)

      hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);  // ***********************
}

It is significantly faster, but the estimates seem different by non-trivial amounts. Do you see any mistakes or errors?

Thanks,

Chris

On Wednesday, November 23, 2016 at 1:10:57 PM UTC-8, Rob Trangucci wrote:

> On your question about length-scale: I would suggest using a distribution for l with a sharper tail, maybe a log-normal or a normal. If the data isn't informative about your length-scale, you'll need to pin it down with a prior. See if you can come up with plausible upper and lower bounds on your length-scale, and then use a distribution to put soft constraints on l. Without specifying stronger priors on l, you can run into trouble where your GP can act as a second constant term in your regression for large draws of length-scale and large draws of alpha. You should also put priors on sig for this reason.
>
> It'll also be good beta, and beta0. Make sure your x, y coordinates and your X variables are standardized, as it'll ensure that your parameters are all on the N(0, 1) scale. If you still have trouble, running a QR decomposition on your X variables and changing your likelihood to:
>
> hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);
>
> can also help the sampler run more efficiently. See here for more info: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/p5vILNIgOYY/MPjb6foPBQAJ
>
>
> In general, it's hard to run complex models in Stan without specifying proper priors (rather than uniform, as you have here) for all your coefficients, especially if your coefficients are on different scales.

There are no updates in a for loop.  The sampling statements
just increment the total log density every time one is
executed.

You probably just want to use a negative binomial rather than
creating your own with a latent gamma and poisson.  It'll be
more efficient, too.

If you need to do inference on a three-component mixture like this
to infer values for the mu parameters or theta, then you want to
do this:

    for (n in 1:10) {
      real lps[3];
      lps[1] = log(0.25) + normal_lpdf(theta | mu1[i], 0.01);
      lps[2] = log(0.5) + ...
      lps[3] = log(0.25) + ...
      target += log_sum_exp(lps);
    }

where that real lps declaration needs to be at the top of a block.

We're close to being able to add array expression to Stan, which will allow
the above to be rewritten as:

  for (n in 1:10)
    target += log_sum_exp({ log(0.25) + normal_lpdf(theta | mu1[i], 0.01),
                            ...,
                            log(0.25) + ... });

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks!

In a case like this with a latent variable, is it better to do the marginalization at the state or observation level. That is:

//Marginalize over the hidden state

ps[1] = log(theta[1]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | 0, 1);
ps[2] = log(theta[2]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | x[n-1], sigma);

//Sum over zero and random walk states
target += log_sum_exp(ps);

y[n] ~ normal(x[n],sig2obs);

VS

x[n] ~ normal(x[n-1], sigma);

ps[1] = log(theta[1]) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | 0, sigma_obs);
ps[2] = log(theta[2]) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | x[n], sigma_obs);

//Sum over zero and random walk states
target += log_sum_exp(ps);

What's nice about the second case is that you are truly allowing the state to be zero, at least in its effect on y.

Thanks!

> is cheap in run time but can be expensive in duplicated

messages.subject: Multiple comparisons example, with questions
messages.subject_clean: Multiple comparisons example, with questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

For some teaching I'm doing, I coded up an example of a scenario where multiple comparisons might be of concern. Andrew posted code to do this analytically on his blog back in the August (http://andrewgelman.com/2016/08/22/bayesian-inference-completely-solves-the-multiple-comparisons-problem/) but I thought it would be useful to show it using Stan. Code is here (https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/a124e7ae144ecdab93f36f87ef8c513e), but a couple questions:

- The thing I initially found curious was that the "unpooled" model actually achieved the same "false positive" rate as the frequentist lm(). This contrasts with my expectation from the plot Andrew posted but looking at the actual paper I see that the Bayesian model used there took the mu/sigma/tau parameters as known where my "un-pooled effects" model doesn't; would this account for the discrepancy?

- As expected, the "partially_pooled" model achieves a 0% false positive rate when the true value of all predictors' influence on the outcome is zero. Then I add one predictor with a non-zero effect on the outcome to see how this affects the standard advice to explicitly model the distributions of beta values as a normal distribution with an mean and sd that are estimated. As I suspected, adding a non-zero effect causes the false-positive rate for the other predictors to jump up again. This motivated the "heavy_partially_pooled" model that uses a heavy-tail student-t distribution for the effects and explicitly estimates the necessary tail-heaviness. This drops the false positive rate back down to 0%, but I notice that the effective sample size for the df & sd parameters of the student-t are rather low for a reasonably high iteration count; is this a problem?

Mike

(p.s. trigger warning: I forgot to convert from tabs to spaces before finalizing the gist, and github won't let me change.)

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
messages.subject_clean: Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,
I have a question regarding the proper way to rank variables in terms of their effect on an outcome. Any papers, books, or ideas are welcome.

Suppose I construct a collection of bayesian models that explain an outcome. These are created by some feature selection algorithm like stepaic or glmnet with bootstraping or some other procedure. So now I have a series of stan models from which I can predict samples. By sampling from this emsemble I can get the posterior of the outcome.

 I would like to get an idea of the importance of each of the variables involved, by perturbing each of them (by setting them to small or large values) and sample from the outcome under each condition (and for each model), and then calculate a "treatment" effect. Some perturbations may have a large effect on the outcome but with a large variance while others may have a smaller effect but with less variance.

 What is the proper way to rank the effect of each perturbation on the outcome? I'm concerned about applying some standard statistical test because I can sample any number of samples from the model so any tiny difference in effect would be significant with enough samples.

 thanks
FKG

Hi James,

If I'm reading the output of the time command correctly, it looks like running in Docker is faster than locally:

At this point, you've got to figure out where all the time is going. I just took a look at your repo: there's a lot more than just rstan in there. Can you boil that down to simple rstan commands so I can run this locally?

Just to give you a point of reference, when I run this on the example-models/bugs_examples/vol1/blocker/blocker.stan, this is my result:

library(rstan)
fit <- stan("blocker.stan")
stan_data <- read_rdump("blocker.data.R")
system.time(fit <- stan(fit = fit, data = stan_data))

   user  system elapsed
  2.298   0.075   2.555

When I enable parallel, this is my result:

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
system.time(fit <- stan(fit = fit, data = stan_data))

   user  system elapsed
  0.191   0.085   4.382

Notice: my elapsed time goes up. My user time + system time drops a bit.

If that's how you're running it, try running it in serial and see what results you get.

Daniel
